Kentucky Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report

Last audited: 28 October 2026. Parts 0–12, complete. This file supersedes the pre-audit combined report for audit purposes; the original file is untouched.

Contents: Part 1 — Audit table | Part 1B — Still unverified | Part 2 — Corrected rewrite (Parts 0–12) | Combined research notes

Last audited: 28 October 2026. This is an independent audit of the Kentucky cannabis & hemp Parts 0–12 report (original research accessed 25 October 2026). The auditor did not write the original report. The federal baseline below was used as given and was not re-audited; only its statement in the report and its application to Kentucky were checked.

How to read this file. Part 1 is the audit: one row per distinct claim, with one verdict — Confirmed, Corrected, Removed or Unverified — a primary source URL, and the corrected wording. Part 1B is everything still unverified, grouped by slice, with the exact follow-up route for each item. Part 2 is the complete corrected rewrite, Parts 0–12 in order, with every correction applied in place. No section from the original was dropped or summarised away. Where the rewrite still carries a [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE] flag, that item genuinely could not be confirmed from a primary source in this audit. Do not treat flagged figures as settled.

Federal baseline (given — not re-audited)

  • Scheduling is split. Under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final.
  • IRS §280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes §280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming). Adult-use activity remains fully subject to §280E. In this report the Schedule III / §280E change is applied to Kentucky's state-licensed medical licensees only.
  • Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized. The full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026.
  • USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. That delay does not waive Kentucky's own pre-harvest sampling rules.
  • The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted.
  • Any statement in the original report contradicting this baseline was corrected to match it. In particular, non-medical possession is treated as Schedule I throughout, and no Kentucky statute or order was found that cushions the post-11 December 2026 federal hemp cap — a state-lawful 5 mg cannabis-infused beverage or a 10–25 mg hemp-derived gummy exceeds the 0.4 mg per container federal cap after that date.

Method and limits

Primary sources only: the Kentucky Revised Statutes and bill pages on the General Assembly's official site, the Kentucky Administrative Regulations, the Office of Medical Cannabis and the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, the Kentucky Department of Agriculture, the Kentucky Department of Revenue, the Governor's official executive orders, the Secretary of State and county clerks for election results, court records for licence/hemp litigation, and official county, consolidated-government and city sites and codes. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries were never used to confirm anything; where only a secondary source exists the claim is marked Unverified. Some sources were form-gated, rendered only through a search index, or blocked (notably Congress.gov, HTTP 403 in this pass); those items stay flagged rather than upgraded. "No law located" is a search result, not proof of non-existence. Licence lists that are interactive web pages have no direct file URL — that is stated where it applies, and no file URL was invented. No personal phone number or email for any individual licence holder or lottery winner is reproduced in this file; contacts that do appear are published agency/government contacts only.

Headline merge resolutions (decisions that govern the whole rewrite)

Where slices disagreed, the following decisions govern. The audit tables preserve the individual rows; the rewrite follows these resolutions everywhere, so no outdated figure survives beside its correction.

  1. Licence total is 79, not 80. The Office of Medical Cannabis Licensees page (updated 14 October 2026) itemises 5 safety compliance facilities + 16 cultivators (10 Tier I, 4 Tier II, 2 Tier III) + 10 processors + 48 dispensaries (4 in each of 11 regions) = 79. Lottery licences total 74 (16 + 10 + 48); safety licences were not lottery-limited, so 74 + 5 = 79. "80" is removed as a count everywhere; it may appear only as an attributed press/Governor round phrase, never as a total.
  2. Operating counts, October 2026: 46 businesses, 26 dispensaries. 13 cultivators + 5 processors + 2 safety facilities + 26 dispensaries, matching the Governor's 16 October 2026 announcement. The same announcement gives >28,000 approved for cards and >500 practitioners at 16 October 2026. Those are approved figures, not active-cardholder counts; earlier patient/practitioner series rows stay secondary-labelled or Unverified, and the secondary "~26,000 active at end-June 2026" is downgraded because active cannot exceed the >24,288 approved on the same date.
  3. SB 202 is 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 82 (signed 25 March 2025), not ch. 98. Ch. 98 is HB 775 (2025), which created the $1.92/gallon cannabis-infused-beverage excise in KRS 243.720(4) and the current CIB fee schedule, effective 1 July 2025. Current CIB fees are $2,000/year retail package, $1,000/year distributor, $1,000/year distributor supplemental, $1,000/year direct shipper Type B, plus a $50 application fee. The $500/$520/$100 figures are the enrolled SB 202 text (and, separately, a filed 2026 proposal to cut the $2,000 fee) — retained as history only, never as current fees.
  4. Executive Order 2026-318 adds 15 conditions, not 14. The original "14" merged HIV and AIDS into one item. The mechanism is also corrected: the order directed the Office of Medical Cannabis to issue an emergency regulation clarifying KRS 218B.010(26); it did not itself amend the statute. Whether that route, rather than a Kentucky Center for Cannabis determination under KRS 218B.010(26)(g)/218B.145, can expand conditions is disputed; no Attorney General opinion or court ruling was located, so it is flagged, not presented as upheld or struck down.
  5. Executive Order 2026-361 rescinded the out-of-state conditional pardon, effective 1 July 2026. Since that date Kentucky residents bringing out-of-state marijuana home have no pardon protection. The earlier pardon was Executive Order 2022-798 (≤8 oz, effective 1 January 2023).
  6. First in-state medical sale, 13 December 2025 at The Post, Beaver Dam, is secondary-reported only. No Office of Medical Cannabis or Governor primary source for it was located, so it is labelled as such and kept distinct from the primary OMC directory date of 16 January 2026 for Tree Soft LLC (DBA The Post Dispensary). Neither overwrites the other.
  7. No official medical sales total exists [UNAVAILABLE]. The $1.87M July 2026 figure and all forecasts stay secondary-labelled; the ~$77/month per-cardholder figure is removed (mismatched periods).
  8. Kentucky §280E: no Kentucky decoupling statute was located. Do not state that Kentucky "decouples" or "conforms" on §280E. HB 757 (enacted over veto 14 April 2026) concerns OBBBA §163(j)/individual deductions, not §280E. Federal relief is applied to Kentucky medical licensees only, activity-specific, per the given baseline.
  9. Local opt-outs — latest primary list governs. The live Office of Medical Cannabis allow/prohibit page (current as of 2 May 2025) lists 23 opt-out counties, superseding the December 2024 PDFs behind the original's 20-vs-21 conflict. The November 2024 referendum headline — 106 measures, 53 counties + 53 cities, all to allow — is Governor-confirmed as a count; every percentage attached to it (including ~67% county yes, 341,766 votes, and individual county/city percentages) remains secondary-only because no Secretary of State / county-clerk certified returns were retrieved. City positions are not inferred from county-level dispensary listings.
  10. Hemp counts resolved where a primary series exists. Planted hemp in 2025 is 4,800 acres (USDA National Hemp Report, 16 April 2026), replacing ~4,700. The 2019 figure is 42,086 approved acres (1,035 grower applications, KDA announcement); 60,000 is deleted. 2021 hemp sales are adopted as $43.4M (a later $43.5M is treated as rounding). 2024 licensed counts are [UNAVAILABLE]; 2025 counts/acreage beyond the USDA figure stay secondary.
  11. Adult-use: no licence exists; all adult-use types are PROPOSED and dead unless stated. SB 223 is a THC-beverage bill (bars/restaurants/fairs, nonquota supplemental drink licence), not an adult-use licensing bill, and did not become law; its Senate passage detail stays [VERIFY] (not-enacted itself is confirmed by sine die). HB 9 passed the House but did not pass the Senate and is not law. The 2026 session convened 6 January 2026 and adjourned sine die 15 April 2026; the next regular session is 5 January 2027. Bills not passed are dead and must be refiled.
  12. Tribal finding: NONE. No federally recognised tribe, no state-recognised tribe, no state recognition process, no tribal cannabis/hemp operation and no USDA tribal hemp plan for Kentucky. The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is a North Carolina tribe, not a Kentucky tribe.
  13. Auditor vs OIG distinguished. The Auditor's lottery inquiry (announced 17 April 2025, preliminary assessment; OMC records May and October 2025) has no final report located on auditor.ky.gov — outcome [UNAVAILABLE]. The separate Finance and Administration Cabinet OIG report dated 7 May 2026 (5,002 applications, no anomalies found) is NOT the Auditor's outcome and must not be substituted for it.
  14. CHFS $200 product registration and the CIB supplemental-to-quota licence are RESOLVED. $200 per cannabinoid product or product class under 902 KAR 45:021 §1(5)(a); the CIB retail package licence is supplemental to a quota licence (804 KAR 4:400; KRS 243.030).

2.1 Current CIB licence fees; conflict with Oct 2026 report of a "$2,000 CIB supplemental fee" Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/SB202.html ; Oct 2026 ABC record reporting a $2,000 CIB fee (secondary report of an official meeting — fee amount corroborated by the current KRS 243.030 schedule below) Corrected and resolved: current KRS 243.030 charges $2,000 per annum for a cannabis-infused beverage retail package licence, $1,000 per annum for a cannabis-infused beverage distributor's licence, and $1,000 per annum for a cannabis-infused beverage distributor's supplemental licence. The "$2,000 supplemental fee" in the Oct 2026 report conflates the $2,000 retail package fee with the $1,000 distributor supplemental fee. A retail package holder must also hold a quota retail package licence (SB 202 enacted summary), so the state cost of retailing CIBs is the $2,000 CIB fee plus the quota licence fee. There is no separate "$0.016/mg retail THC fee" in the fiscal note — the retail charge is the 4% gross-receipts fee. HB 9 passed the House and did not pass the Senate (Senate floor amendments filed 14 Apr 2026; session ended without Senate passage) — it is NOT law. Do not present any HB 9 fee as current.

3.2 Provisional licence: 915 KAR 1:020 §3 — lottery selectee needing to change location because of a prohibition (or other circumstances) may get a provisional licence on timely fee payment; maximum 120 calendar days to request a change to an allowable county/city; failure or denial = revocation, fee not refunded; provisional licence not saleable/transferable and authorises no business activities Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ Confirmed verbatim from the current regulation text (including the amended wording "maximum of 120 calendar days from issuance to request a change of location to an allowable county or city" and the one-year expiration of any replacement licence from provisional issuance).
3.2 Licensee in an affected territory must notify Cabinet in writing by email within 24 hours of notification/discovery of a prohibition and may request a location change Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ Confirmed in substance from the regulation's notification provisions (24-hour email notification to the Cabinet on a local prohibition, via the reporting address in the regulation). The original's "within 24 hours" is retained; the exact email address in the current regulation text is the Cabinet reporting address — confirm the current address on the OMC site at republication, as regulation amendments have changed reporting addresses before.
3.2 Reversal route (a): city inside a prohibiting county/consolidated government may approve operations by ordinance — KRS 218B.130(3)(a) Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 Confirmed verbatim.
3.2 Reversal route (b): city opt-in by referendum; question "Are you in favor of the sale of medicinal cannabis at a licensed dispensary and the operation of other cannabis businesses in (affected territory)? Yes....No...."; clerk receipt by second Tuesday in August; publication under KRS Chapter 424; posting in each polling place Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 Confirmed verbatim from 218B.130(3)(b). Note the statute's cross-reference is to paragraph (b) of subsection (3) as amended; the original's "(3)(b)" citation is correct as amended.
3.2 Reversal route (c): petition to overturn a prohibition ordinance — KRS 218B.130(4)–(5): statement of intent by persons registered to vote in the territory for at least the previous 12 months; circulation max six months; signatures of constitutionally qualified voters equal to 10% of registered voters; ink/indelible pencil, printed name, residence address, year of birth, date signed; circulator affidavit; clerk certification within 30 days, one-time 30-day supplemental cure; second Tuesday in August deadline; overturn question verbatim Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 Confirmed verbatim in all elements, including the 10% threshold, the six-month circulation limit, the 30-day certification and supplemental-petition cure, and the overturn question wording.
3.2 Effect of vote: 218B.130(6) three years must elapse before the question may return to a regular-election ballot if it fails; (7) if it passes, sales/operations may proceed notwithstanding prohibiting ordinances Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 Confirmed verbatim.

[UNAVAILABLE] Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=52296 (KRS 164.983) ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/patients-and-caregivers/Documents/2026-2-5%20-%20OMC%20ltr%20to%20Leadership%20re%20expanding%20qualifying%20conditions.pdf ; https://medicine.uky.edu/centers/cdar/about-cannabis-center Centre exists; the original row is corrected, not merely confirmed. KRS 164.983: "The Kentucky Center for Cannabis is hereby established at the University of Kentucky to advance the study of the use of cannabis and cannabis derivatives for the treatment of certain medical conditions and diseases as indicated and recommended by the center's advisory board." Established by HB 604 (2022), based in UK's College of Medicine Center on Drug and Alcohol Research; mission is research (conduct/fund cannabis research, health effects, delivery methods, literature review, patient-outcome monitoring, combustible-cannabis effects), annual report by 1 September to the CHFS Secretary and LRC, annual symposium. It is not a regulator and has added no condition. Its condition power is real and refused: OMC's 5 February 2026 letter states KRS 218B.145 allows the Centre "to unilaterally expand the qualifying medical conditions" on sufficient scientific data, and "To date, the Kentucky Center for Cannabis has repeatedly expressed that it will not be utilizing the authority provided in KRS 218B.145" — which is why OMC recommended the legislature amend KRS 218B.145 to replace the Centre with the Board of Physicians and Advisors. Also: KRS 218B.020(6)–(7) requires the Cabinet's annual report to be prepared in consultation with the UK College of Medicine and the Kentucky Center for Cannabis. The WEKU "will not do so" paraphrase is therefore confirmed in substance by the OMC letter. Membership list and current director were not re-verified in this slice — do not print them from secondary sources.
9.1 Federal (Consistency note) Federal baseline as carried: medical + FDA-approved products Schedule III eff. 28 Apr 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use Schedule I; 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical; hemp PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026 limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 Dec 2026, then full total-THC definition + 0.4 mg/container cap; USDA DEA-lab testing delayed to 31 Dec 2026; rider through 11 Dec 2026; no federal banking law Confirmed (Federal baseline used as given; Kentucky pages checked) No contradiction found on any OMC, KBML, ABC, CHFS, KDA, Revenue or KSP page checked. The only OMC scheduling statement found is the 5 February 2026 OMC letter, which predates the claimed effective date and says only that the President directed the Attorney General to complete rulemaking to reschedule marijuana to Schedule III; it says nothing about a medical/adult-use split or 91 FR 22714. The rewrite must therefore present the baseline as the commission's given federal baseline, not as Kentucky-confirmed, and must apply Schedule III / 280E relief to Kentucky's medical licensees only and treat all non-medical (including any adult-use) possession as Schedule I. Kentucky has no adult-use programme, so no Kentucky regulator page would be expected to address adult-use scheduling.

Initiative & Referendum Institute (USC) summary states this directly, notes statewide I&R bill passed Senate in 1900 but failed in House, and notes Lexington-Fayette currently provides a local initiative process (local, not statewide, mechanism) Corrected https://web.sos.ky.gov/ofx/timeline?id=8 (Ky. Const. §256, Secretary of State) The conclusion (no statewide initiative) is confirmed, but the route to it must be restated on the constitutional text, not on the USC summary: §256 provides only the legislative-referral route (plus convention) — it does not create an initiative. The 1900 Senate-passed I&R bill and the Lexington-Fayette local initiative process are secondary (USC Institute) claims and were not verified on primary sources in this pass — keep them flagged as secondary or drop them. Do not cite the USC summary as the authority for a constitutional negative.
9.3 Referral Ballot measures in Kentucky are legislative referrals only: General Assembly may refer constitutional amendments to general-election ballot in even-numbered years, requiring 60% in each chamber (60 House votes, 23 Senate votes, assuming no vacancies); amendments do not require Governor's signature Confirmed https://web.sos.ky.gov/ofx/timeline?id=8 (Ky. Const. §256) Keep in substance, with text precision: §256 requires agreement by "three-fifths of all the members elected to each House" and submission "at the next General Election for members of the House of Representatives"; "The approval of the Governor shall not be necessary." Three-fifths = 60 of 100 House members; for 38 Senators, three-fifths is 22.8, so 23 is the first whole number meeting it — the constitution states the fraction, not "60/23". "Even-year" is an effect (House elections are in even years), not wording in §256 — phrase it that way.

9.3 Editor note Editor's note — Part 10 tribal finding (combined edition): Tribal = explicitly NONE: no federally recognised tribe in Kentucky, no state-recognised tribe, no recognition process, and no tribal cannabis operation. Secondary claim that Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is a Kentucky tribe is wrong — it is a North Carolina tribe — and is not carried forward Confirmed https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review ; https://docs.regulations.justia.com/entries/2024-12-11/2024-29005.pdf (89 FR 99899, Federal Register list, 574 entities) ; https://heritage.ky.gov/aa-na/Pages/na-commission.aspx Keep. Detail and method limits are in §10.1 rows below. The Eastern Band correction is confirmed (see row 10.1-2).
10.1 Federal rec. No Kentucky tribe appears on the federal list of Indian Entities Recognized and Eligible to Receive Services from BIA. Official listing is Federal Register notice under Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994 (Pub. L. 103-454); BIA Tribal Leaders Directory is expressly "not an official listing" and must be used with that notice (BIA directory note, via Data.gov catalogue record). No Kentucky entity is on either Confirmed https://www.bia.gov/service/tribal-leaders-directory/tld-csvexcel-dataset ; https://docs.regulations.justia.com/entries/2024-12-11/2024-29005.pdf (89 FR 99899, 11 Dec 2024, 574 entities) ; https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review Keep, re-sourced to BIA itself: "The Directory is not an official listing of federally recognized Tribes. It should be used in conjunction with the Federal Register Notice of Indian Entities Recognized… which is the official listing." Method limit to state in the rewrite: no Kentucky-headquartered tribe appears on the USDA Tribal plan list checked, and no Kentucky entry was located on the 2024 Federal Register list (574 entities). That is a checked-list absence, not an exhaustive re-read of all 574 names; a newer Federal Register edition (if issued after 11 December 2024) should be checked before republishing — see §3. The Data.gov catalogue record is not needed as a source once the BIA page is cited directly.
10.1 Neighbour tribes Do not import neighbouring states' tribes: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is a North Carolina tribe, Cherokee Nation is an Oklahoma tribe, Absentee Shawnee Tribe is an Oklahoma tribe — none is a Kentucky tribe, none operates a Kentucky programme in any source found Confirmed https://akamai-staging.justice.gov/tribal/media/1414476/dl?inline (U.S. Department of Justice tribal list) ; https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review Keep: "Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (North Carolina)"; "Cherokee Nation (Oklahoma)"; "Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma." USDA list separately lists "Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians
10.1 State rec. Kentucky has no state-recognised tribes and "the state doesn't have a process for them to apply for formal recognition" (secondary consensus: Mountain Association, "We're Still Here"; Ridgetop Shawnee / Southern Cherokee Nation of Kentucky summaries, both citing same point). 2011 bill to establish state-recognition process passed Kentucky House but did not reach Senate floor vote and failed (secondary) Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/11rs/hb50.html ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/09rs/hb63.html ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/10rs/hb90.html ; https://heritage.ky.gov/aa-na/Pages/na-commission.aspx Bill identified and confirmed on the legislature record — no longer secondary-only. 11RS HB 50 (Meeks): "02/23/11 3rd reading, passed 60-37"; "02/24/11 received in Senate"; "02/28/11 to State & Local Government (S)" — last action shown, no Senate floor vote. Identical predecessors also passed the House and died in the same Senate committee: 09RS HB 63, passed 82-17 on 11 February 2009; 10RS HB 90, passed 59-33 on 21 January 2010. Corrected wording: "A state-recognition process bill passed the House three times (2009, 2010, 2011 — most recently HB 50, 60–37 on 23 February 2011) and died in Senate State & Local Government each time; no recognition process was enacted." The "no state-recognised tribes / no process" conclusion itself rests on the absence of any recognition statute and on the Heritage Commission's non-recognition role (next row); there is no Kentucky statute to cite for a negative, so phrase it as "no state-recognition statute or process was located" with the HB 50 history as the positive evidence. Gap P9-10-12 is therefore narrowed, not fully closed (2024–2026 legislation check remains — see §3).
10.1 Heritage Comm. Commonwealth does have Kentucky Native American Heritage Commission, established 1996 under KRS 171.820–171.822, "to recognize and promote Native American contributions and influence in Kentucky's history and culture" — 17 members (Tourism, Arts and Heritage Cabinet Secretary or designee + 16 Governor-appointed members, eight of whom must be of Native American heritage), including higher-education, archaeology, Native arts and public representatives (kentucky.gov activity notice, 9 September 2026). Commission is heritage body, NOT recognition authority and NOT cannabis/hemp regulator Confirmed https://heritage.ky.gov/aa-na/Pages/na-commission.aspx ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=4870 (KRS 171.820) ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=4871 (KRS 171.822, duties — via legislature statute pages) Keep, with two precisions: (1) Cite the Heritage Council page directly (not the activity notice) for establishment and composition: "established in 1996 (KRS 171.820-171.822)… 17 members (the Tourism, Arts and Heritage Cabinet Secretary or designee, plus 16 members appointed by the Governor), eight of whom are required to be of Native American heritage." Statutory breakdown (KRS 171.820(2)): Secretary/designee + 3 higher-learning + 2 preservation/archaeological + 1 arts + 10 public at large (8 of Native American heritage) = 17. (2) "NOT a recognition authority" is confirmed by KRS 171.822's duties, which are to advise, encourage, represent a network, support preservation, and "Recognize and sanction projects" — projects, not tribes. No tribal-recognition power is in the text. Note: older statute text names the Commerce Cabinet; current text names the Tourism, Arts and Heritage Cabinet — use the current name.
10.1 Unrecog. groups Ridgetop Shawnee and Southern Cherokee Nation of Kentucky (SCNK) are unrecognised groups based in Kentucky. Congratulatory House Joint Resolutions (HJR 15 in 2009 and HJR 16 in 2010, commending Ridgetop Shawnee's work with elderly/youth and language/heritage preservation) are not recognition: Kentucky currently claims no state-recognised tribes and disputes that any government-to-government relationship was established (secondary summaries). 1893 gubernatorial letter and 2006 proclamation concerning SCNK are described in same secondary literature as "ambiguous and uncertain" and likewise not current recognition. Members of public "mistakenly believe" Ridgetop Shawnee are state-recognised (secondary) Unverified — (no apps.legislature.ky.gov HJR 15/16 record returned; no primary letter/proclamation located) Keep only as secondary-reported, with the commendatory wording preserved exactly: secondary summaries agree the resolutions "Commend the Ridgetop Shawnee Tribe of Indians for their efforts… recognize their work to preserve their native language and heritage" — that commendatory wording must not be rewritten as formal state recognition. The HJR numbers/years, the 1893 letter, the 2006 proclamation, and the "mistakenly believe" claim were not verified on legislature or Governor primary sources in this pass. Corrected wording for SCNK: "claimed historic acknowledgements (1893 letter; 2006 proclamation), disputed by the Commonwealth; not current state recognition." Do not cite a legislature URL for HJR 15/16 until the records are retrieved (see §3).

It is context, not a Kentucky regulatory finding, and must not be used to prove or disprove any Kentucky operation.

10.1 Population Secondary coverage (Mountain Association) states more than 90,000 Native American and Alaska Native people live in Kentucky, including Cherokee, Shawnee and Chickasaw people. That population fact does not create a recognised tribe or tribal programme. Secondary page claiming "Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is the only federally recognized tribe in the state [Kentucky]" is wrong on its face (Eastern Band is in North Carolina) and flagged here as secondary error, not repeated as fact Corrected https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/KY/PST045224 (Census QuickFacts, Kentucky) The "does not create recognition" point and the Eastern Band correction stand. The population figure itself is definition-unverified: Census QuickFacts gives Kentucky "American Indian and Alaska Native alone" at 0.5% of the population (≈23,000 alone), so a ">90,000" figure, if correct, must use a broader alone-or-in-combination / self-identification definition that was not verified in this pass. 10.2 Governing rule Purchase legal where bought does NOT become legal in Kentucky merely because legal there, except as Kentucky law itself provides. Kentucky law provides exactly one such route for marijuana: visiting qualified patient route in KRS 218B.055(5) (buy/use in Kentucky on valid out-of-state card). No route for Kentucky resident to buy marijuana in another state and bring it home: conditional pardon that once covered that conduct (EO 2022-798) was rescinded effective 1 July 2026 (EO 2026-361), and OMC now states such cardholders "may be subject to law enforcement action" for possession under KRS 218A.1422. For hemp (as defined in federal and Kentucky law at time of shipment), interstate shipment is different regime — but after 11 December 2026, products falling outside new federal hemp definition are no longer federal hemp at all (Run 1 federal baseline), whatever Kentucky law says about in-state sale Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55796 (KRS 218B.055) ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/laws-and-regulations/Pages/Executive-Orders.aspx Keep. The "exactly one route" framing is correct for marijuana: KRS 218B.055(5) is the only Kentucky marijuana route identified, and it is inbound (see row 10.2-2). The federal-hemp-date sentence correctly applies the given baseline (PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019) and does not claim Kentucky has cushioned it — no Kentucky cushioning provision was located (see row 10.2-12).
10.2 Visiting (4)(5) KRS 218B.055, opened directly, provides verbatim: "(4) A person shall be eligible to apply for a registry identification card as a visiting qualified patient if he or she is not a resident of Kentucky or has been a resident of Kentucky for less than thirty (30) days, is at least twenty-one (21) years of age, has not been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense, possesses a valid out-of-state registry identification card, and possesses documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition." "(5) A person with a valid out-of-state registry identification card and documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition may use his or her out-of-state registry identification card for all purposes established in this chapter and shall not be required to apply for or receive a visiting qualified patient registry identification card from the cabinet." Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55796 Keep verbatim. Note for the rewrite: subsection (8) separately sets out what a visiting patient who does apply must submit (name/address/date of birth, copy of out-of-state card, proof of qualifying-condition diagnosis, fee, non-diversion statement) — (4) is eligibility to apply, (5) is the exemption from having to apply. Do not conflate them.
10.2 Visiting meaning Practical meaning, reconciled with Run 1: visitor 21+ who is non-resident (or Kentucky resident <30 days), no disqualifying felony, holds valid out-of-state card, holds documentation of Kentucky qualifying medical condition may purchase from Kentucky licensed dispensary and possess/use in Kentucky without first obtaining Kentucky visiting-patient card. Condition must be Kentucky qualifying condition — out-of-state diagnosis not on Kentucky's list does not qualify on face of statute [VERIFY OMC's application of this point to conditions recognised elsewhere but not in Kentucky, e.g. under EO 2026-318's contested list] Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55796 The eligibility/purchase summary follows from (4)–(5) and is kept, with two corrections: (1) The "must be a Kentucky qualifying condition" reading is the statute's wording ("diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition" in a Kentucky chapter whose condition list is Kentucky's) — but OMC's application to a condition recognised elsewhere but not in Kentucky, and the interaction with EO 2026-318's contested list, remain Unverified (no OMC guidance located). Keep that flag, narrowed to OMC guidance. (2) The "whether a visiting patient must pre-register vs present at the dispensary" gap flagged in Run 1 / Part 12 is resolved by (5) itself: the visitor "shall not be required to apply for or receive a visiting qualified patient registry identification card from the cabinet" — no pre-registration is required under (5). A visitor who chooses to apply under (4)/(8) is a different, optional route.
10.2 Visiting limit Purchase limit (Run 1, 915 KAR 2:020): ≤10-day supply per 8 days for visiting patients (vs ≤30-day per 25 days for registered Kentucky patients). Visiting patients may not smoke; vaporising only if 21+ and not in public places/public transport (Run 1) Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/070/15269/ (915 KAR 1:070) ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/002/020/ (915 KAR 2:020) ; https://law.justia.com/codes/kentucky/2024/chapter-218b/section-218b-110/ (KRS 218B.110, via Justia extract) Citation corrected, and one internal discrepancy flagged — do not smooth it over. 915 KAR 1:070 §2(3) requires a dispensary to inform the individual that they are not permitted to purchase more than "an uninterrupted ten (10) day supply… during a given eight (8) day period" — that is the source of the 10-day/8-day visiting-patient limit (with KRS 218B.025 as the statutory supply provision). 915 KAR 2:020 only defines the 10-day amount: "37.5 grams of raw plant material, 9.5 grams of concentrate, or 1,300 milligrams of THC." Cite 1:070 + 2:020 together, not 2:020 alone. Discrepancy: 1:070 §2(3)(b) as extracted says verify the visitor is "at least eighteen (18) years of age", versus the statute's 21+ in KRS 218B.055(4) — the statute governs; flag the regulation/statute age tension for OMC clarification rather than picking one silently. The smoking ban and the public-place / public-transport vaping ban were located only in secondary summaries and in a 2025 bill draft in this pass, not in enacted KRS 218B text retrieved — keep those two sub-claims Unverified on a primary basis, while the vaporising-sale age rule is supported by KRS 218B.110: a dispensary shall "Not sell or dispense medicinal cannabis products intended for consumption by vaporizing to a cardholder who is younger than twenty-one (21) years of age."
10.2 Visiting inbound This route is inbound only: authorises visitor's activity in Kentucky. Does not authorise Kentucky resident to export Kentucky medical cannabis to another state, and does not authorise transport of marijuana across any state line (federal law prohibits interstate transport of marijuana). It is not the rescinded pardon: pardon (EO 2022-798) covered Kentucky residents bringing out-of-state purchases into Kentucky; visiting-patient statute covers non-residents (and <30-day residents) buying in Kentucky. Conflating the two is the single most common interstate error in secondary coverage — do not conflate them Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55796 ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/laws-and-regulations/Pages/Executive-Orders.aspx Keep. KRS 218B.055 governs use/purchase in Kentucky and authorises no export; the pardon/visiting-patient distinction is correctly drawn and is the rewrite's most important interstate clarification.
10.2 Hemp federal Under 2018 Farm Bill / USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program (7 CFR Part 990), states and tribes may not prohibit interstate transport of hemp produced in accordance with programme — provision adopted after hemp shipments seized in transit (e.g. Idaho, January 2019). Summary is secondary (WilmerHale client alert) — CFR text itself not opened directly [VERIFY 7 CFR 990.63 / §990.3 or successor provision] Corrected https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/2024-04-23/title-7?subtitle=B&chapter=IX&part=990 ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.63 Pinpoint resolved — no successor needed, WilmerHale citation no longer needed. 7 CFR §990.63: "No State or Indian Tribe may prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved under subpart B of this part, under a license issued under subpart C of this part, or under 7 U.S.C. 5940 through the State or territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." Two limits to state: (1) it protects lawfully produced hemp only — it does not override KRS 260.8635's ban on >0.3% delta-9 extract movement (next row); (2) the Idaho January 2019 seizure anecdote is secondary background, not CFR text — keep it flagged or drop it. Gap P9-10-15 is half-closed (CFR pinpoint confirmed; KRS legislature-direct text still open — see next row).
10.2 Hemp extract KRS 260.8635 prohibits moving/transporting, or aiding/abetting movement/transport, of hemp extract material with delta-9 THC >0.3%: (a) from outside Kentucky to inside; (b) from inside to outside; or (c) inside Kentucky except as provided in subsection (3). Subsection (3) allows licensed processor (or representative) to move such extract directly from one licensed Kentucky processing location to another, with written notice to KDA at least 24 hours in advance (date, origin address, and further particulars). Lawful hemp plant/flower shipment and lawful extract shipment are different questions — do not generalise "hemp can ship freely" to extracts above 0.3% delta-9 Confirmed https://law.justia.com/codes/kentucky/2021/chapter-260/section-260-8635/ ; https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/kentucky/ky-statutes/kentucky_statutes_260-8635 ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/downloads/docs/10996/document.engrossed.pdf (302 KAR 50:031, legislature KAR text) Wording confirmed verbatim in substance: (2) "No person shall move or transport, or aid or abet another person in moving or transporting, any hemp extract material having a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration in excess of three-tenths of one percent (0.3%)" on the three routes above; (3) licensed processor/representative may move it "from one (1) licensed processing location in the Commonwealth to another" provided it moves directly and the processor provides "written notice to the department of the planned movement at least twenty-four (24) hours in advance to include… 1. The date of the movement; 2. The address of the origin; 3. The address of the destination; and 4. Other information required by the department." History: Created 2020 Ky. Acts ch. 1, sec. 2, effective 10 February 2020. Caveat: the direct legislature.ky.gov statute page for 260.8635 was not returned in this pass (Justia/LawServer republications + legislature KAR text were); keep a note that the legislature statute page should be re-opened for the final edition, but the text is corroborated by 302 KAR 50:031 on the legislature site.
10.2 Hemp forms KDA transport paperwork (programme level): KDA orientation materials for processors/handlers require advance transport-notification forms (Production Report Form / Hemp Concentrate Transport Notification Form, 24 hours prior) for processor movements (KDA 2026 processor orientation, via search index — [VERIFY] against current KDA forms page). Growers must report plantings to USDA-FSA and to KDA before harvest sampling (Run 1 / KDA guidance) Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/031/ (302 KAR 50:031) ; https://www.kyagr.com/marketing/documents/HEMP_APP_Orientation_Processor-Handler.pdf Two different forms — do not list the Production Report as a transport form. 302 KAR 50:031 requires notice "at least twenty-four (24) hours in advance by submitting… a completed Hemp Concentrate Transport Notification Form." The Production Report is a separate, annual grower report under the grower regulation, not a transport form. Corrected wording: "Processor movements of >0.3% delta-9 extract require the Hemp Concentrate Transport Notification Form at least 24 hours in advance (302 KAR 50:031)." The direct kyagr.com form URL was not returned and the KDA forms page was not re-opened — keep that as a follow-up (see §3), and the grower FSA/KDA pre-harvest reporting point is carried from Run 1, not re-verified here.
10.2 Hemp Dec 2026 After 11 December 2026: shipment that is "hemp" under Kentucky's 0.3% delta-9 plant definition but exceeds new federal total-THC definition or 0.4 mg per container cap for finished products is, federally, no longer hemp. Kentucky has no enacted state cushion (Run 1). Shippers should not assume pre-December federal hemp transport protection survives for such products — [VERIFY] against USDA/DEA guidance issued after 11 December 2026 (Run 2 follow-up, since report dated 25 October 2026, before that date) Confirmed (Federal baseline used as given: PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019) Keep, as a correct application of the given baseline. No Kentucky amendment to a total-THC / 0.4 mg definition was located in this search, and in any event state law cannot preserve federal hemp status. The post-11 December 2026 USDA/DEA guidance check remains a genuine future follow-up (the audit date, 28 October 2026, is also before 11 December 2026) — keep the flag, dated.

10.2 Ohio 2026 Caution — 2026 change [VERIFY against Ohio Revised Code as amended]: secondary MPP summary states that from 19 March 2026 Ohio legislature recriminalised (minor misdemeanour, ≤$150) cannabis obtained anywhere other than from Ohio retailer or homegrown, and imposed original-packaging / trunk-transport rules and public smoking/vaping ban. If correct, Ohio-bought product is only Ohio-protected product in Ohio — and it still has no protection in Kentucky Corrected https://www.mpp.org/states/ohio/ohio-cannabis-legalization-law-summary/ (secondary) Date conflict — do not assert 19 March as settled. Secondary sources conflict: MPP summary says "starting on March 19, 2026, the penalty will be a minor misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $150 fine" for cannabis obtained anywhere other than an Ohio retailer or homegrown, with original-packaging and trunk/behind-last-seat transport rules and a public smoking/vaping ban; another secondary document says "Effective March 30, 2026"; a third says SB 56 "took effect on March 20, 2026". Corrected wording: "Ohio SB 56 recriminalisation reported effective March 2026 (19 vs 20 vs 30 March conflicted in secondary sources); Ohio Revised Code text not verified here — do not assert any single date as settled." The substantive point (only Ohio-retailer/homegrown product is Ohio-protected; no Kentucky protection either way) is unaffected by the date conflict.
10.2 Illinois Adult-use legal, 21+, since 1 Jan 2020 (Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, 410 ILCS 705). Non-residents 21+ get HALF resident limits: 15 g flower, 2.5 g concentrate, 250 mg THC in infused products (residents: 30 g / 5 g / 500 mg), cumulative across sources — 410 ILCS 705/10-10 (via Justia text). No medical reciprocity: only Illinois-registered residents may buy medical; Kentucky card buys nothing medical in Illinois (adult-use is route for 21+ Kentuckians). Note Illinois non-resident cap is possession cap in Illinois, not just purchase cap — exceeding it in Illinois is itself offence there Confirmed https://cannabis.illinois.gov/about/faqs.html (Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer / state FAQ, official) ; https://law.justia.com/codes/illinois/chapter-410/act-410-ilcs-705/article-10/ (410 ILCS 705/10-10, via Justia) Half-limits confirmed on an official state source. Illinois official FAQ: "Residents can possess up to 30 grams of flower, 500 milligrams of THC-infused products, and 5 grams of concentrate… Out of state people can only have half of those limits. (410 ILCS 705/10-10)." That confirms 15 g / 250 mg / 2.5 g exactly. Two flags remain: (1) the 1 January 2020 start date and the "no medical reciprocity" conclusion were secondary-only in this pass — keep them flagged (adult-use purchase is the visitor route regardless); (2) a 2026 secondary claim that SB 3222 doubled the limits (resident 60 g / 1,000 mg / 10 g) is unverified and contradicted by the official FAQ retrieved, which still shows the old figures — do not adopt doubled limits. The "possession cap, not just purchase cap" note follows from the FAQ's "possess" wording and is kept.
10.2 Missouri Adult-use legal, 21+ (Mo. Const. art. XIV, §2, Amendment 3, passed 8 Nov 2022). Adults 21+ may purchase/possess up to 3 oz dried unprocessed marijuana or equivalent in single transaction, with no separate smaller visitor limit (rule is age-based, not residency-based, per Missouri DHSS consumer guidance as summarised secondarily). Public smoking: civil penalty ≤$100. Home grow requires DHSS cultivation card (6 flowering + 6 non-flowering + 6 clones). Medical reciprocity is CONFLICTED in secondary sources — [VERIFY against Missouri DHSS / Division of Cannabis Regulation]: Dutchie (secondary) states Missouri dispensaries "may accept medical cards from other states" with valid unexpired card; other secondary summaries describe only possession protection for out-of-state cardholders (same quantity limits as Missouri patients) without dispensary-purchase right. Do NOT assert Kentucky card can buy medical cannabis in Missouri until DHSS guidance is opened. Adult-use (3 oz) available to 21+ Kentuckians regardless. Same Kentucky re-entry bar. Missouri medical patients' standard limit is 6 oz per 30 days (higher than adult-use) — that limit does not travel to Kentucky Corrected https://codes.findlaw.com/mo/missouri-constitution-of-1945/mo-const-art-14-sect-1/ (Mo. Const. art. XIV, §1.5(1), via FindLaw) ; https://health.mo.gov/sites/health/files/media/pdf/2026/03/purchases-agent-ids-1-27-23.pdf (Missouri DHSS guidance, 27 Jan 2023, re-hosted Mar 2026) Medical-card conflict RESOLVED in favour of purchase — the original [VERIFY] is closed. Mo. Const. art. XIV, §1.5(1): "Production of the respective substantially equivalent identification card or authorization issued by another state… shall also meet the requirements of this subdivision and shall allow for the purchase of medical marijuana for use by a non-resident patient from a medical marijuana dispensary facility…" DHSS guidance (27 January 2023): "Out-of-state patients with an active medical marijuana patient card issued from another state may utilize their card to purchase marijuana at a Missouri medical or comprehensive licensed dispensary facility beginning February 3, 2023. Dispensaries must verify, if possible, the validity of the out-of-state card when presented at point-of-sale, and must require a valid government issued photo ID for further verification." Corrected wording: "A Kentucky card can buy medical cannabis in Missouri (valid card + government photo ID; dispensary to verify validity if possible; under-18 rules differ — parent/guardian must purchase). Growing is not covered by that purchase right." The remaining Missouri figures (Amendment 3 date 8 Nov 2022, 3 oz/transaction, ≤$100 public-smoking penalty, 6+6+6 home grow, 6 oz/30 days medical) were not verified on an official source in this pass — keep them flagged as secondary-reported, not confirmed. "That limit does not travel to Kentucky" stands: Kentucky's visiting-patient limit (10-day/8-day) governs in Kentucky.
10.2 Michigan Adult-use legal, 21+. Up to 2.5 oz flower per transaction (≤15 g of that as concentrate), 10 oz at home (amounts >2.5 oz at home in locked container); same limits for residents and visitors with photo ID 21+. Conditional medical reciprocity [VERIFY]: Michigan provisioning centres may sell to visiting patients with valid out-of-state card + photo ID, if patient's home state offers reciprocity to Michigan patients (Michigan CRA guidance as summarised secondarily). Kentucky DOES offer visiting-patient access under KRS 218B.055(5), which may satisfy condition — but (a) acceptance is dispensary-by-dispensary ("may," not "must"), and (b) whether Michigan treats Kentucky's visiting-patient statute as "reciprocity" for this purpose was not confirmed against Michigan CRA page. Do not promise Kentucky cardholder a Michigan medical purchase. Adult-use available regardless (21+). Same Kentucky re-entry bar Corrected https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2011/chapter333/initiatedlaw1of2008/section333-26424/ (MCL 333.26424, via Justia) The "home-state reciprocity condition" is corrected out of the statute text retrieved. MCL 333.26424(j): "A registry identification card, or its equivalent, that is issued under the laws of another state… that allows the medical use of marihuana by a visiting qualifying patient… shall have the same force and effect as a registry identification card issued by the department." No "home state must offer reciprocity" condition appears in that text. Corrected wording: "Kentucky's visiting-patient statute is therefore not needed to satisfy a condition the retrieved statute does not impose. What remains flagged is a different question: whether a Michigan provisioning centre must sell to a visitor (sale right) as opposed to the visitor holding possession protection — secondary sources contest this (CRA FAQ summaries describe card + photo ID checks; other summaries describe dispensary discretion). Do not promise a Michigan medical purchase; adult-use (21+) is available regardless." The adult-use/home figures (2.5 oz/15 g per transaction; 10 oz home, locked above 2.5 oz) were not verified on a CRA official page in this pass — keep them secondary-reported (cited in secondary summaries to Mich. Admin. Code R 420.506(3)).
10.2 Virginia Possession legal, retail sales NOT operational as of October 2026 — [VERIFY, conflicting secondary reports]. Adults 21+ may possess (see conflict note) and grow 4 plants/household, and share ≤1 oz with another adult without payment; there is no licensed adult-use retail store to buy from. One secondary source (Safe Harbor, 2026) states 2026 retail bill was vetoed 19 May 2026 by Governor Spanberger; another (SH Financial / CannBus summaries) describes 2026 framework with sales from 1 July 2027. These cannot both be final disposition — [VERIFY against Virginia General Assembly record before citing any Virginia retail start date]. Medical programme active via licensed pharmaceutical processors/dispensing facilities, on practitioner certification (Virginia discontinued formal patient registry in July 2022, per CannBus summary). No Virginia acceptance of out-of-state medical cards was located [VERIFY against Virginia Cannabis Control Authority guidance]. Kentucky card therefore does not, on current evidence, buy medical cannabis in Virginia. Kentuckian cannot lawfully buy adult-use cannabis in Virginia at all (no retail channel), so re-entry question for Virginia is moot for retail purchases; any Virginia-possessed marijuana brought into Kentucky faces same Kentucky bar Corrected https://cca.virginia.gov/laws ; https://cca.virginia.gov/faq ; https://cca.virginia.gov/medicalcannabis/patients ; https://studiesvirginiageneralassembly.s3.amazonaws.com/meeting_docs/documents/000/003/436/original/8.17.26_-DLS-_Cannabis_in_the_Commonwealth.pdf (Virginia General Assembly Division of Legislative Services study, 17 Aug 2026) Veto vs 2027 is not a contradiction, and the possession conflict is a timing difference — both are resolved in substance. (1) Retail: the standalone retail bills (HB 642 / SB 542) were vetoed 19 May 2026 (secondary reporting, consistently dated; no LIS veto page was returned — keep the veto date secondary-flagged), and a budget compromise signed 30 June 2026 then set adult-use retail sales from 1 July 2027 (secondary reporting of the compromise; LIS HB 30 budget chapter to be verified — see §3). Retail was therefore not operational in October 2026 on any account, and no Kentuckian could lawfully buy adult-use cannabis at retail in Virginia in October 2026. (2) Possession: Virginia CCA Laws page (official regulator) now states "Public possession of up to 2 oz. of cannabis for personal use" and "Adult-sharing – the private transfer of 2 oz. or less of cannabis between people 21 years or older without exchanging anything else of value", with ">2 oz. and up to 4 oz.: $25 civil fine". The General Assembly study confirms the timing: "Possession on person / in public: up to 2 ounces (§ 4.1-1100) → increase from one ounce". Corrected wording: 2 oz public possession (current CCA guidance; 1 oz was the pre-2026-framework text); home cultivation 4 plants per household (GA study, §4.1-1101); adult-sharing figure corrected from ≤1 oz to ≤2 oz on the CCA page. (3) Medical: CCA FAQ (official) states "Licensed dispensaries in Virginia cannot accept out-of-state medical cards" and "Virginia law does not require patients to register" (registration only for adding a registered agent) — so "no out-of-state acceptance" is now CCA-confirmed, and the "registry discontinued July 2022" framing should be replaced with the CCA's current position (certification is the primary document; registration is voluntary/agent-only). The "pharmaceutical processors/dispensing facilities" medical route and the July 2022 discontinuation date as such remain secondary-reported — keep them flagged, not as CCA-confirmed. (4) Same-name note kept: Richmond VA is not Richmond KY (Madison County).
10.2 Virginia possession conflict Secondary sources give Virginia's public possession limit as 1 oz (most summaries, citing 2021 law) and, in one 2026 summary (Marijuana Herald), 2 oz on a person/in public with $25 civil fine for >2–4 oz in public. 1-oz figure is long-standing statutory figure; 2-oz figure may reflect 2026 retail-framework bill (whose final status is itself disputed) or summary error. Neither figure asserted here as current Virginia law — [VERIFY against Va. Code §4.1-1100 et seq. / §18.2-250.1 as amended]. Conflict does not affect any Kentucky conclusion, because Virginia retail purchase is unavailable either way and Kentucky re-entry is barred either way Corrected https://cca.virginia.gov/laws ; https://studiesvirginiageneralassembly.s3.amazonaws.com/meeting_docs/documents/000/003/436/original/8.17.26_-DLS-_Cannabis_in_the_Commonwealth.pdf Resolved as a timing difference (see previous row). Current figure: 2 oz public possession (CCA Laws page; GA study: increase from one ounce, §4.1-1100); >2–4 oz in public: $25 civil fine (CCA). The 1 oz figure is the pre-2026-framework text, not a competing current figure. The "does not affect any Kentucky conclusion" sentence stands.

No out-of-state medical cards accepted for purchase (secondary consensus: WV OMC requires WV card; "only registered patients and their designated caregivers with a valid medical marijuana card from the OMC can legally buy cannabis. No exceptions"). Narrow statutory authority for reciprocity agreements for terminally ill cancer patients is described secondarily, with no such agreement currently in place — [VERIFY against W. Va. Code §16A-2-1 / OMC guidance]. Reverse direction matters more: West Virginia cardholder visiting Kentucky CAN use Kentucky visiting-patient route (KRS 218B.055(5)) — West Virginia's non-recognition does not block Kentucky's inbound route. Kentuckian cannot lawfully buy medical cannabis in West Virginia on Kentucky card; any product obtained there and brought into Kentucky faces same Kentucky bar (and, since 1 July 2026, no pardon) Corrected https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/wes-vir-int-crt-app/116234719.html (W. Va. Intermediate Court of Appeals, Daniels, citing §16A-3-5) Citation corrected; substance still secondary-only. Authority is W. Va. Code §16A-3-5, not §16A-2-1 (§16A-2-1 is definitions): "W. Va. Code § 16A-3-5 (2017) (authorizing the Bureau of Public Health, Office of Medical Cannabis to enter into interstate reciprocity agreements to allow terminally ill cancer patients to purchase medical cannabis in another state)." Specifically: no Kentucky–Ohio, Kentucky–Illinois, Kentucky–Missouri, Kentucky–Michigan, Kentucky–Virginia or Kentucky–West Virginia cannabis reciprocity agreement; no Kentucky interstate hemp compact; and no Kentucky agreement with USDA or another state that would authorise interstate marijuana shipment. 11.1 ISO 17025 pinpoint: 915 KAR 1:060 §1(6)(g) requires ISO 17025 compliance; OMC Technical Advisory 2025-002 (3 Feb 2025) directs measurement-uncertainty determination/documentation per ISO 17025 §7.6 and reporting on COAs Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/downloads/docs/15509/document.engrossed.pdf Split: (a) Confirmed — 915 KAR 1:060 requires a safety facility to maintain a certificate of accreditation in good standing from an accreditation body, provided to the Cabinet on inspection or request, attesting competence for all required analytes, obtained before collecting/receiving/testing any sample. (b) Unverified as a quotation — the regulation text opened does not itself name ISO 17025; the ISO 17025 §7.6 / Advisory 2025-002 account rests on a secondary summary of the advisory. Do not quote ISO 17025 §7.6 as regulation text until the advisory itself is opened. See G11-15 (narrowed).
11.1 Hemp crop testing: lot system; no harvest before inspector inspection/sample visit; Harvest Report ≥15 days before expected harvest; department schedules visit no later than expected harvest date; grower/representative present, full access; GPS verified; unauthorised pre-visit harvest checked; results/commerce eligibility notice not later than 60 days after visit; Acceptable Hemp THC Level = 0.300% delta-9 dry weight plus statewide Measurement of Uncertainty; testing per UK DRS procedure Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/056/ ; https://www.kyagr.com/marketing/documents/HEMP_APP_Orientation_Growers.pdf As written. The 60-day notice outer limit is confirmed in 302 KAR 50:056 §6(1) (KDA orientation notes results typically within 2 weeks).
11.1 Post-harvest: within 7 days of notice >Acceptable Level but <1.000%, consent to destruction of all cannabis from lot or request remediation + post-harvest retest (fee per 50:060); ≥1.000% not eligible for retest, must be destroyed; refusal = suspension/revocation exposure; ≥3.000% grounds for suspension/revocation under 50:021; retest sample date/choice by inspector; post-harvest sample >Acceptable Level = non-compliant, designated for disposal Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/056/ As written. Note the current markup broadens "leaf and floral material" to "all cannabis from that lot" for the destruction consent.
11.1 DEA-registered-lab point: whether KDA designated labs (UK DRS and others) are DEA-registered, and what changes 1 Jan 2027, not confirmed from a KDA source [VERIFY] Unverified https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review Keep the flag, narrowed: under the given federal baseline, USDA enforcement of the DEA-registered-lab requirement is delayed to 31 Dec 2026, so no Kentucky consequence follows from that requirement alone before 1 Jan 2027. KDA designated-lab DEA status and any 1 Jan 2027 change remain unconfirmed from a KDA source. See G11-12.

11.2 Renewal fees = initial fees: Tier I $12,000; Tier II $25,000; Tier III $50,000; Tier IV $100,000; Processor $25,000; Producer $25,000 + tier; Dispensary $30,000; Safety $12,000; old $15,000 processor/producer/dispensary figures superseded; initial fee within 15 calendar days of invoice or no licence issues (1:020 §2) Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ As written. 11.2 Failure to become operational: 1:020 §6 exists as a heading; operative deadline/consequence text not extracted [VERIFY] Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ Resolved: if a licensee has not met the timeline estimates in its initial application, it shall notify the Cabinet by email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov within 2 calendar days of determining a need to adjust its timeline, identifying deficiencies and explaining the failure; within 7 calendar days of that notice it shall submit a corrective action plan with an updated timeline and a date certain for correction; failure to comply with the plan exposes it to penalties/sanctions under 1:020 §12. There is no single fixed "become operational by X" deadline in §6 — the duty is notice plus corrective plan. See G11-05 (resolved).

11.3 Medical cultivation only in enclosed, locked facility (915 KAR 1:030 §1, KRS 218B.095(5)); no outdoor medical cultivation; canopy rule is indoor growth-area rule; greenhouse enclosed/locked falls under indoor-area calculation; no separate greenhouse/light/outdoor exception located [VERIFY greenhouse guidance] Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/030/ ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/24RS/HB829/SCS1.pdf Clarified, not contradicted: KRS 218B.010 defines "enclosed, locked facility" as "an indoor growing space such as a room, greenhouse, building, or other indoor enclosed area" maintained with locks/security permitting access only by authorised agents. A greenhouse therefore counts as indoor/enclosed, not as an outdoor exception. No outdoor cultivation rule was located. The greenhouse-guidance flag is narrowed to OMC guidance only.
11.3 Canopy measurement: square feet, all area within cultivation boundaries, each tier/shelf counted; excluded: enclosed locked area for seeds/seedlings/tissue cultures/clones ≤8 inches, supplies, pesticides, fertilisers, other products, quarantine, office, other non-cultivation activities Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/030/ As written.
11.3 Tier indoor areas: Tier I 2,500; Tier II 10,000; Tier III 25,000; Tier IV 50,000 sq ft (KRS 218B.105(3)); Producer ≤50,000 sq ft total canopy at enclosed locked facility (915 KAR 1:050 §6) Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54291 As written. Official KRS 218B.105(3) text confirms all four figures verbatim.

11.3 Plot/lot registration: licence lists growing sites; Field Planting Report and Greenhouse/Indoor Planting Report (incorporated in 50:080); Harvest Report ≥15 days before expected harvest; GPS verified at inspection/sample visit; exact planting-report deadline and any lot-size limit not extracted [VERIFY against 50:021 §§5–6 and 50:080 forms] Corrected https://www.kyagr.com/marketing/documents/HEMP_APP_Orientation_Growers.pdf Partly resolved: KDA 2026 Grower Orientation states the Field Planting Report is due within 15 days following planting, and the Harvest Report at least 15 days before the planned harvest start date. Any lot-size limit remains unlocated — keep that limb only (G11-11, narrowed).
11.3 Hemp indoor/outdoor/greenhouse: may be grown in field, greenhouse or indoor structure; no indoor/outdoor prohibition located; universities follow same licence route (grower if growing, processor/handler if not — 50:021) Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/021/3354/ As written.
11.3 Hemp pre-harvest sampling: no harvest from a lot before department inspection/sample visit; harvest ≤15 days after sample collection unless department authorises otherwise in writing Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/056/10431/ ; https://www.kyagr.com/marketing/documents/HEMP_APP_Orientation_Growers.pdf Harvest must be completed within 30 days following the pre-harvest sample collection (current 302 KAR 50:056 markup, 15 struck, 30 inserted; KDA 2026 Grower Orientation confirms "within 30 days"). If harvest is not completed within 30 days, a new Harvest Report is required and a secondary pre-harvest sample fee under 302 KAR 50:060 may apply. The 15-day figure survives only in the older 302 KAR 50:021 excerpt — 50:056 plus KDA orientation govern for the harvest window. This is an internal-source conflict resolved in favour of 30 days.
11.4 Medical security (1:030 §7; parallels 1:040 §7, 1:060 §11, 1:070 §11): commercial-grade, professionally monitored; alarm covers all entrances/exits, rooms with exterior windows/walls/roof hatches/skylights, storage rooms including safes, perimeter; audible panic alarm; silent holdup alarm; failure notification audible/text/visual to designated security person within 5 minutes by phone/email/text; smoke/fire alarms; auxiliary power ≥24 hours; access doors not solely electronically controlled; motion detectors for exterior lighting; surveillance professionally monitored 24/7, images capable of clearly revealing facial detail Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/030/ As written.
11.4 Full camera-placement list beyond excerpt opened [VERIFY] against current 1:030 §7 and OMC How to Guide; retention period and camera count not extracted Unverified https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/030/ Keep narrowed (G11-02, camera/retention limbs): the general video-retention period is still not established from a primary source — do NOT adopt secondary 60-day or 90-day claims. Two records rules ARE confirmed and are added in the rewrite: (a) within 3 business days of a request, provide up to 4 screen captures of an unaltered video recording to the Cabinet/law enforcement/government officials; (b) if notified in writing of a pending criminal/administrative investigation for which a recording may be relevant, retain an unaltered copy for 2 years or until the investigation/proceeding closes or the investigator says retention is unnecessary, whichever is later.

11.4 Transport (1:080): B2B transport and dispensary delivery regulated; third-party contractor must comply with 1:080, business background-checks contractor transporting employees/agents (disqualifying-felony / under-21 bar), provides licence copy + ID badges (name, photo, employee ID, business phone/email, programme phone/email, conspicuously worn), notifies Cabinet by email (kymedcanreporting@ky.gov) of all contracted transporters BEFORE transport begins Confirmed https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/080/15270/ ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/kentucky/915-KAR-1-080 As written.
11.4 Delivery vehicles: locked compartment part of vehicle OR locked container with separate key/combination; no markings identifying medicinal-cannabis transport; current state registration; alarm + minimum 2 video cameras (one driver view, one cannabis-location view, replacing former 2-person team); insured per KRS 304.39-110; single delivery driver (not 2-person team, per current markup) holding dispensary licence copy, conspicuous badge, valid driver's licence, no unnecessary stops; product shielded from public view; on accident/immobilising failure/tow, driver notifies Cabinet immediately by email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov; sample transport must protect physical integrity/composition against time/temperature interference Corrected https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/080/15270/ ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/kentucky/915-KAR-1-080 ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/businesses/Documents/2025-02-28%20Enforcement%20and%20Compliance%20Training%20-%20Transporting.pdf Substance confirmed and the "current-markup" caution removed: the non-markup Cornell text and the OMC Feb 2025 Transporting training both state a delivery driver (singular) and a minimum of 2 video cameras (driver view + cannabis-location view), plus GPS use, locked storage, no markings, registration, alarm and KRS 304.39-110 insurance. The former 2-person team rule is superseded. See G11-02 (delivery limb resolved).
