1.6 Hemp

1.6.1 THC limits and measurement — two different measurements, do not conflate them

Crop / plant definition (KRS 260.850, via 902 KAR 45:190's definition cross-reference — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/190/14787/): "hemp" / "industrial hemp" is Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, including seeds, derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids and salts, with a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, excluding medicinal cannabis as defined in KRS 218B.010.

Crop compliance testing (302 KAR 50:056 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/056/; KDA grower orientation — https://www.kyagr.com/marketing/documents/HEMP_APP_Orientation_Growers.pdf): for compliance, all delta-9 THC concentrations are measured post-decarboxylation or by another method including both delta-9 THC and delta-9 THCA (also known as total THC). The "decarboxylated" value is delta-9 THC + 87.7% of delta-9 THCA. The "Acceptable Hemp THC Level" is the 0.300% limit plus the measurement of uncertainty. A crop that is ≤0.3% delta-9 on a neutral-only reading but >0.3% total THC can therefore fail compliance even though the statutory definition speaks in delta-9 terms. Destruction of non-compliant hemp is covered in Run 2 (Part 11), not here.

Finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products (902 KAR 45:190 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/190/14787/): the adult-use list is expressed in Total THC for delta-9 and THCA-A (each 0.3% or less Total THC). The regulation's testing standards give the total-THC calculation: total cannabinoid concentration (mg/g) = (cannabinoid acid-form concentration (mg/g) × 0.877) + cannabinoid concentration (mg/g); the COA must report total THC concentration in percentages, THCA concentration, and mg per serving and mg per package for total THC and the primary cannabinoid marketed (excluding cosmetics). The same section also states that cannabinoid products shall not contain a delta-9 THC concentration of more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis — quote both formulations; do not collapse them into one. Claims that Kentucky applies no total-THC formula are contradicted by the regulation text.

Medical cannabis is NOT hemp: its caps are the 35%/10 mg/70% caps in §1.3, not 0.3%.

1.6.2 What is lawful hemp vs. marijuana in Kentucky today (state law, pre-11-Dec-2026 federal change)

Hemp and hemp-derived products meeting KRS 260.850, 902 KAR 45:190 (for cannabinoid products) and, for beverages, SB 202, are lawful within their thresholds and channels — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/190/14787/ ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/SB202.html — The 902 KAR 45:190 adult-use (intoxicating) list — delta-10-THC; delta-9-THC with 0.3% or less Total THC; delta-8-THC; THCA-A with 0.3% or less Total THC; THCV; THCVA; delta-6; HHC(-); THCP; THCM — means those cannabinoids are regulated, not banned, at state level today. The non-intoxicating list is CBD, CBDA, CBDV, CBDVA, CBC, CBCA, CBGA, CBG, CBN and CBT; all other cannabinoids are prohibited for sale in Kentucky unless pre-approved by the Cabinet. Non-intoxicating products must also meet a ≥25:1 non-intoxicating-to-adult-use ratio and contain ≤2.5 mg adult-use cannabinoid per serving (902 KAR 45:190). Retail sale is further limited: whole hemp buds, ground hemp floral material and ground hemp leaf material shall not be marketed, sold or distributed direct to the consumer in a retail setting, nor any hemp product with total THC above 0.3% (902 KAR 45:012 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/012/15705/). That is the opposite of a ban state. Cannabinoids the cannabis plant cannot naturally produce are a separate federal question from 12 Nov 2026 (see §1.6.5) — not "after 11 Dec".

1.6.3 Product registration, testing, labelling (902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190 / 45:012, CHFS/DPH — NOT KDA, NOT ABC for non-beverage products)

In-state processor/manufacturer/storer/distributor: CHFS permit, non-transferable as to person or address, posted conspicuously, renewed annually (902 KAR 45:021 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/021/REG/; 902 KAR 45:190 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/190/14787/). Permit fees under 902 KAR 45:021 §1(1)(b)4: hemp processing $3,000; hemp manufacturing $1,000; hemp cannabinoid wholesale warehouse and distributor $1,000; hemp cosmetic $200. Product registration fee: $200 per cannabinoid product or cannabinoid product class, 902 KAR 45:021 §1(5)(a), payable by check or money order to the Kentucky State Treasurer (initial fee; a new registration and fee are required on changes to composition, serving size/directions, or label). (902 KAR 45:190 §2(4) separately states $200 per adult-use cannabinoid product.) In-state and out-of-state processors/manufacturers must submit: applicant name/address; brand/company name/address if different; product name; origin name/address of the adult-use product with which the final product was manufactured; a complete copy of the front and back of the label; and a COA from an accredited third-party laboratory for the lot for each product.

Out-of-state processor/manufacturer: annual registration from 1 Jan 2024, renewed by 31 Dec each year, with (a) a copy of the current, valid home-state permit to process or manufacture hemp-derived cannabinoids, (b) a copy of the home-state regulation, and (c) the product registration fee (902 KAR 45:190; current 902 KAR 45:021 wording: complete the department's business registration, renewed annually by 31 Dec).

Testing/COA: the DPH Food Safety Branch industry notice of 16 Feb 2023 (CHFS letterhead; text read in a mirrored copy of the CHFS letter, not on chfs.ky.gov in this pass) required a COA from an ISO-accredited laboratory attesting to composition, including delta-9 THC, other cannabinoids, pesticide residues, heavy metals, mycotoxins, residual solvents and microbiological contaminants, and labelling allowing the consumer to access the COA, the location where the hemp was grown, and the manufacturer/distributor address and phone number. Current regulation (902 KAR 45:190) requires: batch/process-lot sampling and testing on the final product equivalent to what will be consumed; testing only by an independent third-party laboratory fully accredited to ISO 17025 by an ILAC-recognised body, for cannabinoids, microbial impurities, mycotoxins, residual pesticides, heavy metals and residual solvents (if applicable); a limit of quantitation of 1 mg/g or lower for adult-use cannabinoids; and all applicable COAs to accompany the final product (KRS 217.039). At retail, a valid COA must be available upon request.

Labelling — current law (902 KAR 45:190 §3; products packaged/labelled per KRS 217.037, 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 78, and 45:190): tamper-evident seal on every container; child-resistant packaging for adult-use containers (defined as significantly difficult for children under 5 to open, not difficult for adults to use properly, resealable for multi-use/multi-serving products); potency as mg per serving and mg per package for total THC and the primary cannabinoid marketed (excluding cosmetics), other cannabinoids in mg/g per serving and mg per package if listed; labelled amounts must accurately reflect testing results within 80–120% of total cannabinoid content; the common cannabinoid description in the product name (e.g. "Delta-8 THC gummies") in the same or larger font than the product name; adult-use warning statements — "This product is intended for use by adults 21 years and older. Keep out of reach of children.", health risks, additional risks for those pregnant, nursing or planning pregnancy, intoxicating effects delayed by two or more hours, drowsiness/impairment ("Do not drive a motor vehicle or operate machinery while using this product."), and "Use of this product may result in a positive drug screen" (a QR code labelled "Warning Statements" may link to the warnings if smartphone-readable); packaging must not bear cartoons, likenesses to images/characters/phrases popularly used to advertise to children, likeness to/imitation of candy, snack, baked-good or beverage packaging, the terms "candy"/"candies", or a department/Cabinet logo or state seal implying endorsement. The HB 544 6-point labelling list (≥6-point font; identity on the principal display panel; net quantity in English + metric in the lower 30% parallel to the base; ingredients descending by weight; manufacturer/distributor name; total cannabinoid per serving/per container; suggested use; expiration date if any — HB 544 SCS1 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/23RS/HB544/SCS1.pdf) is the Act's direction to the Cabinet and is shown struck through in the current 902 KAR 45:190 text; do not quote it as current labelling requirements.

Packaging/retail: adult-use containers must be tamper-evident and child-resistant (902 KAR 45:190 §3). HB 544 directed retailers to keep covered products behind the counter to prevent theft or easy access by children (HB 544 §(3)(d)); the current operative rule is that adult-use products "shall be secured in the retail setting to prevent theft or other access to persons under 21" (902 KAR 45:190; 902 KAR 45:012).

Minimum age: 21+ to buy and to possess a covered (intoxicating) product; sale, gift or other transfer to a person under 21 is prohibited (HB 544 §(3)(b)–(c)). Current retail rules add: proof of age must be required; only non-intoxicating and cosmetic products may be sold to persons under 21; adult-use products may be delivered/shipped to consumers over 21 (902 KAR 45:190).

Retailer licensing — correction of a common secondary error: HB 544 as enacted directs CHFS regulation and a CHFS permit/registration system; it does not, in the text located, create a KDA "intoxicating hemp retailer licence". Secondary blogs stating "retailers must obtain a licence from KDA" conflate (a) KDA grower/processor-handler licences for the plant, (b) CHFS/DPH permits for cannabinoid processors/manufacturers, and (c) for beverages, ABC retail package licences. Separately, retail and food-service establishments offering adult-use products must be permitted by the Cabinet under 902 KAR 45:012 (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/012/15705/): the permit is non-transferable as to person or address, renewed annually, $2,000 per year, required for every location, with a $250 temporary-event registration fee for unpermitted sellers at temporary events/festivals, and adult-use retail establishments must not be located within 1,000 feet of an elementary, middle or high school (establishments registered before 31 Dec 2024 are exempt from the fee until the next renewal and from the location rule). CHFS's HDCP page confirms the same retail-permit, product-registry and secured-sale requirements (https://chfs.ky.gov:443/agencies/dph/dphps/fsb/Pages/HDCP.aspx). Do not publish a single "hemp retailer licence" without naming the issuing agency and the regulation.

1.6.4 Hemp-derived THC beverages (SB 202 / ABC)

SB 202, signed 25 Mar 2025 (2025 Ky. Acts ch. 82; record — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/SB202.html; enrolled text — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/25RS/sb202/bill.pdf) defines "cannabis-infused beverage" (KRS 241.010(13)) as a properly permitted adult-use cannabinoid liquid product for human consumption with intoxicating properties, containing not more than 5 mg of intoxicating adult-use cannabinoids per 12-ounce serving, excluding medicinal cannabis under KRS ch. 218B, any hemp tincture, and any product containing solely non-intoxicating cannabinoids. Retail sale is only by the package, in wet territory, by the holder of both a quota retail package licence and a CIB retail package licence (KRS 243.401(2)); the CIB retail package licence is a supplemental licence to a quota retail package licence (KRS 243.403, via 804 KAR 4:400 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/804/004/400/REG/). As the practical effect of the dual-licence rule, gas stations, convenience stores and smoke shops cannot sell CIBs. No by-the-drink sales (bars/restaurants cannot serve them) outside the expired window below. Persons under 21 shall not purchase or consume CIBs, and alcohol minor restrictions/offences in KRS chs. 241–244 apply in the same manner (KRS 243.401(3)). Distribution and retail sale are regulated solely by ABC, which was to adopt and exclusively enforce DPH's regulations until ABC promulgated its own on or before 1 July 2026 (KRS 243.401(1)); 804 KAR 4:400 addresses the post-1 July 2026 transition (DPH-permitted sellers wishing to continue after 1 July 2026 must apply for a CIB retail package or distributor licence and pay the statutory fees), but whether it is the complete 243.401 regulation set was not verified in this pass [UNVERIFIED — see §3].

Direct shipping: a DPH-approved CIB manufacturer may self-distribute and may ship CIBs under a direct shipper licence in the same manner as a direct shipper licence allows shipment of alcoholic beverages (KRS 243.401(4)). The direct-shipper "Type B" label and its full holder class were confirmed only from statute mirrors in this pass; open the LRC KRS 243.027 page before quoting Type B holder criteria [UNVERIFIED — see §3].

Fairs/festivals (Acts ch. 82, §38): until 1 Jan 2026, the holder of a CIB retail package licence, a CIB distributor's licence, or a DPH-approved CIB manufacturer's licence could sell and serve complimentary samples of CIBs at fairs, festivals and similar events in wet territory, provided: sales by the drink were permitted in that window; sales by the package did not exceed nine litres per person per day; complimentary samples served by the drink did not exceed one and three-fourths ounces per person per day; and the beverages had been lawfully produced or purchased by the licence holder. That window has ended; by-the-drink CIB sales and that sampling window are no longer available on that section.

Reports: ABC was to report on CIB distribution and sale to the Legislative Research Commission by 1 Nov 2026 (SB 202 record summary) — that date falls after this audit date (28 Oct 2026), so delivery cannot yet be assessed. The University of Kentucky Cannabis Center was to report its work on manufacture, testing procedures and consumer effects of cannabinoid beverages to the LRC by 31 Jan 2026; delivery was not located on a primary source in this pass [UNAVAILABLE].

Fees — current vs enrolled (do not conflate): SB 202 as enrolled set KRS 243.030(36)–(38) at $500/yr CIB retail package, $520/yr CIB distributor, $100/yr CIB distributor supplemental. The current KRS 243.030 schedule is $2,000/yr CIB retail package, $1,000/yr CIB distributor, $1,000/yr CIB distributor supplemental, $1,000/yr direct shipper Type B — evidenced by the legislature's own 2026 HB 9 record summary, which proposes reducing the CIB retail package fee "from $2,000 to $500" (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/26rs/hb9.html), with the same baseline in the 2026 HB 896 summary, and by 804 KAR 4:400's statement that fees are the statutorily prescribed amounts in KRS 243.030. The 2025 HB 775 summary (2025 Ky. Acts ch. 98, sec. 32) states it amended KRS 243.027, 243.030 and 243.040 to require a licence and fee for CIB manufacturers, distributors, direct shippers and retailers. Quote $2,000/$1,000/$1,000/$1,000 as current; quote $500/$520/$100 only as the SB 202 enrolled figures. There is no supplemental-vs-base distinction to explain the difference — it is a later statutory change.

1.6.5 State response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates

No Kentucky law was located in this audit that (a) adopts the federal total-THC definition early, (b) creates a state-law safe harbour for products that cease to be federal hemp on 11 Dec 2026, or (c) bans intoxicating hemp products in anticipation of the federal change. Kentucky's state-law framework (0.3% delta-9 plant definition; 902 KAR adult-use list; 5 mg CIB cap) remains on the books as written. This is a search result, not proof of non-existence.

What the federal dates mean mechanically for Kentucky (applying the fixed baseline as given): (i) 12 Nov 2026: the §781 provisions NOT delayed by §2019 take effect — including exclusions for cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce (i.e. synthetically derived/converted cannabinoids). (ii) 11 Dec 2026: the remainder of §781 takes effect, including the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap for finished products. After that date, a Kentucky hemp gummy, tincture, vape or CIB that today is lawful state hemp (e.g. a 5 mg CIB, a 10–25 mg gummy) would, if it exceeds 0.4 mg total THC per container, cease to be federal "hemp" and would be treated federally as marijuana — Schedule I if non-medical, regardless of Kentucky's 0.3% / 5 mg state rules. That placement (after 11 Dec, not before) is the correct one. Full-spectrum CBD oils with naturally occurring trace THC above 0.4 mg/container are also caught on the face of the cap. Non-intoxicating CBD isolate / products at ≤0.4 mg total THC per container, and fibre/grain hemp, are the categories that survive on the federal definition as described.

The following §1.6.5 items are NOT verified and must not be presented as established: the claim that FDA lists missed a 10 Feb 2026 deadline and that this leaves delta-8's date unsettled [UNVERIFIED — no FDA list or Federal Register item was located in this pass]; the "58 Kentucky hemp farmers, Sept 2025" letter to Sen. McConnell [UNVERIFIED — no primary source located]; the detailed 15 Oct 2026 Interim Joint Committee asks (explicit state protection of compliant cultivation/processing/manufacture/sale/use; financial-services protections modelled on medical-cannabis protections; a single DPH regulator; lower fees; removal of HHC/THCP/THCM/delta-6 from the approved list) [UNVERIFIED — not located on a legislature.ky.gov committee record; a legislator's newsletter confirms only that a hemp hearing occurred]; Rep. Andy Barr's federal bill as a "stricter federal framework" with age limits, testing, manufacturing standards and per-serving caps [UNVERIFIED — Congress.gov returned HTTP 403 for the bill page in this pass; any Barr vehicle is federal, not Kentucky law, but its contents are not verified here]; and the current Congress.gov status of delay bills H.R. 7024 / H.R. 7010 / S. 3686 and repeal bill H.R. 6209 [UNVERIFIED — Congress.gov access denied in this pass; secondary trackers describe them as pending, which does not verify them].

Bottom line: as of this audit, Kentucky operators have no enacted state cushion for 11 Dec 2026 located in primary sources. No Commonwealth statement of a "wait for Congress / legislate in 2027" position was located; do not quote that as the state's position. The next regular session (2027) falls after the federal effective date.

USDA lab-testing delay to 31 Dec 2026 (baseline) matters for Kentucky growers' crop compliance sampling in the interim, but does not change the 11 Dec product cap (crop sampling and finished-product caps are different measures).

1.6.6 Hemp vs. medical interaction

Medical cannabis products are NOT hemp products and are not sold through hemp retailers or ABC package stores (902 KAR 45:190's hemp definition excludes medicinal cannabis; SB 202's CIB definition excludes medicinal cannabis under KRS ch. 218B). Hemp-derived products are NOT a substitute source of "medical cannabis" for cardholders: a cardholder buying a hemp delta-8 gummy is buying a hemp product, not exercising a 218B right, and its purchase/possession is governed by hemp law (21+, secured retail sale, registered product), not the dispensary purchase limits. Conversely, a hemp product that exceeds federal hemp limits after 11 Dec 2026 does not become "medical cannabis" by virtue of being bought by a cardholder — it would need to be a 218B product from a licensed dispensary.

1.7 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning/buffers — medical vs hemp-derived

Medical (915 KAR ch. 1 + KRS 218B): Packaging/labelling (915 KAR 1:100 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/100/14976/): each product package for sale to cardholders must be child-resistant and require at least a two-step process of initial opening; have a tamper-evident seal; minimise oxygen exposure; be light-resistant and opaque; be resealable if applicable; contain the typical onset-time warning, the bold statement "For medicinal use by cardholders only. KEEP OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN", and for raw plant material the statement "NOT INTENDED FOR CONSUMPTION BY SMOKING"; disclose strain (sativa/indica/hybrid), form, and standard delta-9 THC, terpene and CBD amounts (mg per serving and per package for edibles/oils/tinctures; percentages for concentrates/raw plant); disclose any amount-equivalent if applicable and any allergens; clearly and conspicuously display the standardised symbol in navy blue in Appendix A indicating the product contains medicinal cannabis; contain the packager's name and licence number; protect against contamination; impart no toxic/deleterious substance; and provide the National Poison Control Center telephone number. Packaging/labelling must comply with 15 U.S.C. §§1471–1476, must not resemble trademarked food/beverage packaging, must not bear a Cabinet logo/seal implying endorsement, and must not bear any cartoon, image, graphic or feature that may make the package attractive to children or minors. Voluntary packaging/labelling compliance review is available via OMC; a submission must include documentation from the packaging company confirming child-resistance and at least a two-step initial opening, plus clear digital proofs of packaging and label.

Business-to-business labels: [VERIFY] — the LRC renderings of 915 KAR 1:100 conflict (one retains the B2B label paragraph — seller/receiver name, address, phone and licence number; type and amount; unique harvest/production batch identifier; harvest and, if applicable, process date; package date; tested statement with QR code to the COA or a hard/electronic COA copy at sale; B2B sales documented in the designated system — while the LRC markup strikes that paragraph). Do not quote B2B label fields as current law until the operative text is resolved (see §3). Separately, a cardholder label may carry a QR code linking to some or all required information, labelled "Specific Product Information" above or below the code and large enough to be smartphone-readable.

Advertising (915 KAR 1:090 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/services/karmaservice/documents/15512/ToPDF?markup=false): cannabis businesses shall NOT advertise medicinal cannabis sales in print, broadcast, online, by paid in-person solicitation, or by any other advertising device, except that a business may: place appropriate signs on its property identifying the business; place listings in business directories; place listings in trade or medical publications; sponsor health or not-for-profit charity or advocacy events; and maintain an informational website and social media presence. Cultivators, processors and producers shall NOT display any signage, logos, products or other identifying characteristics on the outside of their facilities alerting the public that medicinal cannabis is grown, processed, produced or stored there. No business shall make deceptive, false or misleading assertions on any advertising, device, sign, listing or informational material. An informational website/social media presence may provide: a business/services description; a listing of products cultivated, processed, produced or sold, including prices and inducements allowed under 915 KAR 1:070 §5(5); educational materials and product information; and COAs provided by safety compliance facilities for the business's harvest/production batches (915 KAR 1:090 §2; OMC FAQ — https://kymedcan.ky.gov/FAQs/Pages/Cannabis-Business-Questions.aspx). No additional dispensary-specific exterior-signage ban was located in 1:090.

Delivery (915 KAR 1:080 §2 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/080/; 915 KAR 1:070 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/070/14973/): dispensaries may provide delivery services. Delivery must be accomplished between 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.; a dispensary shall only dispense to a cardholder in an indoor, enclosed, secure facility between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. Delivery requires: 218B and 1:070 dispensing/sale requirements satisfied first; delivery on the date agreed by dispensary and patient/caregiver; a delivery manifest per delivery or series (driver and any accompanying employees, each address, estimated and actual date/time); a receipt per delivery (dispensary name/address/licence; patient/caregiver name/address; dispense date; form/quantity; accessories/educational materials; amount paid); registry-card check at delivery and patient/caregiver signature with a copy of the receipt; delivery only to the Kentucky address identified for the individual in the designated electronic monitoring system.

Business-to-business transport (915 KAR 1:080 §1): GPS; locked storage compartment that is part of the vehicle or locked container with separate key/combination pad; no markings identifying/indicating medicinal-cannabis transport; current state registration; alarm system and a minimum of 2 video cameras (one with a clear view of the driver, one with a clear view of the location of the medicinal cannabis); insurance per KRS 304.39-110; a delivery driver holding a copy of the business licence and a conspicuously worn badge (name, photo, employee ID number, business licence number, business phone/email, programme phone/email); a delivery manifest per delivery. Third-party transporters are allowed if §1:080 §1 is satisfied (business background-checks transporting employees/agents, provides licence copy and badges, notifies the Cabinet before transport begins) (OMC FAQ).

Zoning/buffer (state floor): no cannabis business within 1,000 feet of an existing elementary/secondary school or daycare centre, measured in a straight line from the nearest property line of the school/daycare to the nearest property line of the proposed place of business (915 KAR 1:010 attestation — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/010/15824/). Local governments may impose additional restrictions (OMC FAQ: businesses "may be subject to additional restrictions by local governments") — local detail is Part 3. The 1,000-ft rule is a business-siting rule; no 1,000-ft delivery exemption is stated in 1:080, and delivery is made only to the patient's/caregiver's Kentucky address in the designated system.

Seed-to-sale: see §1.8.

Hemp-derived (non-beverage): packaging/labelling/testing/COA/secured retail sale/21+ as in §1.6.3, plus the 902 KAR 45:012 retail permit ($2,000/yr) and 1,000-ft school buffer for adult-use retail establishments. Advertising: youth-targeted packaging bans DO exist in current 902 KAR 45:190 §3 (no cartoons; no likeness to images/characters/phrases popularly used to advertise to children; no likeness to/imitation of candy, snack, baked-good or beverage packaging; no "candy"/"candies"). No freestanding hemp advertising/marketing ban (as distinct from packaging) was located in the current 902 KAR 45:190/45:012 texts opened, and the HB 544-era health-claims ban appears struck through in the current 45:190 text. Do not assume the medical advertising rules (915 KAR 1:090) apply to hemp — by their terms they govern cannabis businesses under KRS ch. 218B.

Hemp beverages (CIB): ABC three-tier, package-only, wet-territory, dual quota + CIB licence, 21+ (see §1.6.4). CIB advertising/sampling: the 12-oz-per-day CIB sampling provision is SB 223 SCS1 proposal text (sampling licence issuable to a CIB retail package licence, CIB distributor's licence, or DPH-permitted CIB manufacturer — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/26RS/SB223/SCS1.pdf); it is NOT enacted law and must not be cited as a current sampling right. Current CIB sampling rights under KRS 243.0307 as enacted by SB 202 are [VERIFY] (see §3) — SB 202's enacted summary lists no KRS 243.0307 amendment adding CIB sampling.

1.8 Seed-to-sale tracking system

Medical: the Commonwealth's designated electronic monitoring system and seed-to-sale tracking system required by KRS 218B.140. The regulation extracts opened do not name the system — they say "designated electronic monitoring system and seed to sale tracking system" (915 KAR 1:010 attestation; 915 KAR 1:100: any sale/transfer between cannabis businesses shall be documented in that system; 915 KAR 1:070 §12: dispensaries use that system and keep inventory accurate in real time). OMC's official guidance names the system: OMC's 28 Feb 2025 Enforcement and Compliance Training — Dispensary Licensee (https://kymedcan.ky.gov/businesses/Documents/2025-02-28 Enforcement and Compliance Training - Dispensary Licensee.pdf) states "The required track and trace system for all medicinal cannabis licensees in Kentucky is METRC" (citing 915 KAR 1:070 §12(1)), and the companion Cultivator Licensee training (https://kymedcan.ky.gov/businesses/Documents/2025-02-28 Enforcement and Compliance Training - Cultivator Licensee.pdf) states METRC tracks medical cannabis from seed through sale of a finished good to a cardholder, inventory must accurately reflect METRC at all times, and all seeds, seedlings, clones, plants, material, products and waste MUST be tracked in METRC. State it exactly that way: regulations designate the system without naming it; OMC's official training names it Metrc.

No separate hemp seed-to-sale system exists: hemp crop tracking is via KDA lot registration, inspection and sampling/testing (302 KAR 50 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/302/050/056/), and hemp-product tracking is via CHFS permits, product registration and COAs (902 KAR 45:021/45:190) and retail permits/records (902 KAR 45:012), not Metrc. No hemp Metrc rule was located. The OMC–Metrc contract date (secondary reporting: February 2024) was not verified against any contract record in this pass [VERIFY — see §3].

1.9 Employment and drug-testing protections for patients

This is a narrow protection, not a general employment shield — do not overstate it.

What IS protected (KRS 218B.045(1), legislature statute page): "A registered qualified patient or visiting qualified patient who uses medicinal cannabis shall be afforded all the same rights under state and local law, including those guaranteed under KRS Chapter 344, as the individual would have been afforded if he or she were solely prescribed pharmaceutical medications as they pertain to drug testing required by any state or local law." https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55795 — In plain English: for state/local-law-required drug testing, medical cannabis is treated like a prescription drug. It does NOT create a general right to use at work or to test positive on an employer test.

What is NOT required (KRS 218B.040(1), legislature statute page, eff. 1 Jan 2025): "Nothing in this chapter shall: (a) Require an employer to permit or accommodate the use, consumption, possession, transfer, display, transportation, distribution, sale, or growing of medicinal cannabis in the workplace; (b) Prohibit an employer from implementing policies promoting workplace health and safety by: 1. Restricting the use of medicinal cannabis by employees; or 2. Restricting or prohibiting the use of equipment, machinery, or power tools by an employee who is a registered qualified patient, if the employer believes that [such use] poses an unreasonable safety risk; (c) Prohibit an employer from including in any contract provisions that prohibit the use of medicinal cannabis by employees; (d) Permit a cause of action against an employer for wrongful discharge or discrimination; (e) Except as provided in KRS 218B.045, prohibit a person, employer, corporation, or any other entity who occupies, owns, or controls a property from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the use, consumption, possession, transfer, display, transportation, sale, or growing of medicinal cannabis on or in that property; (f) Prohibit an employer from establishing and enforcing a drug testing policy, drug-free workplace, or zero-tolerance drug policy; or (g) Prohibit an employer from exercising his or her ability to determine impairment of an employee who is a cardholder." https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54282 — Good-faith impairment determinations under (1)(g) "shall include behavioral assessments of impairment and a secondary step of testing an employee who is a cardholder for the presence of cannabis by an established method. If an employer determines, pursuant to KRS 218B.015(2)(c), that an employee who is a cardholder is impaired by the use of cannabis from the behavioral assessment and testing, the burden of proving non-impairment shall shift to the employee to refute the findings of the employer."

Two further §218B.040 provisions omitted in the original, now restored: (2) An employee discharged for consuming medicinal cannabis in the workplace, working while under the influence, or testing positive for a controlled substance "shall not be eligible to receive benefits under KRS Chapter 341, if such actions are in violation of an employment contract or established personnel policy." (3) "An employer shall not be penalized or denied any benefit under state law for employing a cardholder." https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54282

Metabolites ≠ under the influence (KRS 218B.015(2)(c), eff. 1 July 2024): a registered/visiting patient "shall not be considered to be under the influence of medicinal cannabis solely because of the presence of tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites, including but not limited to the cannabinoid carboxy THC, which is also known as THC-COOH." https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54278

Other patient rights (§218B.045): custody/visitation/parenting time may not be denied and no presumption of abuse/neglect/dependency arises from permitted use unless the person's actions created an unreasonable danger to the minor as established by clear and convincing evidence (§218B.045(2)); for medical care including organ transplants, authorised medical-cannabis use is equivalent to authorised use of any other practitioner-directed medication, and a health facility (KRS 216B.015) may develop policies to allow on-premises use by a registered/visiting patient (§218B.045(3)); schools: a school shall not refuse to enrol or otherwise penalise a person solely for cardholder status unless failing to do so would violate federal law/regulations and cause loss of a monetary or licensing-related federal benefit, and a school shall not be penalised under state law for enrolling a cardholder (§218B.045(4)(a)–(b)); each local board of education, public-charter board, and certified-nonpublic governing body shall, no later than 1 Dec 2024, establish policies that either prohibit on-property use or permit it as deemed necessary by the pupil's parent/legal guardian — and a permitting policy shall require administration by a school nurse or under supervision of appropriate school staff, or by the parent/legal guardian, out of view of other students, and shall include a process by which a school nurse or other staff member may refuse to administer/supervise (§218B.045(4)(c)). https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=55795 — The original's "private religious schools may refuse" and "boards may (not must)" claims are deleted/corrected above.

Hemp employees: no patient-style employment protection exists for hemp-product use; a hemp delta-8/THC product can cause a positive drug test and is not covered by §218B.045, whose terms cover registered/visiting patients using medicinal cannabis. Whether any hemp-specific employment provision exists anywhere in KRS 260 or 902 KAR [VERIFY — negative search not exhaustively re-run in this slice].

1.10 Pending legislation + session calendar

1.10.1 Session calendar (Ky. Const. §§36 and 42)

Regular sessions in even-numbered years are capped at 60 legislative days and 15 April; in odd-numbered years at 30 legislative days and 30 March (Ky. Const. §§36, 42). 2026 was therefore a 60-day session: convened 6 Jan 2026, adjourned sine die 15 Apr 2026 (HCR 137: the houses adjourning 15 Apr 2026 "do adjourn sine die, and they shall not convene again until the first occurring of the 2027 Regular Session on Tuesday, January 5, 2027, or an extraordinary session upon call by the Governor"). https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/26RS/hcr137/orig_bill.pdf — The next regular session is the 30-day 2027 session convening 5 Jan 2027. Bills that did not pass in 2026 are dead and must be refiled in 2027. (Nuance: Ky. Const. §36(1) carryover applies only within an odd-year session, first part → second part — it does not save 2026 bills.) Special sessions can be called by the Governor.

2.2 Sales-tax treatment — detail

Medical cannabis is exempt from sales and excise taxes per OMC — https://kymedcan.ky.gov/FAQs/Pages/Banking-and-Taxes-Questions.aspx . A dispensary does not add Kentucky sales tax to a cardholder's purchase, and the state collects no sales/excise revenue from medical sales. The exemption's statutory pinpoint (whether in KRS 218B itself, KRS 139.470/139.480 exemptions, or a regulation) was not located — [VERIFY] before citing a KRS section. A secondary "tax guide" claiming medical dispensaries pay "6% + local" monthly is wrong on both points (contradicted by OMC and by the no-local-sales-tax rule) and is not relied on; secondary guides inventing Louisville 8% or Lexington 7% combined rates are likewise rejected — DOR states there are no local sales and use taxes in Kentucky — https://revenue.ky.gov/Business/Sales-Use-Tax/Pages/default.aspx .

Hemp / CIB retail: as tangible personal property sold at retail, the default is 6% sales tax unless the product falls in an exemption (e.g. qualifying "food and food ingredients" under KRS 139.485, which expressly keeps alcoholic beverages, tobacco, candy, dietary supplements, soft drinks and prepared food taxable). Because most intoxicating hemp products are marketed as supplements/edibles/drinks, the practical result for most SKUs is likely taxable at 6%, but product classification (especially tinctures/oils sold as supplements vs food) is fact-specific — [VERIFY] with DOR.

No local add-on: Kentucky's 6% is the total sales-tax rate everywhere; Louisville/Jefferson, Lexington-Fayette and other local governments cannot add a local sales tax. Local revenue from medical cannabis therefore comes, if at all, from reasonable local fees capped at additional costs under KRS 218B.130(2)(b)2 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 — plus a corrections-impact fee where a city opts in inside a prohibiting county (218B.130(8)), subject to the single-fee/shared-fee rule (218B.130(9)), and from general business/occupational taxes that apply to any business (not cannabis-specific, not quantified in this slice) — detail in Part 3.

For a 12-oz can that is $1.92 × (12/128) = $0.18 per can on a proportional basis (arithmetic, not a published per-can rate — the statute levies per gallon proportionally). In addition, DOR states an 11% wholesale sales tax (KRS 243.884) on manufacturer direct-ship/self-distribution and wholesaler distribution, reported monthly by the 20th — https://revenue.ky.gov/Business/Alcohol-Taxes/Pages/default.aspx . The SB 202 regime itself is 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 82, signed 25 March 2025 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/SB202.html ; the KRS 243.720(4) history line is 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 98, sec. 20 — the two chapter numbers are different acts and must not be conflated.

Alcohol excise for comparison (context only, not a cannabis tax): KRS 243.720 also levies distilled-spirits excise at $1.92 per wine gallon (subsection (1)), wine at $0.50 per gallon (subsection (2)), and malt beverages at $2.50 per 31-gallon barrel (subsection (3)) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=56607 ; CIBs were inserted as a new subsection (4) rather than being taxed as beer/wine.

No other cannabis excise (no per-mg, per-gram, potency or wholesale cannabis excise for medical cannabis or non-beverage hemp products) was located. The CIB 11% wholesale tax is CIB-only. The often-quoted "12% excise" for Kentucky medical cannabis was not found in any official source — do not use it.

2.5 IRS §280E and Kentucky decoupling — the critical tax section

Federal (fixed baseline, applied): §280E (IRC §280E) provides, in the OMC FAQ's own quotation — https://kymedcan.ky.gov/FAQs/Pages/Banking-and-Taxes-Questions.aspx : "No deduction or credit shall be allowed for any amount paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business if such trade or business (or the activities which comprise such trade or business) consists of trafficking in controlled substances (within the meaning of schedule I and II of the Controlled Substances Act) which is prohibited by Federal law or the law of any State in which such trade or business is conducted." OMC's FAQ still states this position with no Schedule III update — it is stale and must not be quoted as current without the Schedule III update below.

Before 28 April 2026: all Kentucky medical activity was Schedule I federally, so §280E applied in full; only cost of goods sold (COGS) was excludable from gross income.

From 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714, given baseline): state-licensed medical marijuana is Schedule III. Because §280E reaches only Schedule I/II trafficking, §280E no longer disallows ordinary deductions (rent, payroll, security, marketing, interest, depreciation, admin) for Kentucky's state-licensed medical cultivators, processors, producers, dispensaries and safety compliance facilities to the extent their activity is medical activity under KRS 218B. This is the single largest tax change for Kentucky medical operators in 2026. Practical cautions (analysis, not Kentucky law): (a) the relief is activity-specific — a business that also sells non-medical / adult-use product (which Kentucky does not licence) or, after 11 December 2026, hemp-derived product that is no longer federal hemp, must segregate that activity, which remains Schedule I and within §280E; (b) COGS-vs-deduction reclassification, prior-year amended returns, and state conformity all carry audit risk; (c) Schedule III does not make medical cannabis federally legal — it remains a controlled substance, with CSA, FDA, banking and firearms consequences outside §280E. A secondary law-firm handout found in this audit adds a DEA-registration condition to Treasury's §280E relief; that condition is not in the given baseline and is not adopted here — treat it as secondary-only and unverified.

Adult-use / non-medical: remains Schedule I; §280E remains fully applicable. Kentucky has no adult-use market, so this limb currently bites only on illicit activity and, after 11 December 2026, on formerly-hemp intoxicating products that fall out of the hemp definition (full federal total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap applying after that date, per the given baseline).

Kentucky state decoupling — NOT FOUND: no Kentucky statute was located in this audit that expressly decouples from, or expressly conforms to, §280E for state income-tax purposes (unlike states with explicit "add back / subtract §280E" statutes). Do NOT state that Kentucky "decouples" or "conforms" on §280E. A secondary conformity table stating Kentucky conforms to §280E "to the extent of conformity to the underlying federal deduction" via KRS 141.010 is secondary only and is not adopted. Kentucky's fixed-date IRC conformity date (secondary summaries: 31 December 2024 for tax year 2025) is [VERIFY] on current KRS 141.010. HB 757 (2026) was enacted over veto on 14 April 2026 (House 66–18, Senate 31–5, per the official vote history — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/RECORD/26rs/hb757/vote_history.pdf ) as a revenue-measures bill whose OBBBA decoupling, as described in secondary summaries, concerns IRC §163(j) business-interest and individual OBBBA deductions — not §280E. Nothing located in this audit shows HB 757 addressing §280E at all. The open questions, both [VERIFY] with DOR / current KRS 141.010, are: (1) does Kentucky's IRC conformity date as amended for 2026 bring the federal §280E scope change into the Kentucky starting point, and (2) is there any Kentucky addition/subtraction for §280E? The safe wording is: "No Kentucky-specific §280E decoupling statute was located; state treatment depends on Kentucky's IRC conformity date and any §280E adjustment, both to be confirmed with the Department of Revenue."

Hemp businesses: hemp (while it is federal hemp) was never within §280E, because hemp is excluded from the CSA definition of marihuana. After 11 December 2026, hemp-derived products that exceed the federal cap cease to be hemp and, if non-medical, become Schedule I marijuana for federal tax purposes — i.e. §280E would then apply to them for the first time. Kentucky hemp operators should therefore model a post-11-December world in which their federal (and potentially state-conformity) deductions disappear unless Congress acts. This is analysis from the fixed baseline, not a Kentucky ruling.

3.1 Who does what: state, county, city, consolidated government

The state licence is the licence; local government cannot create a medical cannabis licence. KRS 218B.080(1) (as quoted in the original from the official text; re-open KRS 218B.080 on apps.legislature.ky.gov at republication): "No person shall cultivate, process, produce, possess, test, transfer, transport, or sell medicinal cannabis or otherwise operate a cannabis business in this state without first obtaining a license under this section." The Cabinet for Health and Family Services (CHFS), through the Office of Medical Cannabis (OMC), issues that state licence. A local licence/registration, where a city has created one (Lexington-Fayette, Bowling Green, Covington — see §3.4), is additional to, not a substitute for, the state licence. Covington's own official notice states this expressly: "Businesses in Covington will require a license from both the Commonwealth and the City of Covington. They also must obtain general occupational licenses." — https://www.covingtonky.gov/news/2024/08/14/covington-allows-medical-cannabis-businesses (official city notice as cited in the original; not re-opened live in this audit).

What "local government" means in KRS 218B.130: KRS 218B.130(1), as amended by 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195, sec. 13, effective 17 April 2024 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "For the purposes of this section, 'local government' means a city, county, urban-county government, consolidated local government, charter county government, or unified local government."

Form of government Kentucky example How it acts under KRS 218B.130
Consolidated local government Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government (Jefferson County) One government for the whole county (with small incorporated cities inside Jefferson County retaining their own powers — see below). Its Metro Council ordinance is the county-level act for Louisville/Jefferson County. It also triggers the dispensary-region consequence in 915 KAR 1:020: regions containing a consolidated local government get at least six dispensary licences, two of which must be in the consolidated-government county (see §3.6) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ .
Urban-county government Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (Fayette County) One merged city-county government. Its Urban County Council adopted both the zoning ordinance and the special-fees ordinance (File 0592-24) for the whole of Fayette County — https://lexington.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?From=RSS&ID=6714915&GUID=23395DBC-16AA-4BA4-9C5F-265CA8DD0AC1&FullText=1 . It likewise triggers the "at least six, two in the urban county" dispensary rule.
Ordinary county (fiscal court) + separate cities e.g. Warren County + City of Bowling Green; Daviess County + City of Owensboro; Kenton County + City of Covington; Boone County + City of Florence; Madison County + City of Richmond; Scott County + City of Georgetown; Hardin County + City of Elizabethtown; Christian County + City of Hopkinsville; Franklin County + City of Frankfort; McCracken County + City of Paducah; Pike County + City of Pikeville County and city are separate "local governments". Each can prohibit, allow, zone and fee independently, subject to §3.2. A county prohibition covers unincorporated territory and incorporated cities inside it unless a city opts back in (see §3.2).
Small incorporated cities inside a consolidated government e.g. Kingsley, Douglass Hills, Graymoor-Devondale inside Jefferson County Each is itself a "city" local government and can act on its own territory. Example: OMC's opt-out list includes the City of Kingsley (Jefferson Co.), adopted 7 November 2024, even though Louisville/Jefferson County Metro itself did not opt out — https://kymedcan.ky.gov:443/local-government/Pages/optout-and-optin.aspx . Graymoor-Devondale is on OMC's opt-IN list, adopted 15 October 2024 (zoning ordinance) — corrected date, not merely "October 2024 minutes".

What a local government that permits businesses may do — KRS 218B.130(2)(b), verbatim (as amended 17 April 2024) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "(b) Within whose territory cannabis business operations are permitted, may enact ordinances: 1. That are not less restrictive than this chapter or any administrative regulations promulgated thereunder, relating to the time, place, and manner of cannabis business operations, except that a local government shall not, except as permitted in paragraph (a) of this subsection, enact ordinances that impose an undue burden or make cannabis business operations unreasonable or impractical; and 2. To establish and assess reasonable local fees to compensate for any additional costs caused by the operation of cannabis businesses within its territory. Any fees assessed pursuant to this subparagraph shall not exceed the additional costs caused by the operation of cannabis businesses."

In plain English, the division of labour is: State (CHFS/OMC): who may hold a licence, licence categories and caps, lottery, product and testing rules, the 1,000-foot state buffer (see §3.5), seed-to-sale, and discipline. Local government (county / city / consolidated / urban-county): (a) prohibit all cannabis business operations in its territory, but only before the Cabinet issues a licence there (see §3.2); (b) if it permits them, regulate time, place and manner through zoning and other ordinances, provided the local rule is not less restrictive than KRS Chapter 218B / 915 KAR and does not impose an "undue burden" or make operations "unreasonable or impractical"; and (c) charge reasonable local fees capped at the additional costs the businesses cause. Planning/zoning bodies: the actual zoning text amendments are typically recommended by the local planning commission and adopted by the fiscal court / city commission / Metro Council / Urban County Council (e.g. Louisville Case No. 24-LDC-0007, Ordinance No. 137, Series 2024 — see §3.5). The Louisville Planning Commission hearing date of 30 May 2024 and the Georgetown-Scott County Planning Commission hearing date of 14 November 2024 cited in the original were not confirmed on official planning records in this audit — [VERIFY] against those bodies' minutes.

Hemp-product retailers are NOT covered by KRS 218B.130 — stated as an interpretation of the statute's scope, not as a quoted sentence — [VERIFY] by CHFS/ABC guidance: KRS 218B.130 speaks only of "cannabis business operations" / "cannabis business" as defined in KRS Chapter 218B (medical cannabis businesses) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 . It does not mention hemp or hemp-derived cannabinoid products. On that textual reading, a hemp-derived cannabinoid retailer does not need a KRS 218B.130 opt-in, and a county/city medical-cannabis opt-out ordinance does not by its own terms ban hemp-derived product retail. Such a retailer is instead governed by: (i) general local zoning and business-licensing law; (ii) CHFS permitting and product registration under 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:012 (see Part 4, §§4.6–4.7, outside this slice); and (iii) for cannabis-infused beverages (CIBs), the ABC three-tier system and wet/dry territory law under KRS Chapter 243. A city could still restrict hemp retail through a generally applicable zoning or nuisance ordinance. No example of such a hemp-specific local ban was located in this audit; that absence is [UNAVAILABLE], not proof none exists. (The original's example of Nicholasville as a banning city is removed: Nicholasville allows medical businesses — see §3.3 — and must not be used as a banning example.)

3.2 Opt-out and opt-in: deadline, reversal, and city/county interaction

The statutory mechanism — verbatim core provisions. KRS 218B.130(2)(a) (as amended 17 April 2024) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "A local government: (a) Prior to the cabinet issuing a license to a cannabis business to conduct business operations within its territory, may: 1. Prohibit all cannabis business operations within its territory through the passage of an ordinance; or 2. Enact resolutions directing that the question of prohibiting cannabis businesses from operating within its territory be submitted to the voters of its territory at the next regular election pursuant to subsection (3)(b) of this section; except as provided in KRS 218B.090(5);"

Key consequences, stated plainly:

The prohibition is all-or-nothing by type. A local government may prohibit all cannabis business operations. It may not prohibit only dispensaries, or only cultivators — the statute's word is "all" — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 .

The deadline is framed as a condition, not a single calendar date in the statute text. The statute says "Prior to the cabinet issuing a license". The 31 December 2024 / before 1 January 2025 date used by OMC and the Kentucky Association of Counties (KaCO) in 2024 was a practical translation of that condition around programme launch, not a date written in KRS 218B.130 itself. OMC's current page states the operative principle as automatic opt-in unless a locality enacts an ordinance to restrict/fee or prohibit — https://kymedcan.ky.gov:443/local-government/Pages/optout-and-optin.aspx . Because licences were in fact issued in late 2024, a post-2024 prohibition ordinance in a territory where a licence has already been issued would face the pre-licence limit. Whether a new prohibition remains possible in a territory where no licence has ever been issued is [VERIFY] — KRS 218B.090(5), expressly excepted in §218B.130(2)(a), was not read in full on the primary page in this audit, and its text may qualify this. Do not advise any locality on this point until KRS 218B.090(5) is read.

Notice to the Cabinet within five days. KRS 218B.130(11) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "If a local government elects, pursuant to subsection (2)(a) of this section, to prohibit cannabis business operations within its territory, the local government shall notify the cabinet in writing of its decision to prohibit cannabis business operations within five (5) days after passage of such an ordinance or after the results of a ballot question to prohibit cannabis business operations are certified." OMC gives the notification address as kymedcan@ky.gov — https://kymedcan.ky.gov:443/local-government/Pages/optout-and-optin.aspx .

What happens to an already-licensed business if its territory later prohibits. 915 KAR 1:020, Section 3 (current text) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ — provides for a provisional licence: if a lottery selectee needs to change location because a local government prohibited all cannabis business operations under KRS 218B.130 (or for other circumstances), a provisional licence may be issued on timely payment of the fee; the provisional licensee has a maximum of 120 calendar days from issuance to request a change of location to an allowable county or city; if it fails to request, or the request is denied, the Cabinet shall revoke the provisional licence and the fee is not refunded; a provisional licence shall not be sold or transferred and shall not authorise any cannabis business activities; if the new location is approved, a new licence is issued with an expiration date one (1) year from the date of provisional licence issuance. Separately, the regulation requires a licensee in an affected territory to notify the Cabinet in writing by email within 24 hours of notification or discovery of a prohibition, and it may request a location change — confirm the current reporting email address on the OMC site at republication.

How a prohibition is reversed — three routes:

(a) City inside a prohibiting county/consolidated government opts back in by ordinance. KRS 218B.130(3)(a) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "If a county, consolidated local government, charter county government, or unified local government prohibits all cannabis business operations, the legislative body of a city located within the county, consolidated local government, charter county government, or unified local government may: 1. Approve cannabis business operations within the limits of the city through the passage of an ordinance; or 2. Enact resolutions directing that the question of allowing cannabis businesses to operate within the limits of the city be submitted to the voters who are eligible to vote in that city's elections at the next regular election pursuant to paragraph (b) of this subsection."

(b) City inside a prohibiting county opts back in by referendum. Same subsection, paragraph (3)(b) — the question, if the county clerk receives the resolution not later than the second Tuesday in August preceding a regular election, is: "Are you in favor of the sale of medicinal cannabis at a licensed dispensary and the operation of other cannabis businesses in (affected territory)? Yes....No...." The clerk must publish the full text under KRS Chapter 424 and post a copy in each polling place — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 .

(c) Petition to overturn a local prohibition ordinance. KRS 218B.130(4)–(5) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : if a local legislative body prohibits operations by ordinance, a public question initiated by petition proposing to allow a cannabis business is authorised. The petition must: be preceded by a filed statement of intent (by persons registered to vote in the territory for at least the previous 12 months); be circulated for no more than six months before filing; be signed by constitutionally qualified voters equal to 10% of registered voters for the affected territory, each signature in ink/indelible pencil with printed name, residence address, year of birth and date signed, with a circulator affidavit; be certified sufficient/insufficient by the county clerk within 30 days (with a one-time 30-day supplemental-petition cure for signature insufficiency); and, if certified sufficient not later than the second Tuesday in August preceding a regular election, be placed on the next regular-election ballot with the question: "Are you in favor of overturning the decision of the local government legislative body and allowing the sale of medicinal cannabis at a licensed dispensary and the operation of other cannabis businesses in (affected territory)? Yes....No...."

Effect of a "yes" vote, and the waiting period after a "no" vote. KRS 218B.130(6)–(7) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : "(6) If the question submitted to the voters under subsection (3) or (5) of this section fails to pass, three (3) years shall elapse before the question of medicinal cannabis sales and cannabis business operations may be included on a regular election ballot for the affected territory. (7) If the question submitted to the voters under subsection (3) or (5) of this section passes, medicinal cannabis sales and cannabis business operations may be conducted in the affected territory, notwithstanding any local government ordinances which prohibit all cannabis business operations within its territory."

City opt-in inside a prohibiting county — fee consequence. KRS 218B.130(8) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : operations may proceed within the city limits, and the county/consolidated government "may assess an additional reasonable fee to compensate for any additional corrections impact caused by the approval of cannabis business operations. Any additional fees collected pursuant to this subsection shall not exceed the additional corrections impact caused by the approval of cannabis business operations." KRS 218B.130(9): where neither city nor county prohibits, a business located in both jurisdictions "shall only pay the reasonable established local fees of either the city or the county", shared as negotiated between city and county.

City/county interaction — summary table:

Situation Result
County prohibits; city does nothing No cannabis business anywhere in the county, including inside that city.
County prohibits; city passes opt-in ordinance or wins an opt-in referendum Businesses may operate inside that city's limits only; the rest of the county (unincorporated + other cities) remains prohibited.
County allows; city prohibits by ordinance Businesses barred inside that city; allowed in the rest of the county.
County allows; city allows (or does nothing) Businesses allowed in both, subject to zoning; only one local fee (city or county), shared by negotiation — KRS 218B.130(9) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 .
City prohibits by ordinance; voters petition to overturn Petition route (10% of registered voters, second Tuesday in August deadline) to the next regular election; 3-year wait if it fails.
Either level's voters are asked whether to prohibit (resolution route) Question is the "Are you in favor of the sale…" form; a "yes" allows, a "no" prohibits.

The November 2024 ballot results — [VERIFY against certified results; secondary reporting only in this audit]. Secondary outlets consistently report that 106 jurisdictions put the question to voters — 53 counties and 53 cities — and that all 106 voted to allow medical cannabis businesses, none to ban. The aggregate margin reported in secondary outlets is about 67% in favour across the 53 counties (341,766 votes in favour in aggregate as reported), and a nearly identical percentage in the 53 cities. Largest reported margins: Marion and Nelson Counties over 75% yes; Bardstown reported at 78% in one secondary round-up. Smallest reported margins: Hickman County 54% yes; the City of Union (Boone County) 52% yes in one round-up. Reported examples from secondary round-ups (all [VERIFY] at county-clerk level): Florence (Boone County) 64% in favour; Independence (Kenton County) 63%; Washington (Bullitt County) 67%; Manchester (Clay County) 69% and Clay County 68%. None of these percentages was confirmed against a certified return in this audit. Follow-up: Kentucky Secretary of State / State Board of Elections 2024 general-election certified results, plus each county clerk's certification for the 106 jurisdictions. Do not present 106-for-106 or any percentage as primary-confirmed.

Confirmed asterisk cases on the live OMC page — https://kymedcan.ky.gov:443/local-government/Pages/optout-and-optin.aspx : the City of Union (Boone Co.) adopted an opt-out ordinance on 17 June 2024, then voted to allow businesses in the 2024 election; Coal Run Village (Pike Co.) adopted 12 September 2024, then voted to allow in 2024; and the City of Franklin (Simpson Co.) adopted 24 June 2024, then voted to allow in 2024 (the third asterisk case, omitted from the original's discussion).

Governor's post-election counts — superseded. Secondary reports gave 21 counties opted out by ordinance (another gave 20), 39 counties directly authorised, 53 letting voters decide, and for cities 53 opted out or opted out by their counties and 184 staying in. None of those counts is adopted: the live OMC opt-out list (current as of 2 May 2025) names 23 opt-out counties (see §3.3), and OMC's opt-in lists replace the secondary authorised/staying-in figures. Do not carry the 21-vs-20 conflict forward as unresolved — the primary list resolves it.

3.3 The official allow/prohibit list — what exists, what does not, and the exact URLs

OMC publishes HTML opt-out/opt-in lists, not a downloadable dataset. The hub is the OMC opt-out/opt-in page — https://kymedcan.ky.gov:443/local-government/Pages/optout-and-optin.aspx (current as of 2 May 2025; re-check live at republication). It contains: counties and cities that notified OMC of opt-out (with ordinance links); counties and cities that notified OMC of opt-in via ordinance; and a link to counties and cities that opted in via a ballot resolution. The page warns its map may not reflect all information on the page. The December 2024 OMC PDFs are snapshots superseded by this page; do not cite them as current. There is no jurisdiction that "allows dispensaries but prohibits cultivators" by a §218B.130 ordinance, because prohibition is all-or-nothing (see §3.2). What varies by type is zoning (see §3.5). Any future table that splits allow/prohibit "by type" should therefore be a zoning table, not an opt-out table.

3.4 Local licence / permit fees for cannabis or hemp businesses

State rule (cap). KRS 218B.130(2)(b)2 — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=54619 : local fees must be "reasonable", "to compensate for any additional costs caused by the operation of cannabis businesses", and "shall not exceed the additional costs". KRS 218B.130(8)–(9) add the corrections-impact fee (city opt-in inside a prohibiting county) and the single-fee / negotiated-sharing rule (city + county both allow). No statewide schedule of local fees exists; each locality sets its own.

3.5 Zones and buffers — state floor, then each required jurisdiction

State floor (applies everywhere; local rules may only be more restrictive). 915 KAR 1:020, Section 4 (current text) — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ : "The licensee has submitted its complete physical address and the global positioning system (GPS) coordinates for any cannabis business activities to the cabinet and confirmed its business is not located within 1,000 feet of an existing elementary or secondary school or a daycare center. For the purpose of this administrative regulation, 1,000 feet shall be measured in a straight line from the nearest property line of an existing elementary school, secondary school, or daycare center to the nearest property line of the licensee's place of business."

Additional state siting bars in the same regulation — https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ : no licence for operation within a personal residence or any location where the Cabinet or law enforcement has limited access; no licence for a site on lands owned by the United States or the Commonwealth of Kentucky. A licence is by name and address, valid only for the person/entity and the activity and location specified, for one year from issuance.

For hemp-derived retail, the state buffer is different and narrower: 902 KAR 45:012, Section 1(7) — http://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/902/045/012/ — provides that a retail establishment offering adult-use cannabinoid products "shall not be located within 1,000 feet of an elementary, middle, or high school", with retail establishments registered with the department prior to 31 December 2024 exempted. Note the hemp rule says nothing about daycares, unlike the medical rule.

Under the federal baseline given for this audit, Schedule III covers state-licensed medical marijuana only; adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I and fully subject to 280E.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.1 Medical cannabis licence types at a glance

KRS 218B.080(2) requires the Cabinet to create separate licences, application fees, initial licensure fees and renewal fees for each of: (a) Tier I cannabis cultivator; (b) Tier II cannabis cultivator; (c) Tier III cannabis cultivator; (d) Tier IV cannabis cultivator; (e) Cannabis dispensary; (f) Cannabis processor; (g) Cannabis producer; (h) Cannabis safety compliance facility. Source: https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54038

A licence is valid for one year from issuance; the Cabinet must notify the licensee 90 days before expiry to allow renewal to begin (915 KAR 1:010). Source: https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/010/15824/ A separate licence is required for each location, except that a producer may operate cultivation and processing at separate locations but no more than one cultivation and one processing facility per licence (KRS 218B.080(4)). Source: https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=54038

One-category rule: during an initial application period an applicant may apply for a licence in only one cannabis business licence type (cultivator, processor, producer, dispensary or safety compliance facility), though it may submit multiple applications within that type if each has a separate physical address and separate sufficient capital, with at most one application per cultivator tier and at most one dispensary application per region. Source: https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/010/15824/ ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/FAQs/Pages/Cannabis-Business-Questions.aspx The producer is the designed exception to strict separation, because a producer licence combines cultivation + processing (see §4.2).

Master fee / capital table (state fees). All fees are from the current 915 KAR 1:020 (initial and renewal licence fees) and 915 KAR 1:010 (application fees), plus the sufficient-capital figures in 915 KAR 1:010. Sources: https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/020/ ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/915/001/010/15824/ ; https://kymedcan.ky.gov/FAQs/Pages/Cannabis-Business-Questions.aspx

Licence type What it allows (short) Initial-round cap Application fee (non-refundable) Initial licence fee (pay within 15 days of invoice; licence not issued if unpaid) Annual renewal fee (current 915 KAR 1:020) Sufficient capital to be shown (on deposit or credit extension; same capital may not support two applications)

The current regulation text shows those figures struck through and replaced: processor renewal $15,000 → $25,000; producer renewal $15,000 → $25,000 + tier; dispensary renewal $15,000 → $30,000.
