8.2 What "cannabis-zoned" means in Kentucky (why the list is so thin)

Kentucky does not have a statewide cannabis zoning map or a cannabis-specific zoning district. Siting is governed by (Run 1 Part 3, not re-litigated here — [VERIFY against the cited local codes]): the state 1,000-foot buffer from elementary/secondary schools and daycares for medical businesses (915 KAR 1:020, straight-line property-line measurement; no residence; no US/Commonwealth land); local time/place/manner rules that must not be less restrictive than KRS 218B/915 KAR and must not impose an "undue burden" (KRS 218B.130(2)(b)); and local zoning — e.g. Louisville C-2/C-3 + conditional use permit, Lexington's ZOTA PLN-ZOTA-24-00002 (cultivators excluded from "Commercial Greenhouse"), Bowling Green highway/general business zones, Owensboro's Downtown Overlay exclusion for dispensaries. A property is therefore "cannabis-zoned" in Kentucky only in the weak sense that its local zone + conditional-use position + buffers permit that use — which is why brokers market "potential" and "by right" claims that cannot be verified from a statewide register. Any buyer must verify: (a) the local opt-in status (city vs county split — e.g. a county opt-out does not bind an opted-in city, KRS 218B.130(3)); (b) the local zone and any conditional-use permit; (c) the 1,000-foot state buffer; and (d) that a transferable medical licence exists for the site, since new applications are closed.

8.3 Searched, found, but NOT counted as property listings (with reasons)

Item Why not counted
Region 6 – Kentucky Cannabis Dispensary License – Stanton, KY (BizTrader) — asking price shown as $1,900,000 in one BizTrader index copy and $1,000,000 in another (price conflict [VERIFY]; the two copies may be different vintages of the same licence offer). Described as a "pre-operational medical cannabis dispensary license in Stanton, KY (Region 6)". Licence-only sale. No real property (address, building, land, zoning) is included in the listing text as returned. Per the commission, licence/business sales are NOT fee-simple property listings unless the listing includes real property. Excluded from the §8.1 count; noted here because it is the only other Kentucky cannabis licence offer surfaced in this run. Source: BizTrader listings index, https://www.biztrader.com/listing/page/1/ (secondary marketplace; price conflict preserved).
AgTech Scientific Group 151-acre complex, Bourbon County (Lexington market) — 1.57 million sq. ft. of greenhouses + 155,000 sq. ft. warehouse/office + 150,000 sq. ft. polytunnels at 1077 Cane Ridge Rd, zoned A-1 Agricultural, built for ornamentals, converted to hemp-for-CBD in 2019; plus a 10-acre offsite facility at 333 Cleveland Road, zoned I-1, 24,000 sq. ft. production + 22,000 sq. ft. warehouse + 4,500 sq. ft. office, C1D2 standard. Historic/closed sale, not a current listing. The receivership sale was announced in November 2021 and no asking price was given ("The company gave no asking price"). It is included here as the only Kentucky hemp-facility sale with a full property description located, but it must not be presented as available in October 2026. Source: trade-press article (secondary only) — https://www.sfnet.com/list-pages/article-list---aydan's/2021/11/16/receivership-sale-by-a-g-real-estate-partners-and-murray-wise-associates-features-massive-agricultural-complex-in-lexington-kentucky-market [VERIFY against the receivership sale record / Bourbon County zoning].
16443 Princeton Road, Cerulean, KY 42215 (Christian County) — Land.com, 130 acres (83 acres cropland, 47 acres timber). Listing copy mentions hemp generically ("Kentucky has recently legalized industrial Hemp production… Hemp production for CBD oil at $5000.00/acre. Also, there is a large Industrial Hemp Processing facility in Cadiz, KY about 13 miles away"). Not counted: generic farmland, not marketed as cannabis-zoned, and the hemp copy is stale (the "recently legalized" framing predates the current programme; no price is shown in the search return and no cannabis zoning is claimed). A farm that could grow hemp (any Kentucky farmland, with a KDA grower licence) is not a cannabis-zoned property listing. Source: https://www.land.com/property/130-acres-in-Christian-County-Kentucky/7504952/ (listing only).
NewLake Capital (NLCP) Kentucky dispensary acquisition (August 2026, 8-K) — "In August 2026, the Company acquired a dispensary located in Kentucky for approximately $0.6 million and committed approximately $1.6 million to fund improvements at the property. The property was simultaneously leased to an existing tenant." Not counted: a completed REIT acquisition, not a listing. No Kentucky address, tenant, or property description is given in the filing excerpt, so it cannot be listed as a property. It is noted here only as secondary evidence that Kentucky dispensary real estate is trading (REIT sale-leaseback market). Source: secondary filing summary, https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/NLCP/8-k-new-lake-capital-partners-inc-reports-material-event-4d6246474a83.html [VERIFY against the SEC filing itself before citing the $0.6M/$1.6M figures].
General Kentucky farmland / retail listings on Crexi, LoopNet, Land.com, Realtor with no cannabis claim (e.g. Crexi 4628 Westport Rd, Louisville — R5 residential, $50,000/$25,000 parcels; generic Green County farmland) Not counted. No cannabis/hemp marketing or zoning claim in the listing. They confirm only that general commercial/farm property is available in Kentucky, which is not a Part 8 finding.

8.4 Searches tried (so the negative finding is auditable)

420Property: Kentucky cannabis search — returned only the Louisville Tier 1 licence/lease listing (§8.1, 8-2) as a Kentucky result; all other results on the page were other states (NY, CA, CO, FL, NJ, NV, MI, OH).

LoopNet: "Kentucky cannabis dispensary property for sale lease Louisville Lexington" — returned only the Cave City listing (§8.1, 8-3) as a cannabis-marketed Kentucky property; the remaining results were generic Kentucky retail space with no cannabis claim.

Crexi / Land.com / general web: "Kentucky hemp farm land for sale cannabis zoned property Crexi"; "Kentucky hemp farm for sale land.com acres CBD farm" — returned the historic AgTech sale, the Cerulean generic farm, and non-Kentucky or non-property results (a Colorado hemp-farm sale; a Wilmore, KY hemp farm's marketing pages, which are a farm's own sales site, not a property listing).

Same-name exclusion applied throughout: results for Lexington (VA), Louisville (CO), Glasgow (Scotland), Florence (SC/AL), Paris (France), London (UK), Georgetown (DC/TX) were not counted; none of the §8.1 listings depends on a same-name match (Glasgow, KY is Barren County, Kentucky; Cave City, KY is Barren County, Kentucky; Louisville, KY is Jefferson County, Kentucky — all confirmed by ZIP/state in the listings: 42141, 42127, and "Louisville, KY" respectively).

Part 9 and Part 10

Last audited 28 October 2026. Every fact below carries a source link. Flags appear only where the audit could not resolve the item. No prior-research attribution notes appear in the main text; all corrections from §1 are applied in place. Federal baseline (used as given): under 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III and all other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I; IRS 280E is generally removed as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (Treasury guidance forthcoming), while adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to provisions excluding cannabinoids not naturally produced or synthesised, with the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap applying after 11 December 2026; USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026; the federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026; no federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. Kentucky is medical-only; nothing in this rewrite treats any Kentucky adult-use activity as lawful, and Schedule III / 280E relief is described for Kentucky's medical licensees only. Kentucky's tax-year effect of the Schedule III / 280E change is [VERIFY] with the Department of Revenue (see §9.1, Revenue).

PART 9 — REGULATORS AND HISTORY

9.1 Every state agency regulating cannabis and hemp

Cabinet for Health and Family Services (CHFS) — Office of Medical Cannabis (OMC). Implementation, operation, oversight and regulation of the medicinal cannabis programme: business licensing (cultivator, processor, producer, dispensary, safety compliance facility), patient/caregiver/visiting-patient registry cards, practitioner registry, regulations (915 KAR). Statute: "The Cabinet for Health and Family Services is hereby charged with the implementation, operation, oversight, and regulation of the medicinal cannabis program established in this chapter." — KRS 218B.020(1) (legislature.ky.gov). KRS Chapter 218B; 915 KAR Titles 1–2. Website: kymedcan.ky.gov. Public contacts: card-application assistance 833-727-2828 (OMC application page — this number is given for assistance with applying for a card, not as a general OMC number; technical support on the same page is (502) 875-3733) and kymedcan@ky.gov (OMC local-government rules page). Street address: two different addresses appear in OMC documents — 275 East Main Street, Frankfort, KY 40621 (2024 patient/caregiver guide and business forms) and 500 Mero Street, 5SC14, Frankfort, KY 40601 (5 February 2026 OMC letterhead); use the 2026 letterhead address for current correspondence and note the conflict — no single current OMC street address is settled on these sources alone.

Board of Physicians and Advisors (within CHFS). Advisory only — it does not license businesses or patients. Duties, per KRS 218B.020(5) (legislature.ky.gov): (a) review and recommend daily / 10-day / 30-day supply and raw-plant equivalence protocols; (b) review and recommend quality-improvement metrics and minimum performance standards for cannabis business accreditation; (c) review peer-reviewed data and recommend to the General Assembly on THC limits in production; (d) the same on methods of use; (e) the same on adding or removing qualifying conditions; (f) other duties on request of the CHFS Secretary; and (g) assist in developing the Medicinal Cannabis Advisory Pamphlet under KRS 218B.140(2)(b) (omitted from the OMC page's six-point summary). The Cabinet's annual report is prepared in consultation with the University of Kentucky College of Medicine and the Kentucky Center for Cannabis (KRS 218B.020(6)–(7)). See composition note below. OMC Board page: kymedcan.ky.gov/About/Pages/Board-of-Physicians-and-Advisors.aspx.

Kentucky Board of Medical Licensure (KBML). Authorises practitioners to provide written certifications; appoints the physician members of the Board of Physicians and Advisors. Regulation 201 KAR 9:067 governs authorisation. KRS 218B.050; 201 KAR 9:067. Page: kbml.ky.gov/Pages/Medical-Cannabis.aspx; practitioner questions to kbmlcannabis@ky.gov (public contact shown on that page). Under KRS 218B.050(10), 201 KAR 9:067 covers application and renewal procedures, continuing education, suspension/revocation grounds and minimal standards of care.

Kentucky Board of Nursing. Appoints the two APRN members of the Board of Physicians and Advisors; APRN practitioners are also certifying practitioners under the programme. KRS 218B.020(2)(b). Via the OMC Board page above. No separate nursing-board cannabis page was located.

Kentucky Board of Pharmacy. Appoints the one pharmacist member of the Board of Physicians and Advisors. KRS 218B.020(2)(c), as amended by 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195, §2 (HB 829), effective 17 April 2024. Via the OMC Board page above.

Team Kentucky Medical Cannabis Advisory Committee (2022). Governor-created advisory committee that travelled the Commonwealth, held public hearings/town halls, and reported in September 2022. It was a pre-legislation advisory body, not a licensing regulator, and its work preceded SB 47. EO 2022-338 (14 June 2022), OMC Executive Orders page (kymedcan.ky.gov/laws-and-regulations/Pages/Executive-Orders.aspx). The Committee page confirms 17 members announced by the Governor (co-chairs Kerry Harvey and Ray Perry) (Committee page). The Committee's public work ended with its 30 September 2022 summary; no formal dissolution text was located on OMC/Governor pages, and the OMC Executive Orders page carries no rescission note for EO 2022-338 — absence of a note is not proof of current activity [formal dissolution status Unverified].

Team Kentucky Medical Cannabis Workgroup (2023– ). Governor-created workgroup "to study evolving medical cannabis industry policy and the state of medical cannabis policy in the Commonwealth" and to make recommendations to the programme and other agencies. Advisory only. EO 2023-600 (5 October 2023), same OMC Executive Orders page. The Workgroup's own report text and any Workgroup condition recommendations were not located on official pages in this pass [Unverified] — do not attribute the EO 2026-318 condition list to the Workgroup on secondary coverage alone.

Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, now Department of Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Control (ABC). Regulates cannabis-infused beverages (CIBs): distribution and retail package licensing under the three-tier system; a cannabis-infused beverage retail package licence "shall only be issued as a supplemental license to the holder of a quota retail package license" (KRS 243.403, legislature.ky.gov). Manufacturing of CIBs sits with CHFS/DPH, not ABC; ABC does not issue a standalone CIB manufacturer licence in the sources found. KRS Chapters 241–244; SB 202 (2025), 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 82; 804 KAR 4:400 (CIB application forms, approved and filed with LRC 11 June 2026, legislature.ky.gov). Website: abc.ky.gov — 500 Mero Street 2NE33, Frankfort, KY 40601; board hearings via abc.info@ky.gov (ABC information page); general phone (502) 564-4850 as shown on the Revenue alcohol-taxes page (revenue.ky.gov), not on the ABC static page itself. The 804 KAR 4:400 analysis confirms DPH CIB permits expire after 1 July 2026 and holders continuing must apply for an ABC retail package or distributor's licence.

CHFS, Department for Public Health (DPH), Food Safety Branch — Hemp-Derived Cannabinoid Products (HDCP). Registration and regulation of non-beverage hemp-derived cannabinoid products (adult-use cannabinoids): product registration, retailer/processor/manufacturer/wholesale/cosmetic permits, testing, labelling, child-resistant packaging, 21+ retail rules, under 902 KAR 45:012 / 45:021 / 45:031 (HDCP page) and 902 KAR 45:190 (adult-use regime, Run 1 citation — see §3 note on the 45:031/45:190 numbering). Only CHFS-registered products may be sold. Adverse-event / recall notice within 24 hours. KRS Chapter 217B (food/drug) and 902 KAR 45. Page: chfs.ky.gov/agencies/dph/dphps/fsb/Pages/HDCP.aspx — "You must notify the Cabinet for Health and Family Services within 24 hours by emailing food.safety@ky.gov or calling (502) 564-7181."

Kentucky Department of Agriculture (KDA). Hemp licensing programme: grower and processor/handler licences, plot registration, pre-harvest sampling/testing, USDA-approved State Plan. KDA does not license HDCP retailers or CIB retailers. KRS 260.850–260.869; 302 KAR 50; USDA-approved Kentucky State Plan (operating 1 January 2022, KDA orientation PDF). USDA plan list: ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — "Kentucky | KY Approved Plan (pdf)*". The KDA hemp-pilot landing page (kyagr.com/marketing/hemp-pilot.html) returns only a "Contact Us / AgNet" skeleton with no usable hemp content to a text fetcher; do not cite that page for contacts. Contacts from kyagr.com programme documents: Hemp@ky.gov (grower orientation, processor/handler orientation), (502) 782-4113 (KDA plot-sign document), KDA Hemp Licensing Program, 111 Corporate Drive, Frankfort, KY 40601 (processor-handler application).

Hemp Advisory Board. Advisory board to KDA on the hemp programme. Composition (KRS 260.860, legislature.ky.gov): Commissioner of Agriculture or designee (chair); Dean of the University of Kentucky College of Agriculture, Food and Environment or designee; Commissioner of the Department of Kentucky State Police or designee; President of the Kentucky Sheriffs' Association or designee; President of the Kentucky Association of Chiefs of Police or designee; plus ten at-large members designated by the Commissioner. KRS 260.860(4): "The Commissioner or the Commissioner's designee shall serve as chair." Effective 12 March 2021 (2021 Ky. Acts ch. 12, §11; created 2017 Ky. Acts ch. 45, §5, effective 20 March 2017). Meeting frequency, four-year terms and compensation/travel-reimbursement details are carried as originally cited and should be re-checked against the full KRS 260.860 text before being relied on alone (see §3).

Kentucky Department of Revenue. CIB excise tax and CIB registration; general 6% sales-tax administration (medical cannabis exempt per Run 1). No separate medical-cannabis excise exists. KRS Chapters 131, 243. Correction applied: the $1.92-per-gallon CIB excise tax, effective 1 July 2025, is HB 775, 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 98, §20, amending KRS 243.720 — not SB 202. Revenue page (revenue.ky.gov): "Effective July 1, 2025, a new excise tax on cannabis-infused beverages is established at the rate of $1.92 per gallon and a proportional rate per gallon on all cannabis-infused beverages used, sold, or distributed in any container of more or less than one gallon (KRS 243.720)." The CIB paragraph is subsection (4) in the post-1 July 2025 numbering (exemptions moved to subsection (5)); the Revenue page itself cites KRS 243.720 generally, without a subsection. The same page notes an 11% wholesale sales tax under KRS 243.884. CIB registration: "Department of Revenue / Cannabis-Infused Beverage Registration / 501 High Street, Station 62 / Frankfort, KY 40601", alcoholexcisetax@ky.gov. Whether Kentucky's fixed-date IRC conformity picks up the April 2026 federal Schedule III / 280E change, and for which tax year, remains [VERIFY] with Revenue — no Revenue guidance on this was located, and no Kentucky tax-year conclusion is stated in this rewrite.

Kentucky State Police (KSP). Law enforcement and criminal-background checks for hemp licensees (KRS 260.862) and for medical programme purposes; KSP Commissioner (or designee) sits on the Hemp Advisory Board (KRS 260.860(3)(c)); KSP is a named input to the planned OMC law-enforcement guide (KaCO FAQ — secondary for that detail). KSP does not license cannabis or hemp businesses. KRS Chapter 16. Criminal Identification and Records Branch address in primary KAR text: "Kentucky State Police, Criminal Identification and Records Branch, 1266 Louisville Road, Frankfort, Kentucky 40601, (502) 227-8700" (502 KAR 15:010, legislature.ky.gov). The KSP website itself (kentuckystatepolice.ky.gov/background-checks) lists only headquarters at 919 Versailles Road, Frankfort, KY 40601, (502) 782-1800 — do not present 1266 Louisville Road as KSP-website-confirmed.

Justice and Public Safety Cabinet / Department for Criminal Justice Training. Named by KaCO as contributors, with KSP, to the OMC law-enforcement guide (KaCO FAQ, kaco.org — secondary for this detail). No independent cannabis licensing role was located.

Governor of Kentucky. Executive orders (see §9.2); clemency/pardon power used for EO 2022-798; signs/vetoes legislation; appoints Board members subject to Senate confirmation (KRS 11.160). Ky. Const. §§77, 88; KRS 11.160. Website: governor.ky.gov. EO texts via the OMC Executive Orders page above.

Kentucky General Assembly / Legislative Research Commission (LRC). Enacts/amends KRS Chapters 218B, 218A, 260, 241–244; refers constitutional amendments to voters (see §9.3); publishes KRS and KAR. Ky. Const. §§29, 256. Websites: legislature.ky.gov and apps.legislature.ky.gov.

Kentucky Center for Cannabis (University of Kentucky). Research body, not a regulator. KRS 164.983 (legislature.ky.gov): "The Kentucky Center for Cannabis is hereby established at the University of Kentucky to advance the study of the use of cannabis and cannabis derivatives for the treatment of certain medical conditions and diseases as indicated and recommended by the center's advisory board." Established by HB 604 (2022), based in UK's College of Medicine Center on Drug and Alcohol Research (UK Cannabis Center page); mission: conduct and fund cannabis research, health-effects research, delivery-method efficacy research, literature review, patient-outcome monitoring in states with medicinal programmes, and combustible-cannabis health effects; annual report by 1 September to the CHFS Secretary and LRC; annual symposium. Condition power — real and refused: KRS 218B.145 allows the Centre to unilaterally expand the qualifying medical conditions on sufficient scientific data and evidence that a person diagnosed with that condition is likely to receive medical, therapeutic or palliative benefit from medicinal cannabis. OMC's 5 February 2026 letter (OMC letter) states: "To date, the Kentucky Center for Cannabis has repeatedly expressed that it will not be utilizing the authority provided in KRS 218B.145" — which is why OMC recommended the legislature amend KRS 218B.145 to remove the Centre and replace it with the Board of Physicians and Advisors. The Centre has added no condition. Its membership list and current director were not re-verified in this slice and are not printed here from secondary sources.

Composition note — Board of Physicians and Advisors. The OMC Board page (kymedcan.ky.gov/About/Pages/Board-of-Physicians-and-Advisors.aspx) states the Board "consists of ten members": 7 physicians (KBML) + 2 APRNs (Board of Nursing) + 1 pharmacist (Board of Pharmacy), four-year terms, Senate confirmation, no compensation. The pharmacist seat was added by HB 829, 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195, §2, effective 17 April 2024; the pre-2024 board was nine (7 + 2), which is why older secondary summaries calling it a "nine-member board" must not be used for the current board. The same page, re-opened 28 October 2026, still lists only nine named members: six physicians (Chair Frederick A. Stine, D.O.; AnYu Chen, M.D.; Ryan Grell, M.D.; Linda McClain, M.D.; Charles Roberts, M.D.; Courtney Turner, M.D. — all appointed 17 July 2023, Senate-confirmed 15 April 2024 (Stine SR 326, Chen SR 318, Grell SR 320, McClain SR 279, Roberts SR 325, Turner SR 281), terms expiring 17 July 2027), two APRNs (Jodi Wojcik, appointed 15 June 2023, term to 15 June 2027; Thomas "Perry" Colley, appointed 24 October 2024, term to 24 October 2028), and one pharmacist (Matt Carrico, PharmD, appointed 22 May 2024, term to 22 May 2028). One physician seat therefore remains unlisted on the page — the page labels no vacancy, and no vacant seat-holder is named here. Kristin Dawson, M.D. appears as a Board member in the Board's 15 April 2024 finding letter but not on the current page; her departure is not explained on the page [follow-up: current OMC roster — see §3]. Meeting materials on the page run from October 2023 through October 2026, including two meetings (15 October 2025 and 22 April 2026) at which the Board lacked a quorum to conduct official business ("The Board did not have a quorum to conduct offical [sic] business during this meeting").

9.2 Key dates — timeline

7 April 2013 — SB 50 (Kentucky hemp framework) becomes law without the Governor's signature (2013 Ky. Acts ch. 134): removes industrial hemp from Kentucky's controlled-substances framework at state level and authorises state-sponsored research, contingent on federal rules. Source: Senator McConnell's official release (date and "without the Governor's signature" confirmed); the legislature record page itself was not directly fetched in this pass and should be re-opened before the enrolled text is quoted. (McConnell Senate release via LegiStorm)

7 February 2014 — Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 Farm Bill), §7606 (Pub. L. 113-79, "Legitimacy of Industrial Hemp Research", 7 U.S.C. 5940), authorises state hemp research pilot programmes (state departments of agriculture + universities). (govinfo U.S. Code notes)

Late May 2014; harvest 23 September 2014 — Kentucky's first legal hemp crop in decades [secondary reporting only — no KDA/UK primary release located]: planted late May 2014 at the University of Kentucky Spindletop Farm, Lexington (Fayette County — Lexington KY, not Lexington VA), after a shipment of seed was held at Louisville airport for more than a week (reported as two weeks) and then released; harvested 23 September 2014. Six universities assisted with the 2014 pilot research (contemporaneous reporting) — not "six original pilot participants" overall. (WEKU, 23 Sept 2014; WKYU, 23 May 2014)

20 December 2018 — Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 Farm Bill) signed (Pub. L. 115-334), including McConnell's Hemp Farming Act of 2018: removes hemp (≤0.3% delta-9 THC dry weight) from the federal controlled-substances list and authorises USDA-approved state/tribal plans. Kentucky then moved from pilot to a USDA-approved State Plan (submitted for the 2022 season; operating 1 January 2022 — cite KDA, not the USDA list, for the date). (Federal Register; USDA plan list; KDA orientation)

20 February 2020 — HB 136 (medical cannabis) passes the Kentucky House 65–30 — first time a medical bill was taken up by the full House. It stalled in the Senate. Sponsor: Rep. Jason Nemes (Louisville). (Legislature PIO, 20 Feb 2020) The "first time" characterisation and any COVID-19 session-disruption explanation are secondary glosses, flagged as such.

2021 — Nemes re-files the medical bill for the 2021 session; it does not advance. No chamber passage in 2021 was located [secondary-only; legislature bill-index search for 2021 not completed].

17 March 2022 — HB 136 passes the House again, 59–34 (House Judiciary 15–1 on 10 March 2022 — committee vote secondary-reported). It went to Senate Health & Welfare on 29 March 2022 and died there by session end (15 April 2022). The House and committee votes are consistent across legislature mirrors but were not extracted from a legislature vote sheet in this pass — flag them as mirror-reported; the 2020 vote above is legislature-PIO-confirmed.

14 June 2022 — EO 2022-338 creates the 17-member Team Kentucky Medical Cannabis Advisory Committee; town halls in July 2022; report/feedback summary released 30 September 2022. (OMC Executive Orders page)

15 November 2022 (effective 1 January 2023 — secondary summaries only) — EO 2022-798: "full, complete, and conditional pardon" for possession under KRS 218A.1422 IF AND ONLY IF all conditions are met, including [EO text not opened — secondary summaries only]: lawfully purchased in a US jurisdiction outside Kentucky; written proof of purchase (date, place, physical location); amount legal where purchased and ≤8 ounces; written certification from a Kentucky-licensed healthcare provider of a listed qualifying condition. It did not legalise purchase in Kentucky, did not direct police not to enforce, and did not apply to pre-1 January 2023 possession [same secondary-only flag]. (OMC Executive Orders page — confirms the order, its date and its rescission, but not the condition details.)

15 November 2022 — EO 2022-799 (delta-8 executive order, same day). Governor Beshear issued EO 2022-799 on 15 November 2022, stating that delta-8 is a form of THC, that delta-8 can be derived from cannabidiol (CBD) through further processing, and that products containing delta-8 are sold at retail businesses in Kentucky, and directing CHFS action under KRS 217.125(1) / 902 KAR 45:190 (2023 HB 544 Senate Committee Substitute recitals, legislature.ky.gov). EO 2022-799 does not appear on the OMC Executive Orders page, which lists only six orders. Whether it was formally rescinded or merely superseded by HB 544 / 902 KAR 45:190 remains [Unverified]. The later HDCP regime (902 KAR 45:190, Run 1) now governs adult-use cannabinoids, but whether it formally superseded the 2022 order is likewise [Unverified].

16 March / 30 March / 31 March 2023 — SB 47 passes Senate 26–11 (16 March), passes House 66–33 (30 March), signed by Governor Beshear 31 March 2023 (2023 Ky. Acts ch. 146), "AN ACT relating to medicinal cannabis." (Vote figures consistent across legislature mirrors; a secondary summary giving House "66-32" appears to be a typo against the 66-33 roll call.) Original enrolled summary described it as creating sections of KRS Chapter 218A; the programme was subsequently codified as KRS Chapter 218B. Delayed effectiveness per LRC: licensing portions from 1 July 2024; programme portions from 1 January 2025 (LRC delayed-effective-dates list; SB 47 record). Precision: SB 47 as enacted had delayed portions to 1 January 2025 and portions to 1 July 2024; HB 829 then moved business licensing to July 2024 — SB 47 alone did not move all business licensing to July 2024.

5 October 2023 — EO 2023-600 creates the Team Kentucky Medical Cannabis Workgroup. (OMC Executive Orders page)

January / March 2024 — OMC files programme regulations [not re-verified in this audit]: 10 business regulations in January 2024, 5 patient/caregiver/practitioner regulations in March 2024 (Governor's activity summary); KBML notes 17 regulations filed as of 18 April 2024. Note the unresolved arithmetic: 10 + 5 = 15, not 17 — KBML's 17 may include regulations beyond those two tranches [flagged].

April 2024 — HB 829 (2024) signed (2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195; exact signing date "17 April 2024" appears only in secondary summaries — write "signed April 2024" unless the legislature record is opened): moves the business-licensing timeline forward from 1 January 2025 to July 2024 (application window 1 July–31 August 2024). HB 829 is also the vehicle for the Board pharmacist seat (ch. 195, §2, effective 17 April 2024). (Governor releases)

September 2024 — Governor announces Kentucky's first medical cannabis business licence, to KCA Labs (a hemp testing lab operating in Nicholasville, Jessamine County); OMC had issued 28 total licences as reported 16 December 2024 (not "by November 2024" — the November dating was not established in the releases fetched). KCA's licence category is not printed in the Governor release [flagged]. (Governor, 16 Dec 2024)

28 October 2024 — First lottery drawing: 16 cultivators + 10 processors selected (26 awardees: 10 Tier I, four Tier II, two Tier III cultivators and 10 processors). (Governor, 28 Oct 2024)

25 November 2024 — Second lottery drawing: 36 dispensaries selected. (Governor, 25 Nov 2024)

1 December 2024 — Authorised practitioners may begin issuing valid written certifications; OMC Practitioner Directory opens. (Governor, 16 Dec 2024)

16 December 2024 — Third lottery drawing: 12 dispensaries selected, concluding the initial lottery (48 dispensaries total). (Governor, 16 Dec 2024)

1 January 2025 — KRS Chapter 218B programme effective; medical cannabis lawful for registered qualified patients, designated caregivers and visiting qualified patients within statutory limits. Home grow remains prohibited; smoking remains prohibited (Run 1). KRS 218B.055 (effective 1 January 2025, as amended 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195, §6; created 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 146, §10), (legislature.ky.gov).

2025 — SB 202 (2025 Ky. Acts ch. 82, signed 25 March 2025) establishes the CIB regime (ABC retail/distribution; CHFS manufacturing; ≤5 mg per 12 oz; 21+; package-only in wet territory). House passage 77–17 on 12 March 2025; Senate concurrence 22–13–1 on 13 March 2025 (SB 202 record). The $1.92-per-gallon CIB excise tax from 1 July 2025 is not SB 202 — it is HB 775, 2025 Ky. Acts ch. 98, §20 (see §9.1, Revenue). The SB 202 chapter conflict (ch. 98 vs ch. 82) is closed: both numbers are real, for different bills.

29 May 2025 — EO 2025-335: $25 renewal fee waived in calendar year 2026 for anyone approved for a card in calendar year 2025. (OMC Executive Orders page)

13 December 2025 — First legal in-state medical sale [secondary-only — no Governor/OMC release located]: The Post Dispensary, Beaver Dam (Ohio County, KY — not Ohio the state). The OMC directory "open since 16 January 2026" date for the same dispensary is a separate directory field, not a contradiction of the sale date (Run 1 reconciliation, not re-verified here).

2 June 2026 — EO 2026-318: "clarifying the statutory definition of 'qualifying medical condition'" (OMC page wording). The Governor's official activity stream states: "With the clarification, 15 additional conditions are recognized, including sickle cell anemia, ALS, Crohn's disease, Parkinson's, terminal illness and more" (Governor activity stream). The full 15-condition list is [Unverified on primary sources] (the OMC page gives no list; the Governor stream names only five examples; the EO PDF on governor.ky.gov returned no extractable text in this pass — a fetch failure, not proof the order does not exist). Any claim that legislative leadership challenged whether an executive order can add conditions, and any Board-vs-Workgroup recommendation comparison (including a hepatitis C distinction), rests on secondary coverage and is [Unverified on primary sources] — do not present the EO 2026-318 conditions as settled statutory conditions on that basis. Note the separate OMC proposal (February 2026 letter) to replace the Kentucky Center for Cannabis with the Board of Physicians and Advisors in KRS 218B.145; that is not evidence about EO 2026-318's legal status.

11 June 2026 (effective 1 July 2026) — EO 2026-361 rescinds EO 2022-798. From 1 July 2026, Kentuckians who purchase medical cannabis out of state are no longer eligible for the conditional pardon and "may be subject to law enforcement action" for possession under KRS 218A.1422 (OMC page wording). The OMC page spells the 2022-798 label "RECINDED" [sic]. (OMC Executive Orders page) Any "always planned" rationale is secondary (WEKU, 2 July 2026) and is not stated as a Governor finding here.

12 October / 16 October 2026 — Sunnyside Dispensary, Prestonsburg (Floyd County), opens 12 October 2026 after OMC approval 9 October 2026; Governor announces 16 October 2026 that dispensaries are now open in all 11 licensing regions, with 26 operating dispensary facilities. (Governor, 16 Oct 2026)

Decriminalisation / adult-use bills that passed one chamber — answer: none located. No decriminalisation or adult-use bill was found to have passed either Kentucky chamber in this slice. The only cannabis bills found to have passed a chamber before SB 47 were medical bills: HB 136 in the House in 2020 (65–30) and again in 2022 (59–34), both dying in the Senate. For 2026: HB 401 (conditions/home-grow/smoking), HB 198 (decriminalisation) and HB 199 / SB 168 (constitutional amendments) — no chamber passage located (HB 401 to House Health Services 23 January 2026; HB 198 to House Judiciary 14 January 2026, no votes shown; HB 199 / SB 168 referred to committee and did not advance; SB 168 referral 5 February 2026; HB 199's last legislature action was not retrieved — no committee date is asserted for it). Two 2026 bills did pass one chamber and must not be described as dying in committee without passage: SB 223 (CIB on-premise — bars/restaurants/fairs/festivals) passed the Senate 25–11 on 20 March 2026, then went to the House Committee on Committees; it did not pass the House and did not become law (SB 223 vote sheet; SB 223 record). HB 9 (broader regulated-substances omnibus, including a 4% retail regulatory licence fee — "CIB fees" alone understates it) passed the House 63–31 on 10 March 2026, then stalled in the Senate (floor amendments (1), (2) and (3) filed 14 April 2026; no Senate passage in the record); it did not become law (HB 9 record). An exhaustive chamber-by-chamber search of every decriminalisation/adult-use bill ever filed was not completed in this pass, so the decriminalisation/adult-use statement is "none located", not a proof of a negative.

Executive Orders — what the OMC page actually lists. The OMC Executive Orders page (kymedcan.ky.gov/laws-and-regulations/Pages/Executive-Orders.aspx) lists exactly six entries, in this order, and no delta-8 order: (1) EO 2026-361 (11 June 2026) — rescinds EO 2022-798; (2) EO 2026-318 (2 June 2026) — clarifying "qualifying medical condition"; (3) EO 2025-335 (29 May 2025) — $25 renewal fee waived in 2026; (4) EO 2023-600 (5 October 2023) — Workgroup; (5) "RECINDED: Executive Order 2022-798 (Nov. 15, 2022) / RECINDED: July 1, 2026"; (6) EO 2022-338 (14 June 2022) — Advisory Committee. EO 2022-799 (delta-8) is confirmed from HB 544 recitals (above) despite its absence from this page.

9.3 Ballot history and public opinion polling

Statewide citizen initiative: NO. Kentucky does not provide for initiative or referendum at the state level. The authority is Ky. Const. §256 (Secretary of State constitutional text), which provides only the legislative-referral route (and convention): an amendment agreed to by three-fifths of all members elected to each House is submitted to the voters at the next general election for members of the House of Representatives, and "The approval of the Governor shall not be necessary." Three-fifths is 60 of 100 House members; for 38 Senators, three-fifths is 22.8, so 23 is the first whole number meeting it — the constitution states the fraction, not "60/23". "Even-year" is an effect (House elections are in even years), not wording in §256. Lexington-Fayette's local initiative process (if cited) is a local mechanism, not a statewide one, and the 1900 Senate-passed statewide I&R bill is secondary (Initiative & Referendum Institute) material — neither is verified on primary sources here and neither affects the constitutional conclusion. No statewide cannabis measure has ever reached Kentucky voters by initiative, because the mechanism does not exist.

HB 335 (2025) — initiative proposal, not law. HB 335 would have amended Ky. Const. §29 to reserve initiative power to the people (petition, single subject, filed with the Secretary of State — details from the bill text/fiscal note, not enacted law). Legislature record (apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/hb335.html): "Last Action | 02/07/25: to Elections, Const. Amendments & Intergovernmental Affairs (H)". It never passed and never reached voters.

Polls — read the method warnings before any figure.

Herald-Leader / WKYT Bluegrass Poll (SurveyUSA, January–February 2014, n=1,082 registered voters, ±3 points) — secondary-reported; original SurveyUSA/Herald-Leader release not located. 52% favour, 37% oppose, 12% not sure (medical marijuana in Kentucky). Secondary reports conflict on the field end-date (30 January–3 February vs 30 January–4 February) — flag the conflict; do not pick one. Any age breakdown (highest 18–34, lowest 65+) was not re-verified in this pass — do not cite it without the original release. This is a 2014 poll; do not present it as current opinion.

Foundation for a Healthy Kentucky, Kentucky Health Issues Poll (2019 poll, sponsor release 5 February 2020 — Interact for Health / Foundation for a Healthy Kentucky, conducted by the University of Cincinnati Institute for Policy Research). Sponsor release (Interact for Health; PDF): 90% favour medical cannabis if a doctor recommends; 59% favour allowing adults to buy/use "under any circumstances" (the "60%" figure in a Governor press summary was not found in the sponsor release — use 59%); 49% favour recreational legalisation. Sample/method from secondary reporting of the same poll (1,559 adults surveyed by phone, October–December 2019) — flagged as secondary-reported, since the sponsor release text extracted here does not itself print them. Party breakdowns, 2012 comparisons and the "~4 in 10 know someone who regularly uses" figure were not re-verified against the sponsor release — do not cite them without it; note a further secondary conflict on the 2012 medical figure (sponsor release 78% in 2012 vs one secondary article 76%). No post-2022 scientific Kentucky cannabis poll was located [Unverified whether one exists].

Team Kentucky Medical Cannabis Advisory Committee online feedback + town halls (summer 2022; summary released 30 September 2022) — NOT a scientific poll. Governor release (kymedcan.ky.gov PDF): "the state's medical cannabis website allowed Kentuckians to submit their opinions online. The website received 3,539 comments, 98.64% of which expressed support" and "the advisory committee did not hear any opposition at their town hall meetings" / "Everyone who spoke supported…" — i.e. no one who spoke at the town halls opposed; that is not "zero attendees opposed". "48 opposed" is arithmetic (3,539 − 3,491 = 48) appearing in secondary summaries, not a quotation in the primary release — label it derived. This was a self-selected online straw poll plus town-hall testimony. It must never be cited as "99% of Kentuckians support" — the 99% figure in some headlines is a rounding of this self-selected 98.64%. The Governor's separate statement that "polling suggests 90% of Kentucky adults support" refers to the KHIP scientific poll above, not to this exercise. The number of town-hall meetings (four, as originally cited) was not re-verified here.

2024 local-option referendums. Local-option referendums under KRS 218B.130, not a statewide initiative — they do not contradict §9.3's "no statewide initiative" finding. Headline (Governor-confirmed): on 5 November 2024 (general election), all 106 cities and counties that had medical cannabis on the ballot voted to allow medical cannabis businesses to operate — 53 counties + 53 cities, none failed (Governor, 16 Dec 2024: "On Nov. 7, the Governor announced that all 106 cities and counties that had medical cannabis on the ballot voted to allow medical cannabis businesses to operate"). All percentages and ban counts below are secondary-only (WKYU / Louisville Public Media, 6 November 2024, wkyufm.org) — no Secretary of State or county-clerk certified returns were retrieved in this pass, and no single official statewide table of the 106 certified returns was opened: county voters 67% yes, 341,766 people (the "67%" is ambiguous in the secondary report — aggregate share vs average of county percentages — and must not be presented as SOS-certified); city voters "nearly identical percentage"; largest county margins Marion and Nelson Counties, >75% yes; smallest county margin Hickman County, 54% yes; city examples Bardstown 78%, Shelbyville 72%, Mt. Washington 67%, Florence (Boone County, KY — not Florence SC/AL) 64%; smallest city margin in secondary coverage Union (Boone County), 52% yes — a different universe from the Hickman county figure; both can be true. By ordinance (separate route): "just 20 counties" and "more than 40 cities" had banned by ordinance in the WKYU report; a Governor-summary figure of 21 counties cited in Run 1 was not found in any source in this pass — the 20-vs-21 discrepancy remains unresolved; do not average or reconcile it. Per-jurisdiction certified percentages beyond the examples above remain [VERIFY] against Secretary of State / county-clerk returns. The KRS 218B.130(11) five-day notice rule (notice to the Cabinet within 5 days of passage or certification) is carried as originally cited; the KRS text was not re-opened in this slice.

PART 10 — TRIBAL AND INTERSTATE

10.1 Tribal — explicit finding: NONE

Kentucky has no federally recognised tribe, no state-recognised tribe, and no tribal cannabis or hemp operation located on the lists checked.

Federal recognition. No Kentucky-headquartered tribe appears on the USDA Tribal hemp-plan list checked, and no Kentucky entry was located on the Federal Register list of Indian Entities Recognized and Eligible to Receive Services from the Bureau of Indian Affairs (89 FR 99899, 11 December 2024, 574 entities, Federal Register PDF), published under the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994 (Pub. L. 103-454). The BIA Tribal Leaders Directory is expressly "not an official listing" and must be used with that notice: "The Directory is not an official listing of federally recognized Tribes. It should be used in conjunction with the Federal Register Notice of Indian Entities Recognized… which is the official listing." (BIA directory page) Method limit: this is a checked-list absence, not an exhaustive re-read of all 574 names; a newer Federal Register edition (if issued after 11 December 2024) should be checked before republishing (see §3). Do not import neighbouring states' tribes: the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is a North Carolina tribe, the Cherokee Nation is an Oklahoma tribe, and the Absentee Shawnee Tribe is an Oklahoma tribe — none is a Kentucky tribe, and none operates a Kentucky programme on the lists checked (U.S. Department of Justice tribal list).

State recognition. Kentucky has no state-recognised tribes and no enacted state-recognition process was located. The positive history proves the negative was attempted and failed three times: a state-recognition process bill passed the House in 2009 (09RS HB 63, 82–17 on 11 February 2009), 2010 (10RS HB 90, 59–33 on 21 January 2010) and 2011 (11RS HB 50, 60–37 on 23 February 2011), and died in Senate State & Local Government each time (HB 50: received in Senate 24 February 2011, to State & Local Government 28 February 2011 — last action shown, no Senate floor vote) (HB 50 record; HB 63 record; HB 90 record). A 2024–2026 legislation check for any new recognition process was not completed (see §3).

Kentucky Native American Heritage Commission — heritage body, not a recognition authority. The Commission was established in 1996 (KRS 171.820–171.822) "to recognize and promote Native American contributions and influence in Kentucky's history and culture" (Heritage Council page). It has 17 members: the Tourism, Arts and Heritage Cabinet Secretary or designee, plus 16 Governor-appointed members, eight of whom must be of Native American heritage. Statutory breakdown (KRS 171.820(2), legislature.ky.gov): Secretary/designee + 3 higher-learning + 2 preservation/archaeological + 1 arts + 10 public at large (8 of Native American heritage) = 17. KRS 171.822's duties are to advise, encourage, represent a network, support preservation, and "Recognize and sanction projects" — projects, not tribes. No tribal-recognition power is in the text. The Commission is not a cannabis/hemp regulator. (Older statute text names the Commerce Cabinet; current text names the Tourism, Arts and Heritage Cabinet — use the current name.)

Unrecognised groups — not to be listed as tribes. The Ridgetop Shawnee and the Southern Cherokee Nation of Kentucky (SCNK) are unrecognised groups based in Kentucky [secondary summaries only — legislature/Governor primary sources for the resolutions and proclamations below were not located]. Congratulatory House Joint Resolutions (HJR 15 in 2009 and HJR 16 in 2010, commending the Ridgetop Shawnee's work with elderly/youth and language/heritage preservation) are not recognition: secondary summaries agree the resolutions "Commend the Ridgetop Shawnee Tribe of Indians for their efforts… recognize their work to preserve their native language and heritage" — that commendatory wording must not be rewritten as formal state recognition. Kentucky currently claims no state-recognised tribes and disputes that any government-to-government relationship was established (secondary). An 1893 gubernatorial letter and a 2006 proclamation concerning the SCNK are claimed historic acknowledgements, disputed by the Commonwealth — not current state recognition [secondary]. Members of the public "mistakenly believe" the Ridgetop Shawnee are state-recognised (secondary). The Absentee Shawnee Tribe's Cultural Preservation Department (March 2023) publicly named the Ridgetop Shawnee among groups it identified as recently organised alleged Shawnee bands promoting themselves as the voice of the Shawnee — included here only to show why the distinction matters, not as a finding about any Kentucky operation [secondary].

USDA tribal hemp plans. No Kentucky tribal hemp plan exists, because there is no recognised Kentucky tribe to submit one. Kentucky hemp operates under the Kentucky State Plan (state, not tribal). The USDA state-and-tribal plan inventory (updated 17 February 2026, ams.usda.gov) lists Kentucky as "KY Approved Plan" (state) and lists tribal plans only for tribes in other states (including "Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians | Approved Plan" — a tribal plan, not a Kentucky plan). No tribal hemp producer licence for a Kentucky location was located; caveat: the individual USDA producer-licence register was not separately searched (see §3).

Tribal cannabis/hemp operations in Kentucky: none located, and none should be listed. None was located on the BIA Federal Register list, the USDA State/Tribal plan list, or by a Kentucky tribal-plan route checked. Method limit: OMC/KDA licence rolls were not individually searched for tribal claimants, so this is an absence on the recognition/plan lists, not an exhaustive search of every licensee. If a future search finds a Kentucky-located operation claiming tribal authority, its federal-recognition status and USDA plan status must be verified first — a claim of ancestry or a congratulatory resolution is not authority to operate.

Population note (context only, not recognition). Secondary coverage (Mountain Association) states more than 90,000 Native American and Alaska Native people live in Kentucky, including Cherokee, Shawnee and Chickasaw people. That population figure is definition-unverified: Census QuickFacts gives Kentucky "American Indian and Alaska Native alone" at 0.5% of the population (≈23,000 alone), so a ">90,000" figure, if correct, must use a broader alone-or-in-combination / self-identification definition that was not verified in this pass (Census QuickFacts). It does not create a recognised tribe or a tribal programme. A secondary page claiming "the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is the only federally recognized tribe in the state [Kentucky]" is wrong on its face (the Eastern Band is in North Carolina) and is flagged here as a secondary error, not repeated as fact.

10.2 Interstate issues

The governing Kentucky rule, in one paragraph. A purchase that was legal where it was bought does not become legal in Kentucky merely because it was legal there, except as Kentucky law itself provides. Kentucky law provides exactly one such route for marijuana: the visiting qualified patient route in KRS 218B.055(5) (buy/use in Kentucky on a valid out-of-state card — see below). It provides no route for a Kentucky resident to buy marijuana in another state and bring it home: the conditional pardon that once covered that conduct (EO 2022-798) was rescinded effective 1 July 2026 (EO 2026-361), and OMC now states such cardholders "may be subject to law enforcement action" for possession under KRS 218A.1422. For hemp (as defined in federal and Kentucky law at the time of shipment), interstate shipment is a different regime (see "Hemp shipments" below) — but after 11 December 2026, products that fall outside the new federal hemp definition are no longer federal hemp at all (given federal baseline), whatever Kentucky law says about their in-state sale.

Visiting patients in Kentucky (statutory route — opened directly). KRS 218B.055 (legislature.ky.gov), provides, verbatim in the operative subsections:

"(4) A person shall be eligible to apply for a registry identification card as a visiting qualified patient if he or she is not a resident of Kentucky or has been a resident of Kentucky for less than thirty (30) days, is at least twenty-one (21) years of age, has not been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense, possesses a valid out-of-state registry identification card, and possesses documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition."

"(5) A person with a valid out-of-state registry identification card and documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition may use his or her out-of-state registry identification card for all purposes established in this chapter and shall not be required to apply for or receive a visiting qualified patient registry identification card from the cabinet."

Practical meaning:

  • A visitor 21+ who is a non-resident (or a Kentucky resident of <30 days), has no disqualifying felony, holds a valid out-of-state card, and holds documentation of a Kentucky qualifying medical condition may purchase from a Kentucky licensed dispensary and possess/use in Kentucky without first obtaining a Kentucky visiting-patient card — subsection (5) itself resolves the pre-registration question: no pre-registration is required. Subsection (8) separately sets out what a visiting patient who does apply must submit (name/address/date of birth, copy of out-of-state card, proof of qualifying-condition diagnosis, fee, non-diversion statement); (4) is eligibility to apply, (5) is the exemption from having to apply.
  • The condition must be a Kentucky qualifying condition — an out-of-state diagnosis that is not on Kentucky's list does not qualify on the face of the statute. OMC's application of this point to conditions recognised elsewhere but not in Kentucky, including under EO 2026-318's contested list, is [Unverified — no OMC guidance located].
  • Purchase limit: ≤10-day supply per 8 days for visiting patients (vs ≤30-day per 25 days for registered Kentucky patients). Citation corrected: 915 KAR 1:070 §2(3) (legislature.ky.gov) requires a dispensary to inform the individual that they are not permitted to purchase more than "an uninterrupted ten (10) day supply… during a given eight (8) day period" (statutory supply provision KRS 218B.025); 915 KAR 2:020 (legislature.ky.gov) only defines that 10-day amount: "37.5 grams of raw plant material, 9.5 grams of concentrate, or 1,300 milligrams of THC." Flagged discrepancy — do not smooth over: 915 KAR 1:070 §2(3)(b) as extracted says verify the visitor is "at least eighteen (18) years of age", versus the statute's 21+ in KRS 218B.055(4); the statute governs, and the tension is flagged for OMC clarification.
  • Visiting patients may not smoke [primary-unverified — located only in secondary summaries and a 2025 bill draft in this pass, not in enacted KRS 218B text retrieved]; vaporising products may not be sold/dispensed to a cardholder younger than 21 (KRS 218B.110: a dispensary shall "Not sell or dispense medicinal cannabis products intended for consumption by vaporizing to a cardholder who is younger than twenty-one (21) years of age"); a public-place / public-transport vaping ban is likewise [primary-unverified on the same basis].
  • This route is inbound only: it authorises the visitor's activity in Kentucky. It does not authorise a Kentucky resident to export Kentucky medical cannabis to another state, and it does not authorise transport of marijuana across any state line (federal law prohibits interstate transport of marijuana).
  • It is not the rescinded pardon: the pardon (EO 2022-798) covered Kentucky residents bringing out-of-state purchases into Kentucky; the visiting-patient statute covers non-residents (and <30-day residents) buying in Kentucky. Conflating the two is the single most common interstate error in secondary coverage — do not conflate them.

Hemp shipments.

Federal frame — pinpoint confirmed. 7 CFR §990.63 (eCFR; Cornell LII): "No State or Indian Tribe may prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved under subpart B of this part, under a license issued under subpart C of this part, or under 7 U.S.C. 5940 through the State or territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." No successor provision is needed. It protects lawfully produced hemp only — it does not override KRS 260.8635's ban on >0.3% delta-9 extract movement (below). The Idaho January 2019 seizure anecdote is secondary background, not CFR text.

Kentucky-specific trap — hemp extract >0.3%. KRS 260.8635 (Created 2020 Ky. Acts ch. 1, sec. 2, effective 10 February 2020; text via Justia/LawServer republications, corroborated by 302 KAR 50:031 on the legislature site — the direct legislature statute page was not returned in this pass and should be re-opened for the final edition) prohibits moving or transporting, or aiding/abetting the movement/transport, of hemp extract material with delta-9 THC >0.3%: (a) from outside Kentucky to inside; (b) from inside to outside; or (c) inside Kentucky except as provided in subsection (3). Subsection (3) allows a licensed processor (or its representative) to move such extract directly from one licensed Kentucky processing location to another, with written notice to KDA at least 24 hours in advance (date, origin address, destination address, and other information required by the department). In other words, lawful hemp plant/flower shipment and lawful extract shipment are different questions in Kentucky — do not generalise a "hemp can ship freely" rule to extracts above 0.3% delta-9.

KDA transport paperwork (programme level) — corrected. Processor movements of >0.3% delta-9 extract require the Hemp Concentrate Transport Notification Form at least 24 hours in advance (302 KAR 50:031, legislature.ky.gov). The Production Report is not a transport form — it is a separate, annual grower report. Do not list it as one. The direct kyagr.com form URL and the current KDA forms page were not re-opened in this pass [follow-up — see §3]. Growers must report plantings to USDA-FSA and to KDA before harvest sampling (Run 1 / KDA guidance, not re-verified here).

After 11 December 2026. A shipment that is "hemp" under Kentucky's 0.3% delta-9 plant definition but exceeds the new federal total-THC definition or the 0.4 mg per container cap for finished products is, federally, no longer hemp. Kentucky has no enacted state cushion located in this search, and in any event state law cannot preserve federal hemp status. Shippers should not assume a pre-December federal hemp transport protection survives for such products — [VERIFY] against USDA/DEA guidance issued after 11 December 2026 (a follow-up, since this audit is dated 28 October 2026, before that date).

What can legally be brought INTO Kentucky — summary table.

Item brought into Kentucky Legal? Basis
Marijuana bought legally in another state, by a Kentucky resident, for personal medical use NO (since 1 July 2026). Previously covered only by the conditional pardon (EO 2022-798 — amount, receipt and provider-certification details secondary-only, see §9.2); pardon rescinded by EO 2026-361. Possession is under KRS 218A.1422 (Class B misdemeanour for non-patients, Run 1, not re-verified here). OMC Executive Orders page
Marijuana bought in Kentucky by a visiting qualified patient, then taken OUT of Kentucky NO as a matter of federal law (interstate transport of marijuana), and the destination state's law governs possession there. Kentucky law does not authorise export. KRS 218B.055 — authorises activity in Kentucky only; no export authorisation in KRS 218B was located.
Marijuana possessed in Kentucky by a visiting qualified patient (bought in Kentucky) YES, within KRS 218B.055(5) + 10-day/8-day limit (915 KAR 1:070 §2(3) + 915 KAR 2:020), original-container rules (Run 1, not re-verified here). Smoking ban flagged primary-unverified (see above). KRS 218B.055; 915 KAR 1:070
Lawful hemp (plant/product meeting the applicable federal + Kentucky definition at time of shipment), with required paperwork YES, subject to KRS 260.8635 for extracts >0.3% delta-9 (see above) and to destination-state law. The §990.63 protection covers lawfully produced hemp only. 7 CFR §990.63; KRS 260.8635
Hemp-derived cannabinoid product (e.g. delta-8 gummy, CIB) bought in another state and brought into Kentucky Only if it also complies with Kentucky law: CHFS-registered product, Kentucky labelling/packaging/age rules (21+ for adult-use cannabinoids and CIBs), and — for CIBs — Kentucky's package-only/wet-territory channel. An out-of-state purchase does not exempt the product from Kentucky registration/sale rules, and after 11 December 2026 the federal definition change may remove its federal hemp status regardless of Kentucky sale rules. Product-by-product compliance is [VERIFY] — no blanket "bring it in" rule was located. CHFS HDCP page; 804 KAR 4:400; given federal baseline
A Kentucky patient's medical cannabis taken to another state Governed by destination-state law + federal transport law, not by Kentucky law. Kentucky card status does not travel (see neighbour table). KRS 218B.055

Neighbouring states — current official-rule summaries (for Kentucky residents travelling out, and for visitors coming in). Method warning for the whole table: summaries are for orientation only. Where a row is marked official, the official source is cited; where it is marked secondary, the figure is secondary-reported and must be re-checked with the destination regulator on the travel date. Do not use this table as legal advice for a specific trip — neighbour law changed during 2026 (Ohio SB 56; Virginia budget compromise) and will change again.

Ohio (borders KY on the Ohio River; Cincinnati/Dayton/Covington corridor) [all Ohio items secondary-only — no Ohio Division of Cannabis Control official page was returned in this pass]. Adult-use legal, 21+. Voters approved Issue 2 (7 November 2023; effective 7 December 2023). Adults 21+ may possess/purchase up to 2.5 oz cannabis + 15 g concentrate; home grow 6 plants/adult, 12/residence. Visitors 21+ may buy adult-use with government photo ID; no Ohio residency required for adult-use. Note the purchase/possession distinction in secondary summaries: the daily dispensary limit is described as 2.5 oz flower or 15,000 mg total THC in other products per day — do not merge purchase and possession limits silently. Medical sales are Ohio-registered patients only; Ohio does not accept out-of-state medical cards (dispensary FAQ, Ratio Cannabis — secondary). A Kentucky card therefore buys nothing medical in Ohio (adult-use is the only route for a 21+ Kentuckian). Caution — 2026 change [VERIFY against Ohio Revised Code as amended]: Ohio SB 56 recriminalisation is reported effective March 2026, but secondary sources conflict on the date (19 vs 20 vs 30 March 2026) — do not assert any single date as settled. The substance reported (MPP summary, secondary) is a minor misdemeanour (≤$150) for cannabis obtained anywhere other than from an Ohio retailer or homegrown, with original-packaging / trunk-transport rules and a public smoking/vaping ban. If correct, Ohio-bought product is the only Ohio-protected product in Ohio — and it still has no protection in Kentucky. Adult-use purchase in Ohio is lawful in Ohio; bringing it into Kentucky is not protected in Kentucky after 1 July 2026, and interstate transport is federally prohibited.

Illinois (borders KY at the Ohio/Mississippi confluence; Metropolis, IL is the nearest adult-use market to western KY). Adult-use legal, 21+, since 1 January 2020 (Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, 410 ILCS 705) [start date secondary-only in this pass]. Half-limits confirmed on an official state source: Illinois official FAQ (cannabis.illinois.gov): "Residents can possess up to 30 grams of flower, 500 milligrams of THC-infused products, and 5 grams of concentrate… Out of state people can only have half of those limits. (410 ILCS 705/10-10)." Non-residents 21+ therefore: 15 g flower, 2.5 g concentrate, 250 mg THC in infused products (residents: 30 g / 5 g / 500 mg), cumulative across sources. A 2026 secondary claim that SB 3222 doubled the limits (resident 60 g / 1,000 mg / 10 g) is unverified and contradicted by the official FAQ retrieved, which still shows the old figures — do not adopt doubled limits. No medical reciprocity [secondary-only in this pass]: only Illinois-registered residents may buy medical; a Kentucky card buys nothing medical in Illinois (adult-use is the route for 21+ Kentuckians). Same Kentucky re-entry bar as Ohio. Note the Illinois non-resident cap is a possession cap in Illinois, not just a purchase cap — the FAQ's wording is "possess", so exceeding it in Illinois is itself an offence there.

Missouri (borders KY only via the Mississippi River at the western tip; St. Louis is the nearest large market). Adult-use legal, 21+ (Mo. Const. art. XIV, §2, Amendment 3, passed 8 November 2022) [date secondary-only in this pass]. Adults 21+ may purchase/possess up to 3 oz dried unprocessed marijuana or equivalent in a single transaction, with no separate smaller visitor limit (rule age-based, not residency-based) [secondary-only]. Public smoking: civil penalty ≤$100 [secondary-only]. Home grow requires a DHSS cultivation card (6 flowering + 6 non-flowering + 6 clones) [secondary-only]. Medical reciprocity — conflict resolved in favour of purchase. Missouri Constitution art. XIV, §1.5(1) (FindLaw text): production of a substantially equivalent identification card or authorisation issued by another state "shall also meet the requirements of this subdivision and shall allow for the purchase of medical marijuana for use by a non-resident patient from a medical marijuana dispensary facility". Missouri DHSS guidance (27 January 2023, health.mo.gov PDF): "Out-of-state patients with an active medical marijuana patient card issued from another state may utilize their card to purchase marijuana at a Missouri medical or comprehensive licensed dispensary facility beginning February 3, 2023. Dispensaries must verify, if possible, the validity of the out-of-state card when presented at point-of-sale, and must require a valid government issued photo ID for further verification." A Kentucky card can therefore buy medical cannabis in Missouri (valid card + government photo ID; under-18 rules differ — a parent/guardian must purchase; growing is not covered by the purchase right). Adult-use is available to 21+ Kentuckians regardless. Same Kentucky re-entry bar. Missouri medical patients' standard limit is 6 oz per 30 days [secondary-only] — that limit does not travel to Kentucky; Kentucky's 10-day/8-day visiting-patient limit governs in Kentucky.

Michigan (no land border with KY; nearest via Ohio/Indiana transit — included because Kentuckians commonly travel there). Adult-use legal, 21+. Up to 2.5 oz flower per transaction (≤15 g of that as concentrate), 10 oz at home (amounts >2.5 oz at home in a locked container); same limits for residents and visitors with photo ID 21+ [secondary-only in this pass — cited in secondary summaries to Mich. Admin. Code R 420.506(3); no CRA official page verified here]. Medical reciprocity — condition corrected. MCL 333.26424(j) (Justia text): "A registry identification card, or its equivalent, that is issued under the laws of another state… that allows the medical use of marihuana by a visiting qualifying patient… shall have the same force and effect as a registry identification card issued by the department." No "home state must offer reciprocity" condition appears in that text, so Kentucky's visiting-patient statute (KRS 218B.055(5)) is not needed to satisfy such a condition. What remains flagged is a different question: whether a Michigan provisioning centre must sell to a visitor (sale right) as opposed to the visitor holding possession protection — secondary sources contest this (CRA FAQ summaries describe card + photo ID checks; other summaries describe dispensary discretion). Do not promise a Kentucky cardholder a Michigan medical purchase. Adult-use is available regardless (21+). Same Kentucky re-entry bar.

Virginia (borders KY in the east; Richmond VA is NOT Richmond KY, Madison County). Possession legal; adult-use retail sales were NOT operational as of October 2026. Adults 21+ may possess in public up to 2 oz (Virginia CCA Laws page, official regulator, cca.virginia.gov/laws) — 1 oz was the pre-2026-framework text (General Assembly Division of Legislative Services study, 17 August 2026, GA study PDF: "Possession on person / in public: up to 2 ounces (§ 4.1-1100) → increase from one ounce"); >2–4 oz in public: $25 civil fine (CCA). Home cultivation 4 plants per household (§4.1-1101, GA study). Adult-sharing: private transfer of 2 oz or less between people 21+ without exchanging anything else of value (CCA) — corrected from the original's ≤1 oz. There is no licensed adult-use retail store to buy from in October 2026. Retail history, reconciled (not a contradiction): the standalone retail bills (HB 642 / SB 542) were vetoed 19 May 2026 by Governor Spanberger [veto date secondary-reported; no LIS veto page returned — flag it]; a budget compromise signed 30 June 2026 then set adult-use retail sales from 1 July 2027 [budget chapter (HB 30) to be verified against LIS — see §3]. The veto killed the standalone bill; the budget deal created the 2027 date. Medical programme active via licensed pharmaceutical processors/dispensing facilities, on practitioner certification [secondary-reported as such]; Virginia law does not require patients to register — registration is only for adding a registered agent, and certification is the primary document (CCA FAQ, cca.virginia.gov/faq) — replace the original's "registry discontinued July 2022" framing with this CCA position. No Virginia acceptance of out-of-state medical cards — CCA-confirmed: CCA FAQ states "Licensed dispensaries in Virginia cannot accept out-of-state medical cards." A Kentucky card therefore does not buy medical cannabis in Virginia. A Kentuckian cannot lawfully buy adult-use cannabis in Virginia at all (no retail channel), so the re-entry question for Virginia is moot for retail purchases; any Virginia-possessed marijuana brought into Kentucky faces the same Kentucky bar.

West Virginia (borders KY in the east; the other medical-only neighbour). Adult-use illegal [secondary-only — no WV OMC official page verified here]. No adult-use purchase route for a Kentuckian in West Virginia. No out-of-state medical cards accepted for purchase [secondary-only]: WV OMC requires a WV card ("only registered patients and their designated caregivers with a valid medical marijuana card from the OMC can legally buy cannabis. No exceptions" — secondary consensus). A narrow statutory authority for reciprocity agreements exists: W. Va. Code §16A-3-5 (not §16A-2-1, which is definitions) authorises the Bureau of Public Health, Office of Medical Cannabis "to enter into interstate reciprocity agreements to allow terminally ill cancer patients to purchase medical cannabis in another state" (as cited in Daniels, W. Va. Intermediate Court of Appeals, FindLaw). No such agreement is currently in place [secondary — Drug Policy Watch, July 2026 brief]. Reverse direction matters more: a West Virginia cardholder visiting Kentucky can use the Kentucky visiting-patient route (KRS 218B.055(5)) — West Virginia's non-recognition does not block Kentucky's inbound route. A Kentuckian cannot lawfully buy medical cannabis in West Virginia on a Kentucky card; any product obtained there and brought into Kentucky faces the same Kentucky bar (and, since 1 July 2026, no pardon).

Interstate laws or agreements — answer. No interstate cannabis compact, reciprocity agreement, or transport agreement involving Kentucky was located in this pass. Specifically: no Kentucky–Ohio, Kentucky–Illinois, Kentucky–Missouri, Kentucky–Michigan, Kentucky–Virginia or Kentucky–West Virginia cannabis reciprocity agreement; no Kentucky interstate hemp compact; and no Kentucky agreement with USDA or another state that would authorise interstate marijuana shipment. The only interstate mechanisms found are (a) the federal hemp-transport protection (7 CFR §990.63, above), (b) Kentucky's unilateral visiting-patient statute (KRS 218B.055(5) — unilateral recognition, not a compact or agreement), and (c) other states' unilateral visitor rules summarised in the neighbour table. Method limit: no NCSL interstate-compact index or Kentucky LRC compact-list page was returned in this pass, so this is not an exhaustive compact-database search — do not present it as exhaustively proven non-existence [see §3]. If a future search locates a West Virginia terminal-cancer reciprocity agreement (authority §16A-3-5 above) or any other Kentucky instrument, it must be added here with its instrument and date. The "Michigan–Kentucky understanding" hypothetical in the original is moot in the form stated, since Michigan's statute text retrieved imposes no home-state-reciprocity condition (see Michigan row) — any claimed understanding would still need an instrument and date.

Consistency note vs Run 1 (rewritten). No Run 1 headline figure within Parts 9–10's own scope is changed except as listed in §1. Licence counts (48/16/10/5, 79 vs "80"), operating counts (26/46, October 2026), patient/practitioner trajectory and the opt-out deadline are Parts 3–6 territory and were not re-audited in this slice — they are not presented as audit-confirmed here. Changes within this slice: (1) Board: ten-member composition confirmed; pharmacist seat origin resolved to HB 829 / 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195; page still lists nine names, vacancy still unlabelled. (2) November 2024 margins: Hickman County 54% (smallest county margin) vs Union (Boone County) 52% (smallest city margin in secondary coverage) are different universes, not a conflict — but both figures are secondary-only (no SOS/clerk certified returns retrieved). (3) County ordinance opt-outs: 20 (WKYU) vs 21 (Governor summary cited in Run 1) — unresolved, and the "21" figure was not found in any source in this pass. (4) Missouri medical reciprocity and Virginia possession/retail status are no longer preserved conflicts: Missouri medical purchase is resolved in favour of acceptance; Virginia possession is resolved to 2 oz current / 1 oz prior text, and veto-vs-2027 is resolved as standalone veto + budget compromise (veto date and budget chapter still secondary-flagged). (5) SB 202 chapter is closed (ch. 82; CIB tax is HB 775 / ch. 98); EO 2022-799 number is confirmed, its rescission/supersession still open. (6) First-sale date (13 December 2025) now carries a secondary-only flag. (7) EO 2026-318 count corrected to 15 additional conditions (full list still Unverified). (8) The secondary page's claim that the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is "the only federally recognized tribe in [Kentucky]" is incorrect and is not carried forward.

Part 11 and Part 12

Last audited 28 October 2026. Federal baseline applied as given: state-licensed medical marijuana is Schedule III and all other marijuana is Schedule I under 91 FR 22714 effective 28 April 2026; 280E relief applies to medical licensees only; hemp under PL 119-37 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 limits it until 11 December 2026 to the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized, and the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026; USDA DEA-registered-lab enforcement is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026; no federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. No statement below applies Schedule III or 280E relief to non-medical activity.

PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

11.1 Testing

(A) Medical licensees — 915 KAR 1:110 (Medicinal cannabis testing) and 915 KAR 1:060 (Safety compliance facility). To ensure suitability and safety for human consumption, cultivators, processors, and producers shall test medicinal cannabis in accordance with Section 2 of 915 KAR 1:110. (Source) No laboratory may test medicinal cannabis under that regulation without being issued a licence to operate as a safety compliance facility, and a safety compliance facility shall only send samples for testing to another licensed safety compliance facility in the Commonwealth. (Source)

Batch sizes (915 KAR 1:110 §1). Harvest batches shall not exceed 20 pounds, except raw plant material to be sold to a processor or producer for concentrate, which may be separated into harvest batches of no more than 50 pounds. (Source) Production batches shall not exceed 5 litres of liquid medicinal cannabis concentrate or 9 pounds for non-liquid products, and for final products no greater than 1,000 grams of delta-9 THC. (Source) The same 20-pound / 5-litre figures appear in the Office of Medical Cannabis February 2025 cultivator training. (Source)

Sampling and frequency. An authorised employee or agent collecting samples shall follow the standard operating procedures established by the contracted safety compliance facility for sampling and chain of custody. (Source) Harvest-batch samples shall be obtained and tested post-harvest and prior to sale, transfer, or delivery from that batch; production-batch samples shall be obtained and tested in their final form prepackaging and prior to sale, transfer, or delivery. (Source) Cultivators and producers shall not sell, transfer, or deliver medicinal cannabis from a harvest batch, and processors and producers shall not sell, transfer, or deliver from a production batch, until a sample has passed all tests required by Section 2; dispensaries shall not dispense or sell medicinal cannabis until a sample of its harvest or production batch has passed all required tests. (Source) After sample collection, medicinal cannabis shall not undergo additional processing, transforming, or other changes altering its substance or test results without retesting as required by Section 2 before sale, transfer, or delivery. (Source)

Required tests — finished products for sale to cardholders (915 KAR 1:110 §2(1)). Finished medicinal cannabis products intended for sale by dispensaries to cardholders shall be tested for: (a) tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabinoid concentration; (b) terpenoid type and concentration; (c) residual solvents and processing chemicals (for production batches); (d) residual pesticides; (e) heavy metals; (f) microbial impurities; (g) mycotoxins; (h) water activity (for harvest batches); (i) yeast and mold; and (j) vitamin E acetate. (Source) The Cabinet may conduct additional tests on samples or test samples at its discretion. (Source)

Reduced panels for non-finished transfers. For harvest batches of raw plant material not intended for sale to cardholders in its current form, before sale or transfer to another licensed cannabis business: residual pesticides and THC/cannabinoid concentration. (Source) For production batches of non-finished products not intended for sale to cardholders in current form, before sale or transfer: residual solvents and processing chemicals, heavy metals, and THC/cannabinoid concentration. (Source) Batches passing those items need not be retested for those items in final form if not physically or chemically altered after the prior sale or transfer. (Source)

Cannabinoid / terpenoid detail (§3). Cannabinoid testing shall include: total THC; total CBD; total cannabinoids; THCa; delta-9 THC; delta-8 THC; CBDA; CBD; CBN; CBGa; CBG; THCV; CBC. (Source) Terpenoid testing shall establish the percentage of total terpenes and the most prevalent terpenes expressed in the sample. (Source) Cultivators and producers shall also track the terpene content of the 12 major terpenoids within each strain cultivated and provide a written summary to the Cabinet on request, under KRS 218B.140(1)(c)(9).
