(Source)

Maximum allowable limits (§3, selected). Heavy metals — inhaled products: arsenic 0.2 ppm, cadmium 0.2 ppm, lead 0.5 ppm, mercury 0.1 ppm. (Source) Non-inhaled: arsenic 0.4 ppm, cadmium 0.4 ppm, lead 1 ppm, mercury 1.2 ppm. (Source) Microbial pass: total E. coli not detected above 100 CFU/g; Shiga toxin–producing E. coli not detected in 1 g; Salmonella spp. not detected in 1 g; pathogenic Aspergillus (A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. niger, A. terreus) not detected in 1 g. (Source) Mycotoxins: total aflatoxin B1+B2+G1+G2 ≤20 µg/kg; ochratoxin A ≤20 µg/kg. (Source) Water activity (harvest batches): aw <0.65. (Source) Yeast and mold combined: ≤10,000 CFU/g. (Source) Vitamin E acetate: production batches shall be tested for any detectable level. (Source) Residual solvents and processing chemicals shall not exceed the maxima in Appendix A, and residual pesticides shall not exceed the maxima in Appendix B, each incorporated by reference and dated 4 January 2024; the appendices may be inspected, copied, or obtained at the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, Office of the Secretary, 275 East Main Street, Frankfort, Kentucky 40621, and may also be viewed on the Kentucky Medical Cannabis Program website. (Source) No pinpoint solvent or pesticide limit is stated in this report because the appendices were not opened as readable text in this audit [VERIFY if a pinpoint limit is needed]. (Source)

Failed tests, reanalysis, remediation (§§4–5). A batch failing initial testing may be reanalyzed by the safety compliance facility using the reserve sample. (Source) A batch fails if it exceeds any §3 limit or the KRS Chapter 218B delta-9 cap, on initial test (no reanalysis requested) or on reanalysis. (Source) If a batch fails a test or reanalysis, it may be remediated or sterilised if allowed by Section 5, or if it cannot be remediated or sterilised under Section 5 it shall be deemed medicinal cannabis waste and destroyed by the cultivator, processor, or producer under 915 KAR 1:030 or 1:040 as applicable. (Source) Failed batches shall not be combined with another harvest or production batch; mixed products shall be considered adulterated and shall not be sold, transferred, or otherwise delivered. (Source) Remediation, where allowed, by category: THC over-limit harvest batch — deemed waste, destroyed per 915 KAR 1:030, no remediation. (Source) THC over-limit production batch — may be remediated to reduce THC to allowable levels if the method imparts no toxic or deleterious substance, then resampled and retested, with prior failure and all methods and solvents disclosed to the retesting facility; if not remediated or remediation fails, deemed waste per 915 KAR 1:040. (Source) Residual solvents — same remediate-and-retest pattern; unremediated or still-failing = waste per 915 KAR 1:040. (Source) Microbial failure — may be further processed only if the method effectively sterilises the batch without imparting a toxic or deleterious substance, then resampled and retested with disclosure; failure after sterilisation = waste. (Source) Residual pesticides, heavy metals, mycotoxins, yeast/mold, and vitamin E acetate failures — deemed waste, destroyed per 915 KAR 1:030 or 1:040 as applicable, no remediation route stated. (Source) Water-activity failure (harvest only) — may be further dried and cured, then resampled and retested. (Source) Cap: where remediation is allowed, a harvest or production batch shall only be remediated twice; if it fails testing after a second remediation attempt and second retesting, it shall be deemed medicinal cannabis waste. (Source) Before any remediation, the business shall create and maintain detailed written remediation procedures (provided to the Cabinet within 3 business days on request or at inspection) and document all remediation, sterilisation, resampling, retesting, and disposal. (Source)

Certificate of analysis (COA) (§6). Each safety compliance facility shall generate a COA for each batch sample analysed, containing at minimum: facility name, address, and licence number; cultivator/processor/producer name, address, and licence number; batch number; sample identifiers including matrix type; sample history (dates collected, received, analysed, with results); analytical methods, instrumentation, LOD and LOQ; attestation by an authorised employee that all §2 testing was performed; and any unknown, unidentified, or injurious analytes detected. (Source) Results are reported as overall "pass" or "fail" for the whole batch; qualitative analytes "pass"/"fail"; below-LOQ shown as "<LOQ" (except cannabinoid/terpenoid results); not detected or below LOD shown as "ND"; not performed shown as "NT". (Source) Reserve sample: retained ≥45 calendar days after analyses, securely stored, provided to the Cabinet within 3 business days on request, then destroyed as waste per 915 KAR 1:060. (Source) All COAs shall be documented in the Commonwealth's designated electronic monitoring system and seed-to-sale tracking system. (Source) Cultivators, processors, and producers shall publish or link COAs on their informational websites (per 915 KAR 1:090 §2) so cardholders can easily reach the COA for the batch on the product label. (Source)

Cabinet spot testing and disposal of failures (§1). The Cabinet may select and collect a sample or test sample from a cannabis business at any time, and may require a business to submit a sample at its own expense where the Cabinet has reason to believe product is unsafe or untested. (Source) Except as authorised in Section 5, cannabis businesses shall properly dispose of and shall not use, sell, or otherwise transfer medicinal cannabis that fails to meet any testing standard, with disposal per 915 KAR 1:030, 1:040, 1:060, and 1:070 as applicable. (Source)

Recalls / adverse events — what exists and what does not. Every licensee's standard operating procedures must include "Adverse event reporting and recall" (915 KAR 1:020 §4(1); same SOP list in 915 KAR 1:010). (Source) No standalone Kentucky recall regulation, recall-notice template, or published recall list was located in this audit, and no OMC recall in 2025–2026 was identified in the sources opened — the recall mechanism is therefore SOP-based plus the Cabinet's inspection, suspension, and revocation powers (KRS 218B.100) and the failed-batch destruction duty above. (Source) The detailed recall timeline, notification list, and return procedure are [VERIFY] against OMC enforcement/compliance training and any Cabinet recall guidance, if a step-by-step recall playbook is needed. (Source)

Licensed safety compliance facilities. There is no separate "accredited lab" licence in Kentucky: the licence is the safety compliance facility licence, and testing may only be done by a licensed safety compliance facility (915 KAR 1:110 §1). (Source) The Cabinet shall post a list of licensed safety compliance facilities on kymedcan.ky.gov (915 KAR 1:060 §1). (Source) The OMC licensee page, updated 14 October 2026, lists 5 facilities and states that a licensee approved to operate is indicated with "*******" following its name. (Source) On that page the approved-to-operate safety facilities are KCA Laboratories LLC (DBA KCA Labs, Fayette County) and Aquatic Laboratories LLC (DBA Cannabusiness Laboratories, Fayette County). (Source) The other three listed facilities are STATE38 LLC (DBA STATE38, Graves County; initially licensed in Marshall County, location changed 5 February 2025), COMMONWEALTH ANALYTICS (Barren County; location change within Barren County 4 April 2025), and Commonwealth Cannabis LLC (DBA Commonwealth Cannabis, Marshall County), none of which carries the approved-to-operate stars on the 14 October 2026 page. (Source) Recheck the stars at republication, because approval status changes; do not publish a "6 facilities" figure — the OMC page lists 5.

Director qualifications (915 KAR 1:060 §1(3)). A facility shall employ at least one director to oversee testing, holding (a) a doctorate in chemistry, biology, or a subdiscipline, or (b) a master's in a chemical or biological science plus at least 2 years post-degree laboratory-testing experience for medicinal or pharmaceutical products, or (c) a bachelor's in a biological science plus at least 4 years such experience. (Source) Independence: a principal officer, board member, employee, volunteer, or agent of a cultivator, processor, producer, or dispensary shall not be employed by or affiliated with a safety compliance facility that has a contract with that respective cannabis business. (Source) A facility licence is valid only for the specific site on the licence. (Source) Before testing for a business, the facility shall enter a written contract with that business and provide a copy to the Cabinet within 2 business days of a request. (Source)

Accreditation. A safety compliance facility shall maintain a certificate of accreditation in good standing from an accreditation body and provide a copy to the Cabinet during subsequent inspections or on request; the certificate shall attest to the facility's competence to perform testing, including all required analytes for the relevant test methods, and shall be obtained before collecting, receiving, or testing any sample. (Source) Whether that accreditation is ISO 17025, and the content of OMC Technical Advisory 2025-002 (3 February 2025) on determining and documenting measurement uncertainty and reporting it on COAs, are [VERIFY] against the advisory itself before quoting an ISO 17025 pinpoint as regulation text; the ISO account in the original report rests on a secondary summary of the advisory. (Source)

(B) Hemp / hemp-derived product businesses. Crop (pre-harvest) testing — KDA, 302 KAR 50:056. This is a lot system, not a batch system: "Lot" means a contiguous area in a field, greenhouse, or indoor growing structure containing the same variety or strain of hemp throughout. (Source) A hemp plant shall not be harvested from any lot before a department inspector completes an inspection and sample-collection visit. (Source) The grower submits a Harvest Report at least 15 days before the expected harvest date; the department then schedules the visit no later than the expected harvest date; the grower or authorised representative shall be present and give complete and unrestricted access to all hemp and cannabis plants, land, buildings, structures, and all licensed locations. (Source) The inspector verifies GPS coordinates and looks for unauthorised pre-visit harvest. (Source) The department shall notify the grower of THC results and commerce eligibility not later than 60 days after the inspection and sample visit. (Source) Compliance is judged against the Acceptable Hemp THC Level = 0.300% delta-9 THC dry weight plus the statewide Measurement of Uncertainty (the greater of the designated laboratories' uncertainties). (Source) A sample not exceeding that level is compliant; exceeding it is non-compliant. (Source) Testing procedure is that of the University of Kentucky Division of Regulatory Services. (Source) Kentucky operates under a USDA-approved State Plan (Kentucky began operating under an approved State Plan 1 January 2022; all 302 KAR 50 regulations are incorporated into the plan), and Kentucky appears as "KY Approved Plan" on the USDA list updated 17 February 2026 — growers are licensed by the Kentucky Department of Agriculture, not directly by USDA. (Source) (Source)

Post-harvest retest / remediation (302 KAR 50:056 §§6–7). Within 7 days of notice of a result exceeding the Acceptable Level but less than 1.000%, the grower shall consent to destruction of all cannabis from that lot or request remediation and a post-harvest retest (fee per 302 KAR 50:060). (Source) Samples at 1.000% or greater are not eligible for post-harvest retest and shall be destroyed; refusal to comply with a destruction order exposes the licensee to suspension or revocation under 302 KAR 50:021 or 50:031. (Source) Samples at 3.000% or greater are grounds for suspension or revocation proceedings under 302 KAR 50:021. (Source) The retest sample is collected on a department-determined date, selected by the inspector (not the grower). (Source) A post-harvest sample exceeding the Acceptable Level is non-compliant and designated for disposal (see §11.5(B)). (Source)

DEA-registered lab point [VERIFY — federal baseline interaction]. Under the given federal baseline, USDA enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement is delayed until 31 December 2026, so no Kentucky consequence follows from that requirement alone before 1 January 2027. (Source) Whether the Kentucky Department of Agriculture's designated laboratories (University of Kentucky Division of Regulatory Services and others) are DEA-registered, and what changes for Kentucky growers on 1 January 2027, was not confirmed from a Kentucky Department of Agriculture source in this audit [VERIFY on kyagr.com before advising a grower]. (Source)

Hemp-derived cannabinoid (HDCP) product testing — CHFS, 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190. Retail products shall be from an approved source, packaged and labelled per 902 KAR 45:190, and have a valid certificate of analysis available upon request. (Source) Labelled potency shall accurately reflect testing results and shall not contain less than 80 percent or more than 120 percent of the concentration of total cannabinoid content as listed on the product label. (Source) Potency labelling: ingestible and inhalable products — mg per serving for total THC and the primary cannabinoid marketed, and mg per package for total THC and primary cannabinoids marketed; other cannabinoids, if listed, in mg/g per serving (excluding cosmetics) and mg per package. (Source) All products shall include the common cannabinoid description in the product name (for example "Delta-8 THC gummies", "Full-spectrum CBD extract") in the same or larger font than the product name. (Source) The adult-use warning set (21+, health risks, pregnancy and nursing, delayed effects of at least 2 hours, drowsiness and impairment — do not drive or operate machinery, positive drug screen) applies, with a QR-code option labelled "Warning Statements". (Source)

What was not located for (B). A CHFS analogue of 915 KAR 1:110 — a published panel (pesticides, heavy metals, microbials, solvents) with numeric limits for finished HDCPs, a sampling frequency, a reserve-sample rule, or a failed-test remediation rule — was not found in the 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190 text opened in this audit [UNAVAILABLE / VERIFY]. (Source) Do not import the medical panel into hemp products. Likewise no CHFS published list of "accredited" HDCP testing labs was located; the requirement found is a valid COA available on request. (Source) CIB (hemp beverage) testing: no separate ABC testing panel was located in this audit; CIBs sit under ABC licensing and the CHFS HDCP framework to the extent the product is an HDCP — the exact testing and COA route for a CIB is [VERIFY] against ABC and CHFS guidance before advising a beverage maker. (Source)

11.2 Licence rules

(A) Medical licensees. Term. A licence is valid for one (1) year from the date of issuance as shown on the licence (915 KAR 1:020 §1; KRS 218B.080(5)(a)). (Source) Renewal trigger. The Cabinet shall notify each licensee ninety (90) days prior to the date the licence expires to allow the licensee to begin the renewal process (KRS 218B.080(5)(a)). (Source) Renewal shall be contingent upon successful achievement of minimal performance standards established by the Cabinet as part of the biennial accreditation process (KRS 218B.080(5)(b)) — the current renewal application form, fee-payment deadline, and any grace period were not located in this audit [VERIFY on kymedcan.ky.gov Forms page], and the content of the minimal-performance standards was not located. (Source) Renewal fees (current 915 KAR 1:020). Tier I $12,000; Tier II $25,000; Tier III $50,000; Tier IV $100,000; Processor $25,000; Producer $25,000 plus the applicable cultivator tier fee; Dispensary $30,000; Safety compliance $12,000. (Source) Initial fees are the same schedule. (Source) The old $15,000 processor, producer, and dispensary renewal figures are superseded — do not publish them as current. (Source) The initial fee must be paid within 15 calendar days of invoice or no licence issues (915 KAR 1:020 §2). (Source) The effective date of the fee amendment was not extracted in this audit; read the 915 KAR 1:020 history line at republication if the date is needed. (Source)

One licence per location. A cannabis business shall be required to apply for and obtain a separate licence for each location (KRS 218B.080(4)(a)), except a producer may operate cultivation and processing at separate locations but shall not operate more than one (1) cultivation and one (1) processing facility per licence (§4(b)). (Source) A licence is valid only for the person or entity named and only for the activity and location specified (915 KAR 1:020 §1); no licence for a personal residence or a site where the Cabinet or law enforcement have limited access, or on United States or Commonwealth land (§1). (Source)

Sale / transfer of a licence. The Cabinet shall approve a licence holder's sale of a licence if the purchaser and any new facilities meet the requirements of Chapter 218B (KRS 218B.080(6)). (Source) Under 915 KAR 1:020 §10, a written sale-approval request shall include the sale price, reason or reasons, all initial-application information and documentation for the purchaser showing lottery eligibility, signed purchaser attestations, a transition plan, and a notarised purchaser affidavit (false statements punishable under KRS 523.100). (Source) The Cabinet shall deny a sale to a proposed purchaser who currently holds a licence in a different cannabis business category than the one offered (for example a Tier I cultivator buying a dispensary licence), except a cultivator may sell to another licensed cultivator in the same or a different tier. (Source) Cultivators may hold licences in more than one tier at a time if each licence has a separate and distinct physical address and the licensee is otherwise compliant. (Source) The live OMC licensee page corroborates §10 transfers in practice, recording multiple OMC-approved sales and transfers under KRS 218B.080(6) and 915 KAR 1:020 §10. (Source) Any §10 transfer fee or further condition beyond the contents and denial rule above is [VERIFY] against the current 1:020 §10 full text. (Source)

Change of ownership (not a sale). Under 915 KAR 1:020 §8, if there is a pending change in ownership from the ownership in the initial application, the licensee shall submit a written request for approval by email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov; the Cabinet considers KRS Chapter 218B and 915 KAR Chapter 1 ownership requirements and any other relevant factors, and notifies approval or denial in writing. (Source) For each new individual or entity, include the information required of owners in the initial application, plus names of all outgoing owners. (Source) If the Cabinet finds the request lacking, it notifies the licensee in writing; the licensee has 15 calendar days from the mailing date to supply the missing information or documentation, failing which denial is a ground. (Source)

Ownership caps / cross-category bar. No numeric statewide ownership cap (for example "no more than X licences") was located. (Source) The operative caps are structural: (1) the cross-category sale denial above; (2) the safety-facility independence bar (915 KAR 1:060 §1(4) and 915 KAR 1:010 — a safety-facility principal or board member shall not be a principal or board member of a cultivator, processor, producer, or dispensary applicant, and vice versa); (3) a cannabis business shall not employ, have as a board member, or be owned by, in part or in whole, a medicinal cannabis practitioner (KRS 218B.095(2)(e)); (4) dispensary geography (no more than 1 per non-urban or consolidated county; at least 4 per region, at least 6 in urban or consolidated regions — 915 KAR 1:020 §3). (Source) A general "one licence per person" cap is [UNAVAILABLE] — do not assert one. (Source) The "one-category rule" for applicants in the initial period is an application-period rule, not a perpetual ownership cap; the sale and transfer rules above govern post-licensure accumulation, subject to the cross-category denial. (Source)

Relocation. Under 915 KAR 1:020 §9, a licensee desiring to change a site or facility location shall submit a written request for approval by email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov; no change unless the Cabinet approves in writing. (Source) The Cabinet considers KRS Chapter 218B and 915 KAR Chapter 1 location requirements and other relevant factors. (Source) For dispensaries, the Office of Medical Cannabis will not approve a change of location outside the boundaries of the medical cannabis region for which the licence was issued or otherwise not in compliance with the location restrictions in 915 KAR 1:020 §3(3). (Source) Separately, a dispensary shall not change its retail location to another location within the same region without prior Cabinet approval and shall not change its retail location to outside the region where it was initially licensed (915 KAR 1:020 §3). (Source) Provisional / opt-out relocation: a lottery selectee needing to move because a local government prohibited all cannabis business operations (KRS 218B.130) may receive a provisional licence on timely fee payment, with a maximum 120 calendar days to request a change to an allowable county or city; failure to request, or denial, equals revocation of the provisional licence, fee not refunded; a provisional licence shall not be sold or transferred and authorises no business activities. (Source) A licensee in an affected territory shall notify the Cabinet in writing by email within 24 hours of notification or discovery of a prohibition. (Source)

New licences / quarterly review. Beginning 1 January 2025, the Cabinet shall, on a quarterly basis, review the need for issuance of new licences in each cannabis business category, considering population, active cardholders, condition-list changes, market supply and demand, geographic distribution, workforce development, and other relevant factors; if need is found, it shall issue a notice documenting the basis and factors considered (915 KAR 1:020 §11). (Source) No future window, Tier IV offering, or producer offering announcement was located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source)

Surrender / closure. Under 915 KAR 1:020 (Closure section), a licensee shall not remove or destroy any seeds, seedlings, tissue cultures, clones, medicinal cannabis plants, medicinal cannabis, other plant matter, medicinal cannabis products, equipment, medicinal cannabis accessories, or medicinal devices or instruments until the Cabinet has approved its plan for closing the location, and shall comply with 915 KAR Chapter 1 disposal requirements. (Source) The Cabinet may enter and inspect after receiving the closure plan; if it denies the plan, it notifies the licensee in writing and requires a revised plan within 7 calendar days of denial; the Cabinet decides the revised plan within 7 calendar days of receipt. (Source) If approved, the licensee shall surrender its licence for the closing location to the Cabinet on or before the date for closure provided in the plan. (Source) Note: the original report cites this as §7; surrounding sections have been renumbered in current markup, so confirm the section number at republication if a pinpoint is needed. (Source)

Failure to be operational. Under 915 KAR 1:020 §6, if a licensee has not met the timeline estimates provided in its initial licence application to begin cannabis business activities, the licensee shall notify the Cabinet by email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov within 2 calendar days of determining a need to adjust its timeline, identifying any operational deficiencies and explaining the failure to adhere to its timeline estimates. (Source) Within 7 calendar days of providing that notice, the licensee shall submit a corrective action plan setting forth an updated timeline and a date certain for correcting the deficiencies. (Source) If the licensee fails to comply with its corrective action plan, the Cabinet may impose penalties or sanctions as outlined in Section 12 of the regulation. (Source) There is no single fixed "become operational by X" deadline in §6; the duty is notice plus corrective plan. (Source)

Suspension / revocation. Cannabis businesses are subject to reasonable Cabinet inspection under KRS 218B.100; suspension, revocation, fine, or other penalty requires notice by certified mail to the licence address; the business may, within 30 days after mailing, file a written request for an administrative hearing under KRS Chapter 13B; final orders are subject to judicial review in the Circuit Court of the county where the business is physically located. (Source) During suspension: a cultivator may continue to cultivate and possess plants but shall not transfer or sell; a dispensary may continue to possess existing inventory but shall not acquire, dispense, transfer, or sell; a processor may continue to process and possess existing inventory but shall not acquire, dispense, transfer, or sell; a producer may continue to cultivate, process, and possess plants and existing inventory but shall not acquire, dispense, transfer, or sell. (Source) "Serious violation" (capable of causing death or serious and prolonged disfigurement, prolonged impairment of health, or prolonged loss or impairment of bodily-organ function) is the defined trigger in the statute's definitions. (Source) The enrolled KRS 218B.100 text was not opened in this audit; re-open the official legislature pinpoint before quoting the during-suspension list in a filing. (Source) The OMC enforcement page shows only 3 fines, with no amounts or violation detail, and its completeness is [VERIFY] (see still-unverified list). (Source)

Insurance / bonding. A licensee shall obtain and maintain commercial general liability insurance for, at a minimum, $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 per aggregate; commercial automobile insurance as required by Kentucky law (KRS 304.39-110) for any vehicle used to transport medicinal cannabis or products; and workers' compensation coverage for Commonwealth employees plus Kentucky Office of Unemployment Insurance contributions (915 KAR 1:020 §5 and 915 KAR 1:010 attestations). (Source) Insurance shall begin prior to the licensee's first day of cannabis business activities and continue for as long as the licensee is operating. (Source) No separate surety-bond minimum for medical licensees was located in 915 KAR Chapter 1 in this audit — capital requirements (Tier I $50,000; Tier II $200,000; Tier III $500,000; Tier IV $1,000,000; Processor $150,000; Producer $150,000 plus tier; Dispensary $150,000; Safety compliance $150,000) are Run 1 figures carried here, not re-confirmed in this audit, and the bond question is [VERIFY] against the 915 KAR 1:010 capital and escrow text if a bond is asserted by a counterparty. (Source)

(B) Hemp / hemp-derived product businesses. Grower licence (KDA, 302 KAR 50:021). Sites (growing, handling, storage) shall be in Kentucky; primary residence in Kentucky or within 50 miles of at least one Kentucky growing site, affirmed as the residence from 1 May to 30 September. (Source) Background check: annual Kentucky State Police check, paid for by the applicant or key participant, delivered with the application or renewal; a report more than 60 days old at application is not accepted; failure to submit is grounds for denial. (Source) Ten-year bar: a person convicted of any felony or any drug-related misdemeanour or violation in the previous 10 years (from application or from background-check issuance, as worded in the two provisions) is ineligible, subject to the pilot-programme and pre-20 December 2018 lawful-growing exceptions stated in the regulation. (Source) Substitution of a signing authority requires department approval plus a current background check on the substitute. (Source) The department may inspect and sample at any time; a grower, present or not, shall permit department or law-enforcement entry to any premises where hemp or cannabis seeds, plants, or materials are located and any premises listed on the licence, with or without cause and with or without advance notice. (Source)

Processor/handler licence (KDA). Processor and handler premises, records, and vehicles are subject to Kentucky Department of Agriculture inspection, and non-compliant material is subject to the disposal regime in §11.5(B). (Source) The processor and handler transfer and sale procedure, renewal timeline, and any ownership cap were not located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE].

HDCP permits/registrations (CHFS, 902 KAR 45:021). Processing $3,000, manufacturing $1,000, wholesale/distributor $1,000, cosmetic $200, retail $2,000 per year, temporary-event $250; product registration $200 for each cannabinoid product or cannabinoid product class sold in Kentucky (902 KAR 45:021 §1(5)(a)). (Source) The Cabinet or its duly authorised agent shall conduct an onsite inspection of all permitted cannabinoid processing and manufacturing establishments, storage warehouses, and distribution centres. (Source) The location of the permitted establishment, all general business records, including employee records, and vehicles utilised to transport products are subject to reasonable inspection. (Source) All cannabinoid establishments, whether permitted or not, shall cooperate during any inspections, complaint investigation, and requests for information or data. (Source) All products not in compliance may be seized and destroyed by the Cabinet, with a 10-day appeal notice under §12. (Source) The HDCP transfer, ownership-change, relocation, renewal-timeline, and insurance and bonding rules were not located in the 902 KAR 45:021 text opened [UNAVAILABLE] — do not import the medical 915 KAR 1:020 rules into HDCP businesses. (Source)

CIB licences (ABC). Retail package $2,000 per year supplemental to a quota retail package licence, distributor $1,000 per year, direct shipper Type B $1,000 per year. (Source) ABC transfer, renewal, and insurance rules were not located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source)

No hemp bonding minimum was located for growers, processors/handlers, HDCP permittees, or CIB licensees in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source)

11.3 Cultivation

(A) Medical. Enclosed, locked facility only. A cultivator shall conduct cultivation activities in an enclosed, locked facility in accordance with KRS 218B.095(5) (915 KAR 1:030 §1). (Source) There is no outdoor medical cultivation in the rule as written: the canopy rule is expressly an indoor growth-area rule (below). (Source) "Enclosed, locked facility" means an indoor growing space such as a room, greenhouse, building, or other indoor enclosed area that is maintained and operated by a cultivator or producer and is equipped with locks and other security devices that permit access only by authorised agents — so a greenhouse that is enclosed and locked falls under the indoor-area calculation; it is not an outdoor exception. (Source)

Canopy / tiers (KRS 218B.105(3) via 915 KAR 1:030 §4(3)). A cultivator shall not exceed the indoor growth area specified in KRS 218B.105(3) for its respective cultivator tier. (Source) The surface area of the plant canopy shall be calculated in square feet; measurement shall include all of the area within the boundaries where cultivation of medicinal cannabis plants occurs; if a tiered or shelving system is used, the surface of each tier or shelf shall be included. (Source) Excluded from the calculation: square footage in an enclosed, locked facility used for storage of seeds, seedlings, tissue cultures, or clones 8 inches or less, supplies, pesticides, fertilisers, or other products, and square footage for quarantine, office space, or other non-cultivation activities. (Source) Tier indoor areas (KRS 218B.105(3)): Tier I 2,500 sq ft; Tier II 10,000 sq ft; Tier III 25,000 sq ft; Tier IV 50,000 sq ft. (Source) Producer: shall not exceed 50,000 square feet of total canopy size at an enclosed, locked facility (915 KAR 1:050 §6). (Source)

Plant counts. No per-plant count cap for medical cultivators was located; the control is canopy square footage, not plant numbers. (Source) Do not state a plant-count limit for medical cultivation. (Source) Seed, seedling, and clone inputs: a cultivator shall only grow medicinal cannabis plants from seeds, tissue cultures, clones not taller than eight (8) inches, and seedlings located physically in its facility (915 KAR 1:030 §4(2)); each seed, seedling, tissue culture, clone, or plant acquired shall be recorded in the designated electronic monitoring and seed-to-sale system within 24 hours of receipt (§4(1)). (Source)

Co-location with hemp. If a cultivator intends medical and hemp cultivation at the same licensed location, before its first day of medical cultivation it shall provide: (a) proof it is permitted to operate a hemp business by the appropriate permitting authority and is in good standing; (b) a written plan for keeping medical and hemp activities strictly separated; (c) a site map or blueprint showing which portions are medical versus hemp. (Source) A co-located business is subject to reasonable Cabinet inspection of the entire facility (915 KAR 1:030 §3(5)–(6), citing KRS 218B.100(1)). (Source)

Under-18 / access. A cannabis business shall not permit a person under 18 to enter or remain on its premises (KRS 218B.095(2)(c)); cultivator sites and facilities shall not be open to the general public (915 KAR 1:030, visitor section); visitors must be logged (date, full name, badge number, arrival and departure times, purpose, areas visited) and escorted in limited-access areas; no consideration or compensation may be received for allowing a visitor into a limited-access area. (Source)

(B) Hemp. Lot, not canopy. Hemp cultivation is controlled by lot (contiguous area, same variety or strain, in a field, greenhouse, or indoor structure — 302 KAR 50:056 definitions) and by licensed growing, handling, and storage sites (302 KAR 50:021), not by a canopy square-footage tier. (Source) No hemp canopy cap or plant-count cap was located. (Source)

Plot / lot registration in practice. The grower licence lists growing sites; the grower files a Field Planting Report and, for indoor or greenhouse growing, a Greenhouse/Indoor Planting Report (incorporated by reference in 302 KAR 50:080), plus a Harvest Report at least 15 days before the expected harvest (see §11.1(B)). (Source) The Field Planting Report is due within 15 days following planting, according to the Kentucky Department of Agriculture 2026 Grower Orientation. (Source) GPS coordinates for licensed locations are verified at the inspection and sample visit. (Source) Any lot-size limit was not located [VERIFY against 302 KAR 50:021 §§5–6 and 50:080 forms]. (Source)

Indoor / outdoor / greenhouse. Hemp may be grown in a field, greenhouse, or indoor growing structure (the "lot" definition covers all three). (Source) No hemp indoor or outdoor prohibition was located. (Source) Universities growing hemp for research follow the same licence route (grower licence if the research plan includes growing; processor/handler licence if it does not — 302 KAR 50:021, university provisions; see §11.9). (Source)

Pre-harvest sampling. See §11.1(B) — no harvest from a lot before the department inspection and sample visit; harvest must be completed within 30 days following the date of the inspection and sample-collection visit. (Source) If harvest is not completed within 30 days, the grower shall submit a new Harvest Report and may be required to pay a secondary pre-harvest sample fee established in 302 KAR 50:060. (Source) The Kentucky Department of Agriculture 2026 Grower Orientation confirms the 30-day harvest window. (Source)

11.4 Security

(A) Medical — commercial-grade, professionally monitored, 24/7 (915 KAR 1:030 §7 for cultivators; parallel sections 1:040 §7, 1:060 §11, 1:070 §11 for processors, safety facilities, dispensaries). A cultivator shall have security and surveillance systems, utilising commercial-grade equipment, to prevent unauthorised entry and to prevent and detect an adverse loss. (Source) The alarm system shall include: professionally monitored coverage of all facility entrances and exits; rooms with exterior windows, exterior walls, roof hatches, or skylights; storage rooms including those containing medicinal cannabis and safes; and the facility perimeter; an audible panic alarm (manual activation, life-threatening or emergency, law-enforcement response); a silent holdup alarm (manual activation, robbery in progress); a failure-notification system giving audible, text, or visual alert to a designated security person within 5 minutes of a failure, by telephone, email, or text; smoke and fire alarms; auxiliary power sufficient for at least 24 hours after a power outage; access doors not solely controlled by an electronic access panel (so locks do not release on power loss); and motion detectors for exterior lighting. (Source) The surveillance system shall be professionally monitored, operational 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, recording all activity in images capable of clearly revealing facial detail, with fixed camera placement giving a clear image of all individuals and activities in and around all limited-access areas, any room or area containing a security alarm or surveillance storage device or equipment, and entrances, exits, and other areas detailed in the Office of Medical Cannabis "How to Guide on Security and Surveillance" (Resources tab, kymedcan.ky.gov/businesses). (Source) The full camera-placement list beyond the excerpt opened is [VERIFY] against the current 915 KAR 1:030 §7 text and the How to Guide before specifying a general video-retention period or camera count, neither of which was established from a primary source in this audit; do not adopt secondary 60-day or 90-day retention claims. (Source) Two records rules are confirmed: within 3 business days following a request for records, provide up to 4 screen captures of an unaltered copy of a video surveillance recording to the Cabinet or its authorised agents, law enforcement, or other federal, state, or local government officials if necessary to perform their functions and duties; and if notified in writing by the Cabinet, law enforcement, or other government officials of a pending criminal or administrative investigation for which a recording may contain relevant information, retain an unaltered copy of the recording for 2 years or until the investigation or proceeding is closed or the investigating entity notifies the cultivator that retention is not necessary, whichever is later. (Source)

Limited-access areas (915 KAR 1:001): cultivator and producer — areas where seedlings or plants are growing, being loaded or unloaded, packaged or stored, waste processed, stored, or destroyed, or alarm or surveillance devices stored or maintained; processor and producer — processing, loading or unloading, packaging or storage, waste, devices; safety facility — loading or unloading, storage, testing, destruction, devices; dispensary — loading or unloading, storage, destruction, devices. (Source) All ingress and egress to a limited-access area shall be signed (at least 12 inches by 12 inches, letters at least one-half inch, "Do Not Enter. Limited Access Area. Access Limited to Authorized Personnel and Escorted Visitors") — cultivator section, as indexed. (Source)

Security-equipment rooms. For processors (and by parallel sections, other categories): access limited to persons essential to security and surveillance operations, law enforcement, service employees, the Cabinet and agents, and Cabinet-approved others; a current list of authorised employees, service employees, and contractors with access shall be made available to the Cabinet on request and placed on or next to the doors accessing those areas; rooms housing security equipment shall be kept locked at all times and used for no other purpose or function (915 KAR 1:040 §7). (Source)

Storage (A). Separate locked limited-access areas for (cultivator) seeds, seedlings, tissue cultures, clones, plants, and product that are expired, damaged, deteriorated, mislabelled, contaminated, recalled, or opened or breached, until destroyed or disposed of per the waste section; (processor) the same for product; all storage areas clean, orderly, free from insects, rodents, birds, and pests (915 KAR 1:030, 1:040; parallel dispensary 1:070, safety 1:060). (Source)

Transport (A) — 915 KAR 1:080. Business-to-business transport and dispensary delivery are both regulated; a business may contract a third party for transport or delivery if the contractor complies with §1:080, the business background-checks the contractor's transporting employees and agents (disqualifying-felony and under-21 bar, see §11.8), provides the contractor a copy of its licence and ID badges (name, photo, employee ID number, business phone and email, programme phone and email, conspicuously worn during transport), and notifies the Cabinet by email (kymedcanreporting@ky.gov) of all contracted transporters before transport begins. (Source) Delivery vehicles (dispensary delivery and business-to-business transport): locked storage compartment that is part of the vehicle or locked storage container with separate key or combination pad; no markings identifying or indicating medicinal-cannabis transport; current state registration; alarm system and a minimum of 2 video cameras (one with a clear view of the driver, one with a clear view of the location of the medicinal cannabis); insured per KRS 304.39-110; staffed by a delivery driver (not a 2-person team) who holds a copy of the dispensary licence, wears the employee badge conspicuously, holds a valid driver's licence, and makes no unnecessary stops; all product shielded from public view in the locked compartment or container; GPS used to ensure safe, efficient delivery. (Source) (Source) On accident or vehicle failure rendering the vehicle immobile or requiring a tow, the driver shall notify the Cabinet immediately via email to kymedcanreporting@ky.gov. (Source) Sample transport (to a safety facility): the transporting employee, agent, or contractor shall protect the sample's physical integrity and composition and protect it against factors interfering with testing validity, including time and temperature. (Source)

Notification duties (915 KAR 1:020). During licensure, notify the Cabinet of inventory discrepancies; diversion, theft, or loss; unauthorised destruction; criminal proceedings involving owners, officers, board members, employees, volunteers, backers, or agents arising on premises or using licensee property; security-alarm activation or any event requiring law-enforcement or security response; loss, unauthorised dissemination, or alteration of records; transport accidents; any act creating a health or safety risk; a dispensary declining a sale; a dispensary desiring to prohibit a cardholder from its premises. (Source)

(B) Hemp / hemp-derived. No 915 KAR-style commercial-grade alarm and camera code for hemp growers, processors/handlers, or HDCP retailers was located. (Source) The security-adjacent rules found are: (1) Kentucky Department of Agriculture and law-enforcement entry at any time, with or without cause or notice (302 KAR 50:021); (2) CHFS reasonable inspection of HDCP permitted establishments, records, and transport vehicles, with a duty to cooperate (902 KAR 45:021); (3) HDCP adult-use products secured in the retail setting to prevent theft or other access to persons under 21 (902 KAR 45:190 retail section — see §12.2); (4) CIB retail under ABC quota-licence premises rules — the ABC security and transport detail was not located [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Hemp transport: no hemp-specific locked-vehicle, camera, or unmarked-vehicle rule was located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Do not import the medical 915 KAR 1:080 transport code into hemp. (Source) Interstate hemp shipment issues are Part 10, not this report. (Source)

11.5 Waste disposal

(A) Medical — render unusable, locked container, video + 2-person oversight (cultivator) / locked container (processor). A cultivator and processor shall dispose of undesired, excess, unauthorised, obsolete, adulterated, misbranded, or deteriorated medicinal cannabis in a manner as to render the medicinal cannabis unusable, and shall record medicinal cannabis waste as required in the Commonwealth's designated electronic monitoring system and seed-to-sale tracking system. (Source) Rendered-unusable product shall be discarded into a dumpster with commercial-grade locks or other approved, locked container for removal from the facility by a waste removal company selected by the cultivator or processor, except that ashes resulting from the controlled incineration of medicinal cannabis may be placed in an unlocked dumpster (cultivator version adds: or may be composted in a secured area at the cultivation site for future use at the facility). (Source) Rendering-unusable methods: (a) controlled incineration; or (b) grinding and incorporating the cannabis with one or more non-consumable solid wastes so the resulting mixture is majority non-cannabis waste: paper waste; cardboard waste; food waste; yard or garden waste; grease or other compostable oil waste; soil or other used growth media. (Source) Cultivator disposal shall be performed under video surveillance from the time destruction begins to when it is placed in a locked dumpster or other approved, locked container and removed from the cultivator's site and facility. (Source) A minimum of 2 employees shall oversee and participate in waste procedures, and waste shall be recorded in Metrc and on a separate waste log. (Source) The business shall maintain and make available a separate record of every disposal indicating: the date and time of disposal; the manner of disposal; any unique identification codes associated with the medicinal cannabis scheduled for destruction; the reasoning for and description of the disposal (further record fields in the full section were not fully extracted [VERIFY]). (Source) Note on section numbers: the Office of Medical Cannabis February 2025 Cultivator Training cites the waste rules as 915 KAR 1:030 §13, while the original report cites §15 for cultivators; confirm the cultivator waste-section number at republication before publishing a §15 pinpoint. (Source) Dispensary waste (915 KAR 1:070 §14) and safety-facility waste (915 KAR 1:060, reserve-sample destruction) follow the same render-unusable principle; returned product accepted by a dispensary is for disposal only (see §11.7). (Source)

(B) Hemp — department-supervised destruction; no "majority non-cannabis" mixing rule. Non-compliant harvested material (302 KAR 50:056 §8). If a lot is designated for mandatory disposal, the department shall ensure that all cannabis from that lot is disposed of using one of the procedures established in this section (current markup broadens the earlier "leaf material and floral material" wording). (Source) The costs of disposal, if any are incurred by the department, shall be charged to the licence holder. (Source) Procedures: (1) On-site destruction with department supervision — without removing the material from the licensee's (or other licensed) premises, a department employee shall personally observe destruction (rendering into a useless and non-retrievable state) by (a) grinding it up and incorporating it into the soil, or (b) controlled incineration. (Source) (2) On-farm transfer to a person registered or authorised by the department to accept controlled substances for destruction, loaded and observed by a department employee at the licensee's premises until transfer is complete. (Source) (3) Vehicle transport to a department-approved location (with pre-transport steps in the full section — not fully extracted [VERIFY]). (Source)

Pre-harvest non-compliant plants / university research: universities and colleges growing hemp for research shall ensure the disposal of all noncompliant plants and comply with disposal reporting (302 KAR 50:021 university provisions). (Source) Pesticide-contaminated hemp: hemp seeds, plants, and materials bearing pesticide residue in violation of the label shall be subject to forfeiture or destruction without compensation (302 KAR 50:021 §16(6)). (Source) HDCP / CIB waste: no HDCP-specific waste-disposal method (render-unusable, locked container, and so on) was located in 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190 in this audit; the enforcement route found is seizure (and destruction) by the Cabinet for non-compliant products (see §11.2(B)) [UNAVAILABLE for a step-by-step HDCP waste SOP]. (Source)

11.6 Environmental

(A) Medical. Water / sanitation (facility sections, for example 915 KAR 1:040 §11, 1:030 parallel). The facility shall be provided with a water supply sufficient for its operations, derived from a source that is a public water system, or a nonpublic system capable of providing a safe, potable, and adequate supply of water to meet the operational needs of the facility; adequate readily-accessible restrooms in sanitary condition and good repair; effective non-toxic sanitising cleansers and sanitary towel service or suitable drying devices; and compliance with all other applicable federal, state, and local building code requirements and occupational safety and health requirements. (Source) Spent hydroponic nutrient solution and wastewater are expressly within the definition of "medicinal cannabis waste" (915 KAR 1:001) and therefore subject to the waste regime in §11.5(A) — no separate wastewater-discharge permit rule for medical facilities was located [VERIFY against the Kentucky Division of Water or local sewer authority if a facility discharges process wastewater]. (Source)

Pesticides (A). The medical testing regime caps residual pesticides (915 KAR 1:110 §3, Appendix B, 4 January 2024) and failed pesticide tests equal waste with no remediation (see §11.1(A)). (Source) A cultivator who uses a pesticide on medicinal cannabis shall be certified to apply pesticides by the Kentucky Department of Agriculture pursuant to KRS Chapter 217B (915 KAR 1:030 §8(1)). (Source) The Office of Medical Cannabis publishes a "Notice re Pesticides and Other Chemical Applications" (Resources page, kymedcan.ky.gov/businesses/Pages/Resources.aspx) — its operative list of permitted and prohibited substances was not opened in this audit [VERIFY]. (Source)

Energy. No Kentucky medical-cannabis energy-efficiency, lighting, HVAC, or carbon rule (no PPE or kWh standard, no renewable requirement) was located in 915 KAR Chapter 1 or KRS Chapter 218B in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Facilities are subject only to the general building-code and OSHA compliance clause above and any local code. (Source) Odor: licensee SOPs shall include "Odor mitigation and control" (915 KAR 1:020 §4(1)) — the substantive odor standard, if any beyond the SOP requirement, was not extracted [VERIFY]. (Source)

Worker safety. Licensees shall maintain a physical copy of the "Guide to Worker Safety and Health in the Kentucky Medical Cannabis Industry" readily accessible to employees and agents and ensure annual training on it (915 KAR 1:020); employees shall be trained on the business's SOPs within 30 days of starting employment and once every calendar year thereafter, with training records retained 5 years and made available to the Cabinet on request. (Source)

(B) Hemp. Pesticides (B) — 302 KAR 50:021 §16 (the clearest hemp environmental rule found). (1) A grower who uses a pesticide on hemp shall first be certified to apply pesticides by the department pursuant to KRS Chapter 217B; (2) a certified grower shall not use, or be eligible to use, a Category 10 licence to apply pesticides to hemp in violation of the product label; (3) a licensed grower shall not use any pesticide in violation of the product label; (4) a grower using a pesticide on a site where hemp will be planted shall comply with the longest of any planting restriction interval on the product label prior to planting; (5) the department may perform pesticide testing on a random basis or where it has reason to believe a label violation occurred; (6) label-violating residue equals forfeiture or destruction without compensation (see §11.5(B)). (Source)

Water / energy (B). No hemp-specific water-use, irrigation, runoff, energy-efficiency, or carbon rule was located in 302 KAR Chapter 50 in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Hemp growers remain subject to general Kentucky water, pesticide (KRS Chapter 217B), and local land-use law, which this report does not purport to summarise. (Source) Soil / incorporation: the only soil-related hemp disposal method found is grinding plus soil incorporation under department supervision for non-compliant lots (§11.5(B)). (Source)

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts, promotions

(A) Medical. Samples for testing versus samples for consumers — do not conflate. Testing samples are governed by 915 KAR 1:110 / 1:060 (contracted safety facility, chain of custody, reserve sample — §11.1(A)). (Source) Consumer "samples" (free product to cardholders) are not authorised as a category: the only consumer-facing product-example rule found is the dispensary display example in 915 KAR 1:070 §5(4): a product example shall be marked "NOT FOR SALE OR CONSUMPTION" in bold capitals; packaged in a secure jar protected by a plastic, glass, or metal mesh screen so cardholders can see the product; recorded in the designated electronic monitoring and seed-to-sale system as a product example; and destroyed per §1:070 §14 when it has degraded so it is no longer representative of a new product. (Source) No rule was located authorising a dispensary to give away usable medicinal cannabis to a cardholder [UNAVAILABLE — treat free usable product as unauthorised unless an Office of Medical Cannabis guidance says otherwise]. (Source)

Inducements — expressly allowed, expressly limited (915 KAR 1:070 §5(5)). Dispensaries may utilise inducements to assist cardholders. (Source) Inducements shall not persuade or influence the use of medicinal cannabis outside of medicinal cannabis practitioner recommendations or limitations or the amounts allowed by KRS Chapter 218B. (Source) Authorised inducements may include: (a) the use of coupons, loyalty programs, and discounts; or (b) the giving away of educational materials and branded merchandise. (Source) Inducements therefore cannot be used to push use beyond a practitioner's recommendation or limitation or the statutory supply limits. (Source)

Branded merchandise. A dispensary may sell branded merchandise, including t-shirts, mugs, water bottles, and hats (§1:070 §5(7)). (Source) Smoking accessories — prohibited sale. A dispensary shall not sell any medicinal cannabis accessory that is used solely for the purpose of smoking medicinal cannabis, including rolling papers and lighters (§1:070 §5(8)). (Source) This is the dispensary-side companion to the patient smoking ban (§12.5). (Source)

Returns. A dispensary may accept returns of medicinal cannabis and medicinal cannabis products from a cardholder for the purpose of disposal. (Source) A dispensary shall not offer anything of monetary value in return for medicinal cannabis or medicinal cannabis products received from a cardholder, except clearly defective products may be exchanged for the same or similar product of equal or lesser value with no monetary refund. (Source) All returns and their subsequent destruction shall be documented (§1:070 §5(6)). (Source)

Advertising (915 KAR 1:090). A cannabis business shall not advertise medicinal-cannabis sales in print, broadcast, online, paid in-person solicitation, or other advertising device (KRS 218B.095(2)(f)), except appropriate signs on the licensed property, business-directory listings, trade or medical publication listings, and sponsorship of health or not-for-profit charity or advocacy events. (Source) A business with a website or social media presence shall utilise appropriate measures to ensure that individuals attempting to access the allowable content are eighteen (18) years of age or older (915 KAR 1:090 §2(6)). (Source) The Cabinet may order removal of objectionable or non-conforming advertising on written notice within a reasonable time (§3). (Source) Business-to-business promotion is allowed: cultivators, processors, producers, and dispensaries may directly promote to other cannabis businesses; a safety facility may only promote its testing services and KRS 218B.125 activities to other businesses (§4). (Source)

(B) Hemp / hemp-derived. Sampling / giveaways (B). No HDCP or CIB rule authorising free samples, "tastings", or giveaways of intoxicating hemp products was located in 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190 or in the ABC CIB material opened in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Note the contrast with medical: CIBs were package-only in wet territory with by-the-drink fair and festival sales ending 1 January 2026 — that history points against assuming on-premise sampling is allowed for CIBs. (Source) Do not advise sampling without an ABC or CHFS source. (Source)

Discounts / promotions (B). No HDCP-specific discount, loyalty-program, coupon, or promotion ban or permission was located in 902 KAR 45:021 / 45:190 in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) General advertising restraints that were found for HDCPs: no cartoon images; no likeness to images, characters, or phrases popularly used to advertise to children; no likeness to or imitation of commercially available candy, snack, baked-good, or beverage packaging or labelling; no terms "candy" or "candies" or variations; no department or Cabinet logo or state, county, or municipal seal, flag, crest, coat of arms, or insignia that could mislead a person into believing the product is endorsed, manufactured, or used by government (902 KAR 45:190 labelling section). (Source)

Retailer records (B). Cannabinoid retailers shall maintain records of cannabinoid product purchase, including the name and address of the cannabinoid processor or manufacturer, and the wholesaler or distributor. (Source) (Source)

11.8 Drug testing and background checks (licence holders and staff)

(A) Medical. Background checks — universal, pre-employment, 5-year retention. Every category regulation repeats the same rule (cultivator 915 KAR 1:030 §1; processor 1:040 §1; safety facility 1:060 §1(6)(a); dispensary 1:070 parallel; producer 1:050 parallel): conduct a criminal background check into the criminal history of each person seeking to become a principal officer, board member, agent, volunteer, or employee before that person begins work, and retain records of these background checks for five (5) years and provide them to the Cabinet during subsequent inspections or on request. (Source) Pre-first-day confirmation (915 KAR 1:020 §4(1)(c)): the licensee has conducted and shall continue to conduct such checks and shall not employ, take on as a volunteer, or have as a board member, principal officer, or agent any person who was convicted of a disqualifying felony offense or is younger than twenty-one (21) years of age. (Source) Employment records (individual file: full legal name, job description, background-check documentation, training record, employment dates, days and hours worked, disciplinary actions) shall be maintained at least 5 years after the employee's last date of employment. (Source) ID badges (name, photo, employee ID number, business phone and email, programme phone and email) shall be conspicuously worn on premises and during transport. (Source) Third-party transporters' employees and agents are background-checked on the same disqualifying-felony and under-21 bar (915 KAR 1:080, see §11.4(A)). (Source)

"Disqualifying felony offense" — definition. Under KRS 218B.010(11) (as amended by HB 829), "disqualifying felony offense" means: (a) a felony offense that resulted in the person being classified by the Department of Corrections as a violent offender under KRS 439.3401; or (b) a violation of a state or federal controlled substance law that was classified as a felony in the jurisdiction where the person was convicted, except: (1) an offense for which the sentence, including any term of probation, incarceration, or supervised release, was completed five (5) or more years earlier; or (2) an offense that, as determined by the Cabinet, consisted of conduct for which Chapter 218B would likely have prevented a conviction, but the conduct either occurred prior to the enactment of Chapter 218B or was prosecuted by an authority other than the Commonwealth of Kentucky. (Source) Do not assume the hemp 10-year rule (below) applies to medical. (Source)

Drug testing of staff (A). No Kentucky rule was located in 915 KAR Chapter 1 requiring medical licensees to drug-test their own employees, or prohibiting them from doing so. (Source) What the law does say is on the patient side (KRS 218B.040 and 218B.045: an employer may run drug-testing and zero-tolerance policies; the prescription-drug-like protection applies only to testing required by state or local law) and on impairment determination (KRS 218B.040(1)(g): good-faith impairment determinations may include behavioural assessment plus a secondary step of testing a cardholder-employee for cannabis by an established method, with the burden shifting to the employee to refute — see §11.8 and Part 12 employment cross-reference). (Source) A licensee's own staff drug-testing policy, if any, is therefore an employer-policy matter under general Kentucky employment law, not a 915 KAR mandate found here [UNAVAILABLE as a mandate]. (Source)

Practitioner / owner bars. A business shall not employ, have as a board member, or be owned in whole or part by a medicinal cannabis practitioner (KRS 218B.095(2)(e)); safety-facility independence bar (§11.1(A)). (Source)

(B) Hemp / hemp-derived. Grower background check — 10-year rule (see §11.2(B)). Annual Kentucky State Police check, paid by applicant or key participant, no more than 60 days old at application, felony or drug-related misdemeanour or violation within 10 years equals ineligible (with pilot and pre-20 December 2018 exceptions). (Source) This is stricter in time-bar terms and different in scope from the medical "disqualifying felony" rule — the two must not be merged. (Source)

Processor/handler, HDCP, and CIB staff checks. No processor or handler, HDCP-permittee, or CIB-licensee background-check or staff drug-testing rule was located in the 302 KAR 50:031, 902 KAR 45:021, or ABC material opened in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) HDCP inspections do reach "employee records" (902 KAR 45:021, §11.2(B)), but that is an inspection-access rule, not a background-check mandate. (Source)

Drug testing (B). No hemp-employer drug-testing mandate or prohibition was located [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) The HDCP label warning "Use of this product may result in a positive drug screen" (902 KAR 45:190) is a consumer warning, not an employment rule. (Source)

11.9 Research and university work

Kentucky Center for Cannabis — University of Kentucky (KRS 164.983). The Kentucky Center for Cannabis is established at the University of Kentucky to advance the study of the use of cannabis and cannabis derivatives for the treatment of certain medical conditions and diseases as indicated and recommended by the centre's advisory board. (Source) Mission (§2): (a) conduct and fund research related to cannabis and cannabis derivatives; (b) conduct and fund research on health effects including potential risks and side effects; (c) conduct and fund research on efficacy and potential health effects of various delivery methods including vaporizing, ingestibles, topical applications, and combustion; (d) review current and future research literature, clinical studies, and clinical trials; (e) monitor, to the extent appropriate and sufficient data are available, patient outcomes in states with medicinal cannabis programs; (f) examine, to the extent sufficient data are available, health effects of combustible cannabis. (Source) University duties (§3): develop and maintain the centre under its multidisciplinary-centre regulations; establish an internal advisory board appointed by the University of Kentucky president to oversee activities, research agenda, and finances; report to the Secretary of the Cabinet for Health and Family Services and the Legislative Research Commission by 1 September each year for the preceding fiscal year, outlining activities and expenditures; comply with §4 (employ a director and necessary staff; seek, accept, and expend gifts, grants, and donations; conduct clinical research, studies, and trials as approved by appropriate federal agencies). (Source) History: established by HB 604 (2022) (became law 26 April 2022, per secondary summaries; University of Kentucky College of Medicine announcement 21 September 2022: based in the Center on Drug and Alcohol Research (CDAR), initial $2 million appropriation over two years, director Shanna Babalonis, PhD — secondary details, carried as such). (Source) Whether the Centre's September report (for the preceding fiscal year) was delivered or published was not located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE — check University of Kentucky CDAR and Legislative Research Commission postings]. (Source) The Centre's role in the condition list is statutory: "qualifying medical condition" includes any other medical condition or disease for which the Kentucky Center for Cannabis established in KRS 164.983, or its successor, determines that sufficient scientific data and evidence exists to demonstrate that an individual diagnosed with that condition or disease is likely to receive medical, therapeutic, or palliative benefits from the use of medicinal cannabis (KRS 218B.010(26)(g)). (Source) Executive Order 2026-318 was issued 2 June 2026, clarifying the statutory definition of "qualifying medical condition" (Office of Medical Cannabis executive-order page); its full text and any Attorney General opinion, legislative resolution, or court challenge were not opened in this audit [VERIFY]. (Source)

University of Louisville — hemp (not medical cannabis). The University of Louisville's Conn Center for Renewable Energy Research has begun growing industrial hemp to enhance its research in fuels and manufacturing, in partnership with the Kentucky Department of Agriculture and the University of Kentucky Agriculture Department, on a 40-by-40-foot plot at the Phoenix House, Belknap Campus, Louisville, Kentucky (University of Louisville News, undated in the source opened, describing the pilot-era planting; seven other Kentucky universities were then also researching hemp, the University of Louisville being the only one focused on hemp as a fuel resource). Researchers named: Jagannadh Satyavolu (biofuels theme leader), Noppodon Sathitsuksanoh (assistant professor, chemical engineering), Eric Berson (associate professor, chemical engineering); director Mahendra Sunkara. Later University of Louisville hemp-fibre work (secondary, Journal of Bioresources and Bioproducts, via Labroots summary): methane sulphonic acid (MSA) hydrolysis of hemp seed hulls, 1.8% acid loading, 26.15 g/L xylose, 31% higher yield than sulphuric-acid hydrolysis at the same loading, for C-5 biorefinery and activated-carbon applications — secondary figures, not quoted as primary data. No University of Louisville medical-cannabis clinical programme was located in this audit; the University of Louisville's located work is hemp as fuel and fibre. Do not describe the University of Louisville as a medical-cannabis research centre.

Other Kentucky university hemp programmes (secondary summaries, dates as given — [VERIFY] against each university and the Kentucky Department of Agriculture before relying). Murray State University — among the first Kentucky universities on industrial hemp, agronomic practices, production systems, and processing; Western Kentucky University College of Agriculture, Food Science and Sustainable Systems — Industrial Hemp Research Initiative (economics and agronomics); Morehead State University Office of Regional Outreach and Applied Research — Cannabis Science Certificate Program (medical-cannabis cultivation, production, processing, dispensing education); Eastern Kentucky University — listed in the same secondary round-up, detail truncated [VERIFY]. (Source) The Kentucky Department of Agriculture university route itself is primary: an authorised faculty, administrator, or staff member of an eligible institution (accredited, degree-conferring, principal campus or office in Kentucky) who wishes to possess or conduct academic research involving living hemp plants, leaf or floral material, or viable seeds shall submit a Hemp License Application; if the research plan includes growing, a Hemp Grower License issues; if not, a Processor/Handler License issues; university applications are accepted at any time of year; no fees for licences issued to faculty, administrator, or staff if the project is research-only and not for commerce; sampling and testing by the department if harvested material is intended for commerce; universities growing for research shall ensure disposal of all noncompliant plants and comply with disposal reporting (302 KAR 50:021). (Source)

Medical research by licensees / practitioners. KRS Chapter 218B practitioner provisions carve out research protocols, clinical trials, and investigational new drug applications from the standard certification rules (secondary summary of SB 47 §9) — the primary text pinpoint was not re-opened here [VERIFY]. (Source) No Kentucky medical-licensee "research licence" type separate from cultivator, processor, producer, and safety-facility licences was located. (Source)

Hemp research and the federal hemp dates. No Kentucky university or Kentucky Department of Agriculture statement was located in this audit addressing how the post-11 December 2026 federal total-THC and 0.4 mg cap affects research hemp (which is already tested on a total-THC basis for crop compliance — see §11.1(B)) [VERIFY on kyagr.com and University of Kentucky Division of Regulatory Services if research material is to move in commerce after that date]. (Source) The baseline split is: PL 119-37 takes effect 12 November 2026, PL 119-103 limits it until 11 December 2026 to the non-naturally-produced and synthesized-cannabinoid exclusions, and the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. (Source)

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL RULES

Headlines. No per se THC driving limit; no automatic marijuana expungement; no Kentucky gun disqualification found — but the federal 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) conflict for patients is live and unresolved on the effect of Schedule III. (Source) School on-property use is district policy (HB 829 / KRS 218B.045(4)(c) / KSBA 09.2242 permit-or-prohibit); see §12.10. (Source)

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke-shop rules

General paraphernalia offence — KRS 218A.500(2) (still in force for non-medical use). It is unlawful for any person to use, or to possess with intent to use, drug paraphernalia for the purpose of planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analyzing, packing, repacking, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing into the human body a controlled substance in violation of this chapter. (Source) Delivery, possession with intent to deliver, and manufacture with intent to deliver paraphernalia, knowing or reasonably should know it will be used with controlled substances, is likewise unlawful under KRS 218A.500 (seller and buyer intent both matter; "for tobacco use only" labelling is not a legal shield where surrounding evidence points to drug use — secondary analysis, marked as such). (Source) Penalties: any person who violates any provision of KRS 218A.500 shall be guilty of a Class A misdemeanour (KRS 218A.500(5), as quoted by the Kentucky Supreme Court in Blane v. Commonwealth). (Source)

Medicinal-cannabis accessories carve-out. The term "drug paraphernalia" does not include medicinal cannabis accessories as defined in KRS 218B.010. (Source) In practice: accessories used in connection with the medical programme by a qualified patient do not fall under the paraphernalia definition; the exemption does not protect items connected to recreational marijuana or other controlled substances. (Source) The dispensary-side rule is stricter than the possession rule: a dispensary shall not sell any medicinal cannabis accessory that is used solely for the purpose of smoking medicinal cannabis, including rolling papers and lighters (915 KAR 1:070 §5(8) — §11.7(A)). (Source)

Smoke shops / hemp retailers — no separate "smoke shop licence" located. No Kentucky statute or regulation creating a smoke-shop licence, a smoke-shop zoning class, or a smoke-shop age-gating rule distinct from (a) the HDCP retail registration and adult-use securing rules (902 KAR 45:190) and (b) the general paraphernalia offence above was located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) A shop selling only non-intoxicating hemp or CBD products, only smoking accessories, or only CIBs therefore sits under different rule sets (HDCP registration, paraphernalia intent, ABC quota licensing respectively) — do not assume a single "smoke shop" permit covers all three. (Source) Local (city or county) business-licence and zoning rules for tobacco and vape retailers may additionally apply and were not surveyed here. (Source)

Federal hemp-date interaction for shops. PL 119-37 takes effect 12 November 2026, but until 11 December 2026 PL 119-103 limits it to the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized; only after 11 December 2026 do the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply. (Source) After 11 December 2026, an intoxicating hemp product that exceeds the federal 0.4 mg per container cap ceases to be federal hemp even if it remains Kentucky-lawful as an HDCP or CIB — a smoke shop's federal exposure (interstate shipment, banking, mail) changes even though its Kentucky retail permission does not automatically change. (Source) No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted under the given baseline, so no banking safe harbour is claimed here. (Source) No Kentucky shop-specific guidance on that date was located [VERIFY on chfs.ky.gov and abc.ky.gov]. (Source)

12.2 Minimum age for hemp-derived THC products

21+ for adult-use HDCPs (902 KAR 45:190). Adult-use hemp-derived cannabinoid products shall bear: "This product is intended for use by adults 21 years and older. Keep out of reach of children." (Source) All adult-use products shall be secured in the retail setting to prevent theft or other access to persons under the age of 21, and shall not be sold, gifted, or otherwise transferred to any person under the age of 21. (Source) Any person who sells adult-use products at retail shall require proof of age of the buyer to verify the buyer is age 21 or older, and may deliver or ship adult-use products to consumers over 21 in packages clearly marked "Adult-use only". (Source) The adult-use list in the original report (delta-8, delta-10, THCA, THCV, HHC, THCP, THCM, delta-6) is a Run 1 finding carried here. (Source)

Non-intoxicating products — no 21+ floor. Only non-intoxicating and cosmetic cannabinoid products may be sold to persons under the age of 21. (Source) Do not impose 21+ on all CBD by analogy with the adult-use rule. (Source)

CIBs: 21+ (Run 1, SB 202 / ABC). (Source)

Medical vaporising products: 21+ for purchase (915 KAR 1:070 — a dispensary shall not sell vaporising-intended products to a cardholder under 21 or to a caregiver for a patient under 21). (Source) Medical patients under 18 may only use with a parent or legal-guardian designated caregiver (KRS 218B.025(2)); persons under 18 may not enter or remain on cannabis-business premises (KRS 218B.095(2)(c)). (Source)

Web/social access. Cannabis businesses' websites and social media shall use measures ensuring persons accessing allowable content are 18 or older (915 KAR 1:090 §2(6) — §11.7(A)). (Source) Note the 18 (web) versus 21 (purchase, vaping, HDCP) distinction — do not merge them. (Source)

12.3 THC driving limits and impairment testing

No per se THC limit in Kentucky law as opened. Kentucky has not adopted a 5 ng/mL (or any ng/mL) per se THC limit for driving. (Source) The 2025 proposal to create one — HB 34 (2025), and the jacketed bill text for SB 230 / BR 1897 proposing a new subsection (1)(g), "Having a marijuana concentration of 6 or more" in blood within 2 hours of cessation — did not become law in the material opened. (Source) Do not quote 5 or 6 ng/mL as Kentucky law. (Source)

What the law does prohibit (KRS 189A.010(1), current). A person shall not operate or be in physical control of a motor vehicle anywhere in Kentucky: (a) with alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more (0.02 or more if under 21) by a scientifically reliable breath or blood test within 2 hours of cessation; (b) while under the influence of alcohol; (c) while under the influence of any other substance or combination of substances which impairs one's driving ability; (d) while the presence of a controlled substance listed in subsection (12) is detected in the blood, by a scientifically reliable test within 2 hours of cessation; (e) while under the combined influence of alcohol and any other impairing substance. (Source)

Marijuana-specific rule — impairment, not presence. The subsection (12) controlled-substance list is: (a) any Schedule I controlled substance except marijuana; (b) alprazolam; (c) amphetamine; (d) buprenorphine; (e) butalbital; (f) carisoprodol; (g) cocaine; (h) diazepam; (i) hydrocodone; (j) meprobamate; (k) methadone; (l) methamphetamine; (m) oxycodone; (n) promethazine; (o) propoxyphene; and (p) zolpidem. (Source) Because subsection (1)(d) specifies that marijuana will never fall into subsection (12), a marijuana DUI will always be prosecuted under subsection (1)(c) — that is, it must be proved by actual impairment (driving, behaviour and observations, field sobriety, blood evidence, expert testimony) rather than mere THC presence. (Source) A blood THC number alone does not automatically prove impairment in Kentucky. (Source) The contrary secondary reading describing Kentucky as "zero-tolerance" for controlled substances including marijuana is rejected; it conflicts with the express (12)(a) exception. (Source) Note for the federal baseline: marijuana is expressly excepted in (12)(a) whether non-medical marijuana is Schedule I or state-licensed medical marijuana is Schedule III — the Kentucky (12) text does not depend on the federal schedule. (Source)

Medical card is no driving defence. KRS 218B.035 preserves DUI prosecution, and KRS 218B.035(4) provides that nothing in Chapter 218B supersedes statutory laws relating to driving while under the influence of intoxicants, including KRS 189A.010. (Source) Office of Medical Cannabis General Questions: cardholders may not operate vehicles or machinery while under the influence of medical cannabis, keep medical cannabis in arm's reach when operating machinery, or use medical cannabis if it impairs their ability to perform tasks safely.
