(Source) A registered or visiting patient using medicinal cannabis has prescription-drug-like rights for state and local-law drug testing (KRS 218B.045(1)) — that protection does not extend to driving while impaired. (Source)

First-offence DUI penalties (secondary summary, dated — [VERIFY] current penalty text). First offence within 5 years: fine $200–$500 and/or county jail 48 hours–30 days; second: $350–$500 plus 7 days–6 months; third: $500–$1,000 plus 30 days–12 months; fourth or subsequent: Class D felony, mandatory minimum 240 days. (Source) These are general DUI penalties, not THC-specific, and the summary is dated — re-check the current KRS 189A.010 penalty text before quoting. (Source)

12.4 Expungement and record clearing for marijuana offences

No Kentucky medical-cannabis expungement programme and no automatic clearing for marijuana convictions was located. There is no provision in KRS Chapter 218B creating expungement for pre-legalisation marijuana offences, and no automatic (non-petition) marijuana expungement statute was found. (Source) What exists is the general expungement and sealing framework, which marijuana offences can enter only if they meet its ordinary conditions. (Source)

First-possession sealing — KRS 218A.276(8)–(11). For a person convicted of possession of marijuana (also synthetic drugs and salvia), the court may set aside and void the conviction upon satisfactory completion of treatment, probation, or other sentence, and issue a certificate to that effect. (Source) A conviction voided under this subsection shall not be deemed a first offense or deemed a conviction for purposes of disqualifications or disabilities imposed by law. (Source) If voided, the court shall order the sealing of all records in the custody of the court and any records in the custody of any other agency or official, including law enforcement records (except as provided in KRS 27A.099), on an Administrative Office of the Courts form; every agency shall certify sealing completed within 60 days of the order. (Source) After sealing, proceedings shall not be used against the defendant, agencies shall reply to any inquiry that no record exists, and the person need not disclose the record on employment, credit, or other applications. (Source) Inspection thereafter only by court permission or on the subject's motion, only to persons named in the motion. (Source) Re-open the enrolled legislature pinpoint for §218A.276 at republication; the substance above is as reproduced in the original report and corroborated by the National Reentry Resource Center Kentucky summary.

General misdemeanour expungement — KRS 431.078. A person convicted of a misdemeanour, violation, or traffic infraction (or series arising from a single incident, or series not arising from a single incident) may petition the convicting court for expungement of the record within that judicial district, including dismissed or amended charges in the action. (Source) Except as provided in KRS 218A.275(8) and 218A.276(8), the petition shall be filed no sooner than five (5) years after the completion of the person's sentence or five (5) years after the successful completion of the person's probation, whichever occurs later. (Source) Hearing no sooner than 30 days after filing, with notice to the county attorney, any identified victim, and others with relevant information. (Source) For single-incident petitions, the court shall order expungement if it finds (among other conditions in §4) the offence was not a sex offence or offence against a child, the person had no previous felony conviction, and had not been convicted of another misdemeanour or violation in the 5 years before the conviction sought to be expunged — read the full §4 and §5 conditions before advising eligibility, including for multi-incident petitions. (Source)

Felony expungement — KRS 431.073. Any person convicted of a Class D felony violation of a statute enumerated in §431.073(1)(a) — including KRS 218A.1423 (marijuana cultivation) and KRS 218A.500 (paraphernalia) — or a series of such violations arising from a single incident, or granted a full pardon, or convicted of a Class D felony (or pre-1 January 1975 offence punishable by not more than 5 years' incarceration) that was not a violation of KRS 189A.010, 508.032, or 519.055, abuse of public office, a sex offence, or an offence committed against a child, and did not result in serious bodily injury or death, may file an application to have the judgment vacated. (Source) (Source) The application shall be filed no sooner than 5 years after completion of sentence, or 5 years after successful completion of probation or parole, whichever occurs later. (Source) A marijuana cultivation felony under §218A.1423 (for example, 5 or more plants, Class D) is therefore expressly listed; a trafficking felony under §218A.1421 is not in the (1)(a) list, so its eligibility depends on the (1)(d) catch-all and case-specific facts — do not promise felony marijuana trafficking expungement without that check. (Source)

Dismissed charges. A criminal offence dismissed without prejudice may be expunged after 3 years (felony) or 1 year (misdemeanour) per the National Reentry Resource Center Kentucky summary (secondary) — official pinpoint [VERIFY] against the enrolled KRS 431.076 text before advising. (Source)

Certification. Every expungement petition or application shall include a certification of eligibility for expungement from the Department of Kentucky State Police and the Administrative Office of the Courts, which certify a background check was conducted and whether the petitioner is eligible (KRS 431.079(1)). (Source)

Proposed, not law. SB 33 (2025) would have removed penalties for possession, cultivation, and trafficking up to 8 ounces and 5 plants and created a new KRS Chapter 431 marijuana-expungement process (retroactive in part) — it is a 2025 bill, not law, and must not be presented as current relief. (Source) HB 420 and SB 186 (earlier adult-use bills with expungement sections) are likewise dead or proposed only. (Source)

Governor's pardons. The conditional-pardon executive order for out-of-state medical purchases (EO 2022-798, issued 15 November 2022) was rescinded effective 1 July 2026 by EO 2026-361, issued 11 June 2026. (Source) Beginning 1 July 2026, Kentuckians with certain conditions who purchase medical cannabis out-of-state are no longer eligible for a conditional pardon for the criminal offense of marijuana possession afforded by EO 2022-798, and Kentucky medical cannabis cardholders who purchase medical cannabis from an out-of-state dispensary may be subject to law enforcement action and are no longer eligible for a pardon for marijuana possession under KRS 218A.1422. (Source) No general marijuana-conviction pardon programme replacing it was located in this audit [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source)

12.5 Consumption rules

Who may consume. Only registered qualified patients, visiting qualified patients, and their designated caregivers acting for the patient, within the supply limits. (Source) Diversion to any non-cardholder is prohibited; a cardholder who sells, distributes, or dispenses to a person not permitted to possess or use medicinal cannabis shall have the card revoked and be subject to criminal prosecution (915 KAR 2:010, citing KRS 218B.075(1)). (Source)

Smoking: banned everywhere for patients. Using or consuming by smoking is unauthorised; the violator shall not be considered to be in possession of medicinal cannabis or engaged in the use of medicinal cannabis and shall not benefit from the legal protections afforded by Chapter 218B, and may face card revocation and prosecution under KRS 218A.1421 and 218A.1422 (KRS 218B.035(1)(g)). (Source) Odour or smell of uncombusted raw plant material is not evidence of smoking. (Source)

Vaporising: 21+ only for purchase, and banned in the places below. A dispensary shall not sell vaporising-intended products to a cardholder under 21 or to a caregiver for a patient under 21 (915 KAR 1:070). (Source) Using or consuming marijuana by vaping while on any form of public transportation, in any public place as defined in KRS 525.010, or in any place of public accommodation, resort, or amusement as defined in KRS 344.130 is not authorised (KRS 218B.035(1)(h)). (Source)

Office of Medical Cannabis published prohibited-place list (General Questions). Cardholders may not: operate vehicles or machinery while under the influence; keep cannabis in arm's reach when operating machinery; use it if it impairs safe task performance; possess or use on school property unless the school's policies allow registered qualified patients to use at school, administered by a school nurse or appropriate staff; possess or use at correctional facilities or on federal property; consume by combustion (smoking); or grow their own without a cannabis business licence. (Source) The school limb is governed by the district-policy rule in §12.10. (Source)

No consumption lounges / social-consumption licences. No Kentucky medical consumption-lounge licence, on-premise consumption licence for dispensaries, or social-consumption establishment rule was located [UNAVAILABLE — treat as not authorised]. (Source) Dispensary premises are for dispensing, not consumption, on the rules opened. (Source)

Hemp-derived consumption. No HDCP or CIB on-premise consumption rule was located (see §11.7(B) on sampling). (Source) CIB by-the-drink sales ended 1 January 2026 — package-only consumption off-premises is the CIB model found. (Source)

Private-property rule (landlord and tenant bridge). KRS 218B.040(1)(e) expressly does not prohibit a person, employer, corporation, or any other entity who occupies, owns, or controls a property from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the use, consumption, possession, transfer, display, transportation, sale, or growing of medicinal cannabis on or in that property (except as provided in KRS 218B.045) — see §12.7. (Source)

12.6 Visitor and out-of-state patient rules

Visiting qualified patient — definition and proof (KRS 218B.010, 218B.025, 218B.055). A visiting qualified patient means a person who has registered as such through the Cabinet as required under Chapter 218B or who possesses a valid out-of-state registry identification card and documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition. (Source) A person is eligible to apply for a registry identification card as a visiting qualified patient if he or she is not a resident of Kentucky or has been a resident of Kentucky for less than thirty (30) days, is at least twenty-one (21) years of age, has not been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense, possesses a valid out-of-state registry identification card, and possesses documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition (KRS 218B.055(4)). (Source) The Office of Medical Cannabis Patient and Caregiver Questions list the same five criteria. (Source) A person with a valid out-of-state registry identification card and documentation of having been diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition may use the out-of-state card for all purposes established in Chapter 218B and shall not be required to apply for or receive a visiting qualified patient registry identification card from the Cabinet (KRS 218B.055(5)). (Source) A dispensary may therefore dispense to a visiting patient presenting that card and documentation even without a Kentucky card. (Source) A Kentucky visiting card is an optional application route: the Office of Medical Cannabis FAQ describes the application, documentation, $25 fee, and 1-year card, and states the same steps as for a registered qualified patient apply once the criteria are met. (Source) Whether any particular state's card is excluded was not confirmed in this audit [VERIFY]. (Source)

Limits (915 KAR 2:020). Visiting patients: no more than a 10-day supply during a given 8-day period (versus in-state: a 30-day supply during a given 25-day period). (Source) A daily supply consists of 3.75 grams of raw plant material, 1 gram of concentrate, or 130 milligrams of delta-9 THC infused into a medicinal cannabis product; an uninterrupted 10-day supply consists of 37.5 grams of raw plant material, 9.5 grams of concentrate, or 1,300 milligrams of THC infused into a medicinal cannabis product; an uninterrupted 30-day supply consists of 112 grams of raw plant material, 28 grams of concentrate, or 3,900 milligrams of THC infused into a medicinal cannabis product. (Source) Non-consumable medicinal cannabis products (ointments, soaps, lotions, and other topical agents) shall not count toward a patient's supply limits. (Source) Outside the residence, product must be in the original dispensary container and the cardholder must carry the valid registry card (visiting: out-of-state card plus diagnosis documentation). (Source) Note on the 18-versus-21 distinction: KRS 218B.110 dispensary verification (verify the presenter is at least 18 years of age and is the person identified on the card) is a verification step, not the visiting-patient eligibility floor, which is 21 under KRS 218B.055(4). (Source)

No reciprocity list. No list of states whose cards are accepted or excluded was located beyond the card-plus-documentation rule above. (Source) Out-of-state patients may not bring their home-state cannabis into Kentucky as a matter of course — see Part 10 (interstate); this report does not authorise importation. (Source) Since 1 July 2026, the EO 2022-798 conditional pardon for out-of-state purchases no longer applies (see §12.4). (Source)

Cardholder protections on the road (KRS 218B.030). Possession of or application for a registry card (or out-of-state card, or business licence) shall not constitute probable cause or reasonable suspicion, nor shall it be used to support the search of the person, property, or home of the holder or applicant (without prejudice to probable cause on other grounds); there is a rebuttable presumption of lawful use where the cardholder holds a valid card (or visiting card plus diagnosis documentation) and possesses no more than the allowed amount. (Source)

12.7 Landlord and tenant rules

No Kentucky landlord and tenant statute protecting medical-cannabis use in rented housing was located. The governing provision points the other way: KRS 218B.040(1)(e) preserves a property occupier, owner, or controller's right to prohibit or regulate use, consumption, possession, transfer, display, transportation, sale, or growing of medicinal cannabis on or in that property (except as provided in KRS 218B.045). (Source) In practical terms: a landlord may, by lease terms or property rules, ban smoking, vaping, possession, or growing on the premises, and a tenant has no KRS Chapter 218B right to override that ban on the text found. (Source)

What KRS 218B.045 does protect (and does not). §218B.045(1) gives prescription-drug-like rights only for drug testing required by state or local law; §218B.045(2) protects custody, visitation, and parenting time (no denial, no presumption of abuse, neglect, or dependency for permitted conduct, absent clear-and-convincing evidence of unreasonable danger to the child); §218B.045(3) treats authorised medical use as equivalent to other practitioner-directed medication for medical care including organ transplants, and allows health facilities to develop policies permitting on-premises use; §218B.045(4) protects school enrolment (see §12.10). (Source) None of these provisions mentions housing, tenancy, eviction, or rent — a housing-protection claim under Chapter 218B is therefore [UNAVAILABLE] on the sources opened. (Source)

General tenancy overlay (not cannabis-specific, flagged not surveyed). Kentucky's general landlord-tenant law (KRS Chapter 383, including the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act as adopted in certain jurisdictions) and any federal housing rules (for example federally assisted housing, where federal controlled-substance status matters) were not surveyed in this audit and may independently restrict or permit action against a tenant for cannabis use, particularly smoking. (Source) Federal assisted-housing consequences are [VERIFY] before advising a tenant in public or federally assisted housing — do not advise that a state card protects a federal tenancy, and do not treat the given Schedule III status of state-licensed medical marijuana as answering that question. (Source)

Growing in rented property. Home grow is prohibited for all, so a tenant has no lawful home-grow right to assert against a landlord in any event; a landlord's ban on growing is therefore consistent with state law, not in tension with it. (Source) The Office of Medical Cannabis General Questions state: "Can I grow my own medical cannabis? No. Kentucky law prohibits individuals from growing their own medical cannabis." (Source)

Hemp in rented property. No hemp-specific landlord or tenant rule was located [UNAVAILABLE]; the general property-control principle in KRS 218B.040(1)(e) is a medical-cannabis provision and does not by its terms govern hemp or CBD possession in a rental. (Source)

12.8 Gun ownership conflicts for patients

Kentucky state law: no state firearms disqualification for cardholders found. No KRS Chapter 218B provision disqualifies a registered or visiting patient from owning or possessing firearms under Kentucky law, and the medical programme and firearms licensing systems are not linked in the sources opened (secondary dispensary guidance: "Kentucky law does not prohibit medical cannabis cardholders from possessing or owning firearms… applying for a medical card does not require you to forfeit any firearm or permit" — secondary, marked as such). (Source) No Kentucky statute was located creating a state safe harbour for a cardholder's federal firearms purchase either. (Source)

Federal law: the conflict is live. Under 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3), it is unlawful for a person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" to ship, transport, possess, or receive firearms or ammunition in or affecting commerce; ATF Form 4473 asks whether the purchaser is an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana or other controlled substances; ATF's 2011 open letter told federal firearms licensees that possession of a state marijuana authorisation card is reasonable cause to believe the person is an unlawful user (secondary summaries). (Source) In late 2024, ATF officials warned Kentucky residents that participating in the then-imminent medical programme would prohibit them from buying or possessing firearms under federal law, while noting existing owners were not "expected to" turn firearms over but must "make the decision to divest themselves" to follow federal law (secondary reporting of the 2024 warning and a bipartisan Kentucky resolution urging Congress to amend federal law — no action taken on that bill as reported). (Source)

Schedule III effect — unresolved, no safe harbour. Under the given federal baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III on 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714), while all other marijuana remains Schedule I. (Source) Whether that move, by itself, removes a Kentucky medical patient from §922(g)(3)'s "unlawful user" category, or whether ATF has issued a Kentucky-specific or general safe harbour for Schedule III medical users, was not resolved from a primary ATF or Federal Register source in this audit. (Source) ATF's interim final rule effective 22 January 2026 rewrote 27 CFR 478.11 to require regular use continuing into the present: a person is not an "unlawful user" if the person has ceased regularly unlawfully using the substance, or if the person's use is isolated or sporadic, with no bright-line abstinence period stated. (Source) That rule does not by itself create a safe harbour for a currently, regularly using Kentucky medical patient, and secondary sources in this audit still describe the federal prohibition as applying to medical users. (Source) Practical position to carry forward: a Kentucky patient faces a state-lawful and federally-prohibited conflict on purchase and possession; card expiry plus cessation of use is the only route described in secondary sources for falling outside §922(g)(3), with no defined waiting period. (Source)

Supreme Court — Hemani (narrow, not a safe harbour). Under the given federal baseline, United States v. Hemani, No. 24-1234, was decided 18 June 2026 (Gorsuch): a status-only 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, is inconsistent with the Second Amendment (as-applied, narrow). (Source) Hemani does not hold that all Kentucky medical patients may purchase or possess firearms, does not address purchase from a dealer or possession outside the home, and does not resolve the Schedule III question — do not advise any patient to purchase or retain a firearm on the basis of Hemani. (Source) The outcome of United States v. Baxter, cited in secondary sources, was not located in this audit [VERIFY on court dockets before advising any patient]. (Source)

Caregivers. A designated caregiver who does not personally use cannabis is not an "unlawful user" on the statute's terms (secondary analysis), but may still face point-of-sale denial if a dealer treats card possession as reasonable cause — a practical obstacle, not a legal disqualification on the sources opened [VERIFY]. (Source)

Enhanced penalties note (not a gun-ownership rule). KRS 218A.992 enhances certain drug offences where the offender possessed a firearm at the time (court example: possession plus paraphernalia, each Class A misdemeanours, enhanced to Class D felonies by a firearm-possession finding) — a patient whose conduct falls outside Chapter 218B protection (for example smoking, over-limit possession, diversion) therefore faces a compounded exposure that a compliant patient does not. (Source) Official pinpoint [VERIFY] for §218A.992. (Source)

12.9 Pet and veterinary products

No Kentucky veterinary cannabis or pet-CBD statute or regulation was located. There is no Kentucky law in the sources opened that (a) authorises veterinarians to prescribe or recommend cannabis for animals, (b) creates a pet-CBD product category with its own THC limit, labelling, or registration, or (c) bans pet CBD. (Source) Medical cannabis under KRS Chapter 218B is for human registered and visiting patients only; giving a patient's medicinal cannabis to an animal would be diversion outside Chapter 218B protection. (Source)

Kentucky Board of Veterinary Examiners (KBVE) position (official board page). KBVE "cautions that selling, prescribing, or advising on the use of cannabidiol (CBD) in animals is at your own risk in the event a patient has an adverse reaction." (Source) Background stated by KBVE: the 2018 Farm Bill descheduled hemp and assigned crop regulation to USDA-approved state plans; regulation of CBD, hemp extracts, and derivatives "remains with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act"; until FDA issues a clear written statement or federal law defines extract products as supplement versus drug, "Kentucky will continue to view CBD as a supplement and treat it accordingly" (citing KRS 218A.010(23)–(24), KRS 260.850, KRS 260.852). (Source) "There is no prohibition in Kentucky for carrying this product in a store or clinic as a product with an off-label use." (Source) Hemp-grain and extract regulation in animal feed remains with AAFCO and the University of Kentucky Division of Regulatory Services Feed Program; the UK DRS Feed Program policy statement (26 September 2023): "Current Policy on Use of Hemp Products in Animal Feed" — contact the UK DRS Feed Program directly for detail (the policy text itself was not opened here [VERIFY]). (Source)

Product legality baseline for pet products. "In Kentucky, CBD products are legal when derived from industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L. with a THC concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis)" (KBVE, same page). (Source) That is the hemp definition, not a pet-product approval: a pet product exceeding 0.3% delta-9 THC dry weight is not hemp, and an intoxicating HDCP sold for animal use would still be an adult-use (21+) human product under 902 KAR 45:190 on the framework found — no animal-use HDCP rule was located [UNAVAILABLE]. (Source) Human CBD products should not be assumed safe for dogs or cats (secondary veterinary-safety guidance, Bluegrass Hemp Oil and Kentucky Cannabis Company, October 2025): discuss with a licensed veterinarian, bring label, batch COA, ingredients, and medication history; THC exposure can be dangerous for dogs and cats and may require urgent care. (Source) These are safety recommendations, not Kentucky law, and are marked as such. (Source)

Federal hemp-date note for pet products. PL 119-37 takes effect 12 November 2026, but until 11 December 2026 PL 119-103 limits it to the non-naturally-produced and synthesized-cannabinoid exclusions; only after 11 December 2026 do the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply — so a pet CBD product that is hemp under the pre-11 December 2026 definition but contains more than 0.4 mg total THC per container would fall outside the post-11 December 2026 federal hemp definition. (Source) No Kentucky pet-specific response to that date was located [VERIFY]. (Source)

12.10 Medical cannabis in schools

Enrolment protection (KRS 218B.045(4)(a)–(b), effective 1 January 2025). A school shall not refuse to enroll, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for his or her status as a cardholder, unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations and cause the school to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations, or would violate the school's sincerely held religious beliefs, if the school is a private, religious institution. (Source) A school shall not be penalized or denied any benefit under state law for enrolling a cardholder. (Source)

On-property use — the rule is district policy. Under KRS 218B.045(4)(c) as amended by HB 829 (2024 Ky. Acts ch. 195, effective 1 January 2025): each local board of education, each board of directors of a public charter school, and the governing body of each certified nonpublic school shall, no later than 1 December 2024, establish policies related to the use of medicinal cannabis by a pupil who is a registered qualified patient on school property. (Source) Policies enacted under this paragraph shall either prohibit the use of medicinal cannabis on school property or permit the use of medicinal cannabis on school property by a pupil who is a registered qualified patient as deemed necessary by the pupil's parent or legal guardian. (Source) If a board or governing body enacts a policy to permit use, that policy shall: (1) require medicinal cannabis to be administered (a)(i) by a school nurse or under the supervision of appropriate school staff, or (ii) by the parent or legal guardian of the pupil, and (b) out of view of other students; and (2) include a process by which a school nurse or other school staff member may refuse to administer or supervise the administration of medicinal cannabis. (Source) The operative rule today is therefore not "all schools must permit" — it is "each board or governing body must have a policy, and that policy may prohibit or permit (with nurse, staff, or parent administration, out of view, and a staff refusal process)." (Source) The July 2024 "permit" deadline in the original SB 47 summary and the December 2024 "permit or prohibit" deadline in the KSBA material describe different enactments (SB 47 as passed versus HB 829 as amending) — the HB 829 and current KRS 218B.045 text governs. (Source) The KSBA model policy (09.2242, 2024) frames the same choice, effective 1 January 2025: the policy shall either prohibit use on school property or permit use by a registered-patient pupil as deemed necessary by the parent or legal guardian, with administration by a school nurse or under appropriate staff supervision, or by the parent or legal guardian, out of view of other students, and a written-acknowledgement refusal process (09.2242 AP.2) — note that "written acknowledgement" is KSBA form language; the statute itself requires "a process by which" staff may refuse. (Source) No statewide list of which districts permit versus prohibit was located [UNAVAILABLE — check the individual district's 09.2242 policy]. (Source)

Possession and use default (OMC). Cardholders may not possess or use on school property unless the school's policies allow registered qualified patients to use at school, administered by a school nurse or appropriate staff (Office of Medical Cannabis General Questions — §12.5). (Source) KRS 218B.035(1)(e)(1) likewise prohibits possessing medicinal cannabis, or otherwise engaging in its use, on the grounds of any preschool or primary or secondary school, except as permitted in accordance with policies enacted pursuant to KRS 218B.045(4). (Source) School buses, preschool, primary, and secondary grounds, correctional facilities, and federal property appear in pre-SB 47 bill summaries as prohibited places; the SB 47 and HB 829 school-policy regime above is the current framework found — do not cite a 2019 bill summary as current law. (Source)

Under-18 patients generally. A registered qualified patient under 18 shall not be permitted to possess, purchase, or acquire medicinal cannabis and shall only engage in the use of medicinal cannabis with the assistance of a designated caregiver who is the registered qualified patient's parent or legal guardian responsible for providing consent for medical treatment (KRS 218B.025(2)). (Source) Persons under 18 may not enter or remain on cannabis-business premises (KRS 218B.095(2)(c)). (Source)

Hemp-derived products in schools. No school-specific HDCP rule (for example CBD in schools) was located [UNAVAILABLE]; the general school tobacco and drug policies of the district and the 21+ adult-use HDCP rule (§12.2) are the only adjacent rules found — an adult-use HDCP may not lawfully be sold to a school pupil in any event. (Source)
